query_dims.consensus_text: The room is split with no clear consensus; two abstain days have passed with no lynch, and the discussion centers on the claimed sentinel's single visit claim rather than any agreed target.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong vote is recoverable but costly, and the game cannot end within one more elimination, so keeping visibility low this day preserves room for later body use.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible move (a vote, a claim, a body-use hint) commits me to a stance that cannot be undone once read by the village; the day-3 vote is public and permanent, so voting with the majority keeps my visibility low.
query_dims.heat_now: Moderate and rising: I voted to eliminate a player on day 2 who then abstained, and one accuser has said my day-2 vote named no one substantive, so I am a visible but not focal target.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel claim with one visit, two day-2 votes with no stated evidence, and no confirmed results; the only hard datum is that a single visit reached a dead trailseer on night 1.
query_dims.my_position: With the majority on the abstain side in practice, holding out of the early accusations and not driving any lynch.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the necromancer I privately know my own role and that I am not visible to anyone's night checks, while the public sees only a day-3 accusation thread between a claimed sentinel and the player who accused them; my private knowledge is that I am the lone killer and no one on the table can verify that.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 after two abstain days: a claimed sentinel named a single visitor to a dead trailseer on night 1, and the accused player is demanding the sentinel explain it, while the village debates whether to vote on either. I have two dead bodies (a trailseer and a vigilante) whose night abilities I could later use, which the village does not know about.
query_dims.target_landscape: Two accusers and one claimed sentinel are in play: a claimed sentinel (unverified) whose single watch result names one visitor, a player being voted on for a day-2 push with no new evidence, and a player accused by two others with only a stated night-1 reason; all bases are claims and day-2 votes, not confirmed roles.

lessons.why: A claimed watcher's report against an accused player who disputes it is exactly the live dispute (player_4's sentinel claim vs player_5), and the advice (test the report against the visit rules, then vote with the side the rules support) is usable now.
lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

lessons.why: Needs an endgame with 3-4 alive and the seat personally cornered; eight are alive and the seat is not accused.
lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.why: Needs the seat's claimed result to have been exposed as impossible; the seat has made no claim.
lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

query_dims.consensus_text: No current village alignment is visible: today's discussion has not started, and the previous summary records no accusations.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive; five eliminations from the leading evil faction's win threshold, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so a single result is not yet a swing.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible claim about the concealed player's role or the hidden kill trace would commit you to information the village cannot verify during play and could expose your private knowledge. No such public claim or other visible move is currently on record.
query_dims.heat_now: No suspicion of you is recorded in today's discussion, which has not begun; the public record contains no accusation against you.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved publicly: the attacks and concealment are confirmed, but the victim's role and will are unavailable to the village. You alone know the victim was the Vigilante; there are no discussion claims or accusations yet today.
query_dims.my_position: No position relative to a forming village consensus is established; there is no current discussion or consensus to align with or oppose.
query_dims.public_private_text: The public knows that the player killed by both the wolves and the serial killer had their role concealed. Privately, you know they were the Vigilante and that you concealed the body; the village has no public role or will from them.
query_dims.situation: The opening night removed one player through both a wolf attack and a serial-killer attack, while your concealment withheld that player's role and will. This leaves the village without the dead player's role information as day two begins, while you privately know the concealed player was the Vigilante.
query_dims.target_landscape: No candidates are currently being debated; there are no public role reveals or claims to compare. The only confirmed event is that the concealed player was attacked by both the wolves and the serial killer and died.

lessons.why: Needs a revealed dead wolf partner and a public record tying the seat to it; nothing of the kind exists on day 2 opening.
lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.why: Early day, wolf holding private pack knowledge, speak low-content versus pass is the real choice; but no claimants are comparing logs yet and the pack's kill did not hit an immune target.
lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.

lessons.why: Needs a dead wolf partner and a Town result to use as a defence; neither exists.
lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been revealed and killed. You are pressured over a lone vote against a dead Town player, while a Town player's result (a non-triggering sigil) is available as a defense. Information landscape: Moderate: public voting records and a privately held Town result that can be used to clear you, but no hard role confirmations on the quiet alternative suspect. Stakes: Each vote now decides whether the last wolf survives. Moving even a couple of swing voters off you keeps the wolf team alive into the final few players. Consensus: The village is split. Some players press you over the vote record, while players holding a clearing result and neutral voters are open to another suspect. My position: holding out Heat: High. Players cite your isolated vote against a now-dead player as the basis for suspicion. Forward exposure: Citing a Town player's result ties you to a non-attacking story that you cannot take back, and later tracking evidence could break it. The alternative-suspect push can be adjusted as new information arrives. Target landscape: Candidates are you, under pressure from the vote record, and a quiet player with no confirmed role who was targeted by the dead wolf. Suspicion of the quiet player is behavioral, while the case against you is the vote record. Public vs private: Privately you are an active wolf, but the partner carried the kill that night, so a Town result such as an un-triggered sigil looks exculpatory. The room reads that result as evidence you are not the killer.
lessons.action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Use only what the rules show: the sigil not triggering means only that you did not attack on that night, and it does not clear you of being a wolf. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.

lessons.situation: Late game with four players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A confirmed town player or a will points at your past votes or kills, and you must redirect the final lynch toward the lone killer or unconfirmed player. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed roles, dead players' wills, announced attack types and public vote history sharply limit which roles could be evil. Stakes: At four alive, a single lynch decides the game. If you are voted out, the wolves lose. If another player is lynched, the wolves get closer to parity. Consensus: The remaining players are largely aligned against the illusionist. They rely on the confirmed roles, dead players' wills and the voting record rather than on speculation. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High to severe. Dead players' wills and prior votes against you, plus cleared players' pointed remarks, make you the favorite target. Forward exposure: Your last speeches before the day-four vote are irreversible. If you don't move the table onto another player, you are the default lynch. A weak or unsupported push gets rejected by cleared players and hardens consensus against you. Target landscape: Two or three players remain. One or two are confirmed or cleared town (such as the sigilist or vigilante), and one unconfirmed player is a lone killer or neutral. The choice is between you and that unconfirmed player, and the evidence is public facts and vote records. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving wolf and who really made the recent kills. Publicly the town has confirmed or cleared players and a vote record, so you must look like an innocent townsperson.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf at four alive and the table is converging on you, spend your speech on a counter-case against the one unresolved player. Build it only from announced facts (the morning's attack-kind report, confirmed roles, public vote records) and say which of the two remaining suspects those facts fit. Don't just acknowledge the vote record against you, and don't attack a player with a flimsy argument. Each failed attempt left you as the consensus target.

lessons.situation: A trailseer claims to have seen the illusionist visit a player who died that night with a hidden role, and the illusionist has to answer in daytime discussion. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed death with a hidden role plus a direct tracking report that matches what the illusionist actually did. Stakes: An elimination of the illusionist here leaves the surviving wolf alone and closer to losing, so avoid a flat denial that the room can disprove. Consensus: The majority takes the tracker's findings at face value; only a couple of players are confused about how concealment affects visits. My position: opposing the forming consensus Heat: Critical; directly accused of visiting a murder victim on the night they died. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits you to calling the trailseer a liar and rules out any later switch to a benign visiting claim. A benign-visit explanation stays open and can be adjusted if the town pushes back. Target landscape: The accused visitor (you) against the single claimed tracker; the town has no competing account of the night, so the report counts as hard eyewitness evidence. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the reported visit is true, because it concealed the body, while publicly it insists it never left home.
lessons.action: When a trailseer or sentinel report places you at the door of a victim whose role was hidden, do not flatly deny the visit. Offer a benign reason for being out that night (for example, a claim of a visiting town role, or that you checked on that player), and stress that the report only shows a visit, not who attacked. Do not claim that illusionist concealment makes the report invalid: if you were not the carrier, your own visit to hide the body is still seen, and a flat denial against a tracker report the town trusts loses you the room.

lessons.situation: Day two with several town investigative and protective claims surfacing, a night death that flipped information, and the room absorbed in checking one claimant. The illusionist wolf knows about an unannounced immune target. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, with three town role claims and a dead trailseer's visit reported, but nothing confirms wolf alignment. Stakes: Mid-early game; the pack still has room, but one revealed slip about the immune target would expose a wolf and tilt the count toward town. Consensus: The town is coalescing around abstaining and picking apart one claimant's lack of results, based on claimed night results. My position: Staying out of the main debate and moving with the room, ready to join it. Heat: Low. Reported town information frames me as an innocent subject of night information, and attention sits elsewhere. Forward exposure: Accusing the immune player would require explaining how I know about an unannounced failed kill, instantly revealing wolf knowledge and being irreversible. A mild on-topic comment commits me to little and can be revised later. Target landscape: The room is scrutinizing a newly claimed role with thin results and accepting a cleared target. The immune player is publicly unverified and not under pressure. Public vs private: Privately the pack knows a quiet player survived our unannounced night attack and is night-immune, while the town sees only an unverified player talking mechanics.
lessons.action: When the room is focused on another debate, such as verifying a claimed role, and your night-immune or already-known target sits among the discussants, join the discussion on its stated topic only. Voice a mild opinion on the claim under scrutiny or on the emerging abstain, and don't accuse or defend the immune player, since explaining how you know would expose wolf knowledge. Staying aligned with the room's current direction keeps heat low while you preserve your concealed information.

lessons.situation: A claimed watcher reports a visitor at the dead wolf partner's door, and the accused denies it while the village weighs the two stories. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed dead wolf, a watcher's claim about its visitors, and a supporting investigator result. Stakes: Removing the lone killer is necessary before wolves can win and costs the pack nothing, while staying unscrutinized keeps the illusionist alive for the endgame. Consensus: Town converges on the accused and the vote is nearly unanimous. My position: with majority Heat: None: no one has linked the illusionist to the kill or questioned its behavior. Forward exposure: Backing the watcher commits the illusionist to treating that claimant as credible later, though that is easy to revisit if the watcher is contradicted. Target landscape: The accused visitor, who claims town and denies the visit, versus the claimed watcher whose report is plausible given the dead wolf. The basis is a watch result, not behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows its partner was killed by an outside night killer, so the accused visitor is probably that killer, and the public read matches this.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is already dead and a claimed sentinel or other watcher accuses an outside killer, back the watcher's report and press the accused to explain their visit. This helps the town remove the lone killer without any suspicion falling on you. Keep your wording the same as the rest of the village's.

lessons.situation: A claimed watcher or tracker reports visits to a player who survived or died, and I (a wolf-side illusionist) am among the visitors named or about to be exposed. Information landscape: Information-rich: visit reports, an attack that was thwarted or a body, and several role claims on the table, though none verified. Stakes: Mid-game with a wolf exposed by a visit report; a single failed explanation risks a vote on me, while a convincing cover keeps the wolf pack on course toward parity. Consensus: The room is information-rich and willing to act on visit reports, but has not settled on who is lying; it accepts any claim that plausibly explains the visits. My position: Driving; I set the narrative right after the report by claiming first and redirecting focus. Heat: High; named as a visitor at a sensitive door by a claimed night-information role on the exact night of the event. Forward exposure: A fake role claim locks me in publicly and guarantees a collision if the genuine role-holder is alive; it is hard to retract, but it buys immediate safety and can set up removing the real role-holder. Target landscape: The unverified observer who reported visits, the genuine role-holder whose action matches my claim, and the surviving target; the observer's claim is unverified while my cover story is plausible. Public vs private: Privately I know the visit was a wolf action (kill attempt or ability use), but publicly the visit must be framed as a Town role's action to explain being seen.
lessons.action: When an unverified watcher or follower reports your visit at a victim's or target's door and you are exposed, immediately claim a Town role whose action explains that visit (e.g. Healer protecting the target), and tie it to the night's outcome. If the claim fits the report and the room accepts it, steer the town toward the player who raised the report, and plan the later collision with the real role-holder.

lessons.situation: A claiming tracker names me as a visitor to the night-one victim while a separate dual-claim conflict dominates the room. Information landscape: Information-rich: two investigative claims with direct visit reports on both night deaths, plus a hard counterclaim. Stakes: A named wolf-side visitor who survives today by deflection but leaves the accusation unresolved; it can return at the next vote and cost a wolf while the pack still needs several eliminations. Consensus: The room is split and distracted by a bigger role-claim dispute, so it can be redirected but has not cleared me. My position: With majority; I am following the room's focus on the other conflict while deflecting from my own accusation. Heat: High; named by a claimed tracker as a visitor to the night victim, though partly diluted by another player caught at a different body. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits me to calling the reporter a liar without any role alibi; it is reversible only by building a story later, and if the reporter survives or is validated it brings me down. Target landscape: The claiming tracker who named me, a rival dispute (conflicting claims of the same role) in the room, and myself; the reports are unverified but the tracker's claim is accurate. Public vs private: Privately I know the report is accurate because I carried out the kill, while publicly the room is split over a different dispute and can be pointed away from me.
lessons.action: When a claimed tracker or watcher reports you at a victim's door, do not rely on a bare denial: pair it with a coherent counter-story, such as a plausible role claim with a believable alibi. Use any competing role conflict in the room to draw attention off yourself, but keep the counter-story ready so the report cannot resurface later.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator reports a suspicious result on the illusionist, or counter-claims against a real investigator, and the village treats it as a binary choice that favors the accuser. Information landscape: Information-rich: a specific investigative report, town deductions that verify it, and sometimes an announced save, leaving little room for an unsupported denial. Stakes: Losing the illusionist halves the wolf pack and leaves the partner alone against a village that has already shown it can work out the mechanics, so the day's speech should protect the partner's standing first. Consensus: Near-unanimous and fast: town members are checking the mechanics themselves and agree that only a wolf fits the result. My position: holding out against a consensus that is already forming Heat: Critical; a claimed investigator directly named you and the town has independently confirmed the logic against you. Forward exposure: Calling a mechanically checkable result fabricated, or counter-claiming a unique investigative role, commits you to a 1-for-1 credibility duel that cannot be undone. Naming an alternative target keeps a fallback and keeps your partner out of the fight. Target landscape: The accuser is a lone claimed information role with no rival claimant. The only other candidates are quiet or unclaimed players, and the accuser's report is hard evidence while your counter is behavioral. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the accusing investigator's check is accurate, while publicly the only option offered is to call it false, which the room can test against the rules.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator names you suspicious and the room can verify that only a wolf could read that way, skip the "fabricated check" argument and the counter-claim. Instead pair a brief, calm denial with a concrete alternative suspect (an unexplained claimant, a quiet player, a vote pattern), and say nothing that ties or defends your partner. If the room is still locked on you, spend your remaining speech turns pulling suspicion off your partner and onto that alternative rather than winning the duel.

lessons.situation: A sentinel or trailseer publicly lists the illusionist among several visitors to one player, creating a risk of an investigation trap. Information landscape: Fairly rich in visit data from several claimed watchers, but nothing is verified by deaths and the data converges on an odd target. Stakes: A single named-visitor result could expose the pack on day 2; defusing it keeps both wolves alive and the vote at abstain. Consensus: The village treats the multi-visit pile-up as a puzzle and has no single suspect, so it leans toward abstaining. My position: with majority Heat: Moderate: explicitly named by a sentinel as a visitor, diluted by other claimants reporting the same visits. Forward exposure: Admitting a visit commits the illusionist to being a visiting role in later claims, and it is only partly reversible. Avoiding a specific role claim keeps flexibility. Target landscape: The quiet visited player and the other visitors defending their own overlapping actions. All are unverified claimants, and the evidence is visit lists rather than behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the visit was the wolf kill or another wolf action, whereas the town sees an inexplicable convergence of visits on one quiet player.
lessons.action: When a claimed watch or tracking result names your partner or you as a visitor, acknowledge only the visit that cannot be disproved. Frame it as a casual check-in and point the room at the strangest part of the data, such as several players visiting the same target. This keeps your claim consistent with the visits other players can report while avoiding a specific role claim.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear village consensus; the room is split between a vote on player_5 and calls to test the sentinel claim further, with the accusers relying on the watch record and the accused relying on the block report contradiction.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong lynch is recoverable but costly, since it would bring the evil side closer to parity and the wolves and necromancer remain unidentified.
query_dims.heat_now: Moderate on me as the Speculator: I have not been heavily accused, but I am a living voter whose pick is already announced as Town, so my vote is watched for alignment with the Town pick.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel watch, one roleblock report with no source, and one admitted visit; no confirmed role claims survive and no night results have been announced beyond the dead players' roles.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out from the forming pressure on player_5, with a low profile and no night result of my own.
query_dims.situation: A claimed Sentinel's night-3 watch shows only player_5 at player_1's door, while player_1 says they were roleblocked that night, so the block is unexplained; player_5 admits the visit, denies being blocked, and claims no role. Several players are pressing a vote on player_5 while the accusation rests on one watch record against one block report.
query_dims.target_landscape: Player_5 (unrevealed, living) who admits a night-3 visit to player_1 with no role claimed; player_1 (unrevealed, living) who reports being roleblocked that night; player_2 (claimed Sentinel, unverified, living) whose night-3 watch shows only player_5 at player_1's door. Public role status: no one confirmed beyond the dead.

lessons.why: Needs four alive with one wolf left; six are alive with two evil factions.
lessons.situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.
lessons.action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.

lessons.why: Speculator already picked Town, split day vote at about six alive with both wolves and a lone killer alive: same decision and dynamic, advice (vote the unconfirmed player whose claims conflict, not a claimed Town power role) is usable.
lessons.situation: The speculator has already picked a side (Town) and sits in a split or deadlocked day vote where its single vote can decide a tie or prevent a bad elimination of a claimed Town role. Both wolves and a lone killer may still be alive. Information landscape: Moderate and muddled: night kills, a hidden role, conflicting role claims and night-result claims, but no confirmed wolf or killer. Mostly unverified claims plus voting records. Stakes: With about six players alive and two killing factions active, one vote can decide an elimination or block a Town loss. A mistaken Town elimination moves evil toward parity and weakens the Town side the speculator picked. Consensus: The village is scattered or split into near-equal camps with no single dominant target; the push is based on muddled claims and behavioral reads. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none; nobody has directed accusations at the speculator, and its speech has been neutral. Target landscape: Several candidates split the room: claimed Town power roles (healer, trailseer, sigilist, vigilante) versus an unconfirmed quiet or counter-accusing player. The evidence is partly claims and conflicting timelines, partly behavior and past votes, with no confirmed wolf.
lessons.action: When you have already picked Town and the day vote is split among several candidates, cast your vote sincerely on the unconfirmed player whose behavior or claims look most evil. Prefer the candidate whose claims conflict with other players' reports over a claimed Town power role. Your vote can swing a split or tie, so use it to stop a Town-aligned elimination and to remove the likeliest killer, which keeps Town the winning side you picked.

lessons.why: Needs four alive and evil one step from parity; not the case at six.
lessons.situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.
lessons.action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.

lessons.situation: Final-wolf vote at four alive: the village must eliminate the last wolf now or face parity at night, and the Speculator is one of the two unverified players. Information landscape: Information-rich: the dead Investigator's will clears one player, the Sigilist's abilities are logged and spent, and the lone killer is confirmed dead. Stakes: Eliminating the last wolf wins immediately for Town and for a Town pick, while a miss leaves three alive with parity at night. Consensus: Two confirmed Town players treat the vote as a choice between the two unverified players and are open to a clear case. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the cleared players. Heat: Exposed: the remaining suspect openly pushes to eliminate the agent based on a quiet record, and the confirmed Town players see it as a binary choice. Target landscape: Two unverified players, the Speculator and one suspect who survived earlier scrutiny, among four alive. The other two are cleared or confirmed Town, by a dead Investigator's will and spent, logged abilities. The suspect's push on the Speculator is behavioral, while the confirmed Town players are the deciding votes.
lessons.action: When four are alive, one wolf remains, and the Speculator has picked Town, join the cleared Town players in eliminating the one unverified suspect rather than the other. Ignore the suspect's counter-accusation of you when it rests only on a quiet record, because eliminating the last wolf ends the game with a Town win and your pick wins.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room shows limited agreement that the visit accounts are consistent but do not prove roles or alignments. At least two speakers favor restraint, and there is no clear consensus on a vote target.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive, and the leading evil faction is at least five eliminations from winning; five is the closest possible distance for town because the concealed player's side is unknown. A single elimination cannot end the game or flip which faction is winning, though its result can affect later decisions.
query_dims.forward_exposure: You are publicly unclaimed and have made no statement about the night. Staying quiet commits you to no account and is reversible; a visible push or role claim would create a public position that could be compared against the unverified night claims and the concealed kill.
query_dims.heat_now: No one has accused or questioned you in the public discussion; suspicion on you is low, with no stated basis.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information is limited and mostly claim-based. The visit accounts corroborate who went where, not anyone’s role or alignment; the Investigator result has no public confirmation. The only system-confirmed night facts are that the concealed player was attacked by both wolves and the serial killer and died; their role remains unknown publicly.
query_dims.my_position: You have made no public statement and have not taken a visible position in the discussion; you are not driving or publicly opposing the restraint expressed by others.
query_dims.public_private_text: The public knows a player was killed by both the wolves and the serial killer, but the role was concealed. Privately, you know the pack killed that player and that your block on another player did not affect them; neither fact is public. Your living wolf partner has not been revealed.
query_dims.situation: On day 2, three unverified information-role claims produce a mutually consistent visit trail: a claimed Sentinel says a claimed Trailseer came to their watched target, and the Trailseer says that target visited no one. The trail corroborates routes but supplies no alignment evidence, while a separate claimed Investigator’s Not-suspicious result is also unverified. The village is weighing this sparse, non-conclusive information without a clear target.
query_dims.target_landscape: No one is under a clear public push. A player claiming Investigator says another player was Not suspicious; this is an unverified claim and does not clear them of being the serial killer. A player claiming Sentinel says the player followed by a claimed Trailseer visited the watched target; the Trailseer’s account corroborates that route, but neither claim establishes alignment. No candidate has system-confirmed role evidence.

lessons.why: Needs the wolf partner already exposed and killed; the partner is alive.
lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.why: Needs the partner eliminated and a stumbling claimant to pile onto; neither holds.
lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.why: Needs a three-player final day; nine are alive.
lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator has outed your wolf partner with a suspicious check, or a true investigator is dueling the partner's counterclaim. The room is forming an elimination consensus while you are unsuspected. Information landscape: Moderately to highly informative. There are role claims, a check report, and possibly sentinel or healer-save evidence that backs the investigator, so the town has concrete leads. Stakes: The partner is likely lost, so the wolf side's survival now depends on you staying unsuspected. Staying uncorrelated with the partner is worth more than a failed rescue that could expose you next. Consensus: The village is converging quickly on eliminating the accused partner. Its basis is the investigator's report and supporting mechanical logic from other town roles, and the room is largely ignoring pleas to slow down. My position: holding out Heat: Low to none. You are not named, but speaking up for the accused partner would put you in the spotlight. Forward exposure: Any defense of the partner is permanent on the record and becomes an associative link once the partner flips wolf, and it cannot be undone. Silence or neutral talk commits you to nothing and leaves later options open. Target landscape: The candidates are the accused wolf partner and the claimed investigator, possibly with a counterclaimer. The room is deciding on the strength of check reports and mechanical deductions, such as a healer save or ruling out other roles, rather than on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you know the accused partner is a wolf and the accusing investigator is accurate or at least credible. Publicly the room is still debating the check, and you have no suspicion on you.
lessons.action: When a credible investigator accusation or counterclaim is pulling the room against your wolf partner, stay out of the partner's defense: do not urge caution, vouch for them, or advocate for them. Keep your day talk short and about other players, or stay silent, so nothing visibly ties you to the partner and the room's attention stays on the duel. If you must speak, give only neutral points that would still stand if the partner flipped wolf.

lessons.situation: The endgame has 3-4 players left, you are the last wolf, and an unconfirmed player is pushing a case built on your voting record. A claimed Town role's result could clear the swing player and make them an ally. Information landscape: Information-rich: full public voting records, a claimed trailseer result, and a dead player's final vote are all available. These details can be used to rebut the accuser. Stakes: One vote or one night kill decides the game: winning this vote brings the wolves to parity at the next kill, while losing it eliminates the last wolf. Consensus: The room is split with no majority. Everyone is working from public vote history and one or two claimed results, and one swing player is deciding whom to believe. My position: Driving a counter-narrative to form a defensive voting coalition with the swing player. Heat: High: the accuser has laid out your voting record and tied you to a dead wolf on a key mis-elimination. Forward exposure: Answering the accuser head-on commits you to a specific story about your old vote and to a coalition with one other player. If the swing player sides with the accuser, you are voted out right away and cannot undo it. If the swing player sides with you, you can win the vote or at least split the room. Target landscape: A field of three or four: the vocal accuser citing voting records, a claimed Town role whose claim has some support (such as a cleared visit report), and possibly another claimed role. The case against you rests on past votes, evidence rather than behavior; the case against the accuser rests on behavior and on the dead players' positions. Public vs private: Privately you are the last wolf who drove the earlier kills and mis-eliminations, while publicly you pose as an innocent Town player who made an honest deduction alongside the room.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf in a tiny endgame (3-4 alive) and are accused with hard evidence like voting records, answer the accusation directly. Reframe your past vote as a reasonable reaction to the situation, then cite a result or vote from a still-living or already-dead Town player that undercuts the accuser. Aim to win over the swing Town player; if they are not yet persuaded, shift your pitch to the accuser's inconsistencies and to the accuser as the likelier wolf.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a single wrong lynch is recoverable but narrows the margin for the remaining wolves and the Serial Killer.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible move by the agent (naming a player, claiming a result, or voting against a claimed info role) commits it publicly; a vote is permanent on the record and cannot be undone, while a verbal claim can be contradicted later by another claimant.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only public hard facts are the dead players' records (Sentinel watched one player and saw no one; Healer protected two players with no attack announced). All living role claims are unverified claims.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 after a healer was lynched; the village is split between a Trailseer claim whose night-1 visit to the dead Sentinel's watch target is unverified and a shot claim that openly challenges it, and two accusers are voting against each other. The agent, a Serial Killer with no public result, must avoid drawing attention while the room coordinates votes against the most accusing players.
query_dims.target_landscape: Five living candidates other than the agent: a claimed Trailseer whose chain was partly confirmed by the healer's will (player_3), a player holding an unverified shot claim (player_8), and three quieter players whose roles are unknown. Public role status: the Sentinel, Investigator, Fortune Teller, and Healer are dead and revealed; the Serial Killer is the agent itself. Basis is behavioral and claimed, with no announced confirmation of any living player's role.

lessons.why: Same decision (SK night target) and the 'don't repeat the obvious protected target' idea is generic, but it assumes a living healer and a just-saved leader; the Healer is dead here.
lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

lessons.why: Needs a claimed Investigator who cleared the seat and singled out a suspect; the Investigator is dead.
lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.why: Night-1 blind kill; the seat has day-3 information and four public deaths.
lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear consensus; the village has abstained on every vote so far and day discussion is about requesting concrete night 1 visit directions from anyone claiming a result, with no shared accusation forming.

query_dims.my_position: Holding out from any accusation, with no side pick yet; the village is not forming a consensus the agent needs to join or oppose.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 with the investigator killed on night 2 and no vote yet succeeding. Players are asking whoever claims a night result to give specific visit directions for night 1, while one player states a night 1 roleblock with nothing to share. The agent is an unpicked speculator who must avoid dying unpicked, so its survival and eventual pick depend on the board tilting toward a side.
query_dims.target_landscape: Nine living players, none publicly claimed or confirmed beyond the public abstain record; the only role-revealed death is the investigator (player_9), killed night 2. Candidates for any future vote are all unverified; no one has a public accusation on record except the day-2 vote where player_9 targeted player_8, who is now a claimant of a night 1 roleblock with no verifiable result.

lessons.action: When four are alive, one wolf remains, and the Speculator has picked Town, join the cleared Town players in eliminating the one unverified suspect rather than the other. Ignore the suspect's counter-accusation of you when it rests only on a quiet record, because eliminating the last wolf ends the game with a Town win and your pick wins.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.
lessons.action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: With 8 alive and 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, tonight's death does not make the game immediately endable by one more elimination. A correct death bet advances my separate point goal, while a self-bet trades that chance for protection; the faction balance is not on a one-action knife edge.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the Investigator and Trailseer were revealed dead, and the Sentinel claim and visitor result are unverified. There is no public attack pattern or confirmed role evidence pointing to tonight's victim; any victim or role prediction is uncertain.
query_dims.situation: After the village abstained on day 2, no one was eliminated and the vote record contains no decisive consensus. At night, the wolves and lone killer can each attack; the public Sentinel claimant may be exposed, but there is no confirmed target. I have 0 points and two self-bets remaining, so the decision is between predicting another player's death and using a self-bet that would make me immune to attacks but earn no points.
query_dims.target_landscape: The exposed player claiming Sentinel is a plausible night target because of the public claim, but that role is unverified. Other living players have no confirmed roles from the public record; there is no clear evidence identifying a likely victim or their role. Betting on myself would prevent an attack on me but score no points that night.

lessons.why: Needs three alive and a necromancer lone killer; eight are alive in a serial-killer game.
lessons.situation: Last wolf voted out and three players left. A lone killer (the necromancer, who can attack through a reanimated body) wins by killing one more player, so the Fortune Teller is a live kill target and no other player's death is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead, the dead roles are confirmed, and the remaining Town sigilist is confirmed out of sigils. This makes the only remaining attacker and its available bodies clear. Stakes: The lone killer wins if anyone else dies tonight, so a bet that fails to cover your own life can end the game with the Fortune Teller short of two points. A self-bet keeps you alive for another night. Target landscape: The suspected necromancer (alive and holding a usable body, so unlikely to die), a confirmed sigilist with no sigils left (no threat), or a self-bet. Roles are confirmed from the graveyard, and nothing makes the suspect likely to die tonight.
lessons.action: With three alive and a lone killer that can attack, you are one of only two possible victims. If no other victim is predictable, spend a self-bet, because an attack on you fails that night. Don't bet on the suspected killer: a killer that is immune or about to win is unlikely to die, and a wrong bet leaves you open to the attack.

lessons.why: Needs a late game with a publicly protected top target and a known surviving killer; neither exists on day 2 with eight alive.
lessons.situation: Late game with the wolves dead or nearly dead and one killer left (serial killer, necromancer or last wolf). The Fortune Teller stands at 0-1 points and needs a death, and the most obvious target is publicly protected, so a bet on them fails to the save or the killer switches targets. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of the dead wolves are confirmed, claims and protection histories are public, and the surviving killer's identity or kill pattern is mostly known. Stakes: Few players remain and the game can end any night. Each night spent without scoring risks being voted out or the game finishing before the second point, so the bet must follow where the killer can actually kill, not just where it wants to. Target landscape: The investigator or leader shielded by a public healer claim, the claimed healer who is exposed, other claimed power roles (sigilist, sentinel, trailseer), and unconfirmed players. Hard evidence of who is protected, not behavior, drives the choice.
lessons.action: When the healer has publicly announced protecting the obvious top target (the confirmed or claimed investigator), place the bet on the next-most-valuable unshielded Town role the surviving killer must remove, such as the claimed healer or another power role. If the killer's last pick is predictable, name that role in the bet for the two-point payoff.

lessons.why: Bet decision with no hard lead, and 'keep self-bets for later' is usable; but it is written for night 1 with no claims or deaths, and the seat has two deaths and a Sentinel claim.
lessons.situation: Night one after a discussion-only opening day. Several killers (wolves, and possibly a lone killer) will each attack someone, and no public mechanical constraint limits their choices. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigative findings, deaths, confirmed roles, or vote record exist. Stakes: Very low board pressure. A miss costs nothing but a night, and multiple attackers raise the chance that the chosen player dies. A hit on night one puts the win one successful bet away. Target landscape: All other living players, with no public claims, revealed alignments, or voting history to separate them. Any pick is close to a random draw among the candidates.
lessons.action: On a night with no evidence at all (no claims, no deaths, no votes), bet on any one quiet living player without naming a role, since the bet scores on any death by any cause. Keep both self-bets unspent for later nights when you may become a target.

lessons.situation: Three-player endgame tie between a confirmed Town power role, a suspected wolf and the Fortune Teller. The wolves need a kill to close the game, and the Fortune Teller needs points to win. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed by earlier night results and blocked actions, so the wolves' likely victim can be read from the board. Stakes: Each night is nearly decisive. A correct victim-and-role bet gives two points and wins the game for the Fortune Teller, while a miss wastes a night when the kill can end the game. Target landscape: A publicly confirmed Town role (e.g. a claimed vigilante whose shots were blocked), a suspected surviving wolf, or a self-bet. The Town player is the most likely kill target, backed by confirmed evidence from earlier nights and blocks rather than just behavior.
lessons.action: With three alive and a night kill that is predictable (a publicly confirmed Town role whose own actions are blocked or spent, with a wolf free to carry the kill), bet on that player to die and name their confirmed role. A correct victim plus role scores two points and can finish the win.

lessons.situation: After a day elimination or accusation, the remaining killer needs to silence the player who exposed it or holds a deadly tool against it. The Fortune Teller must choose between betting on the accused (who survives) and betting on the exposing claimant (who is attacked). Information landscape: Information-rich: a public claim or result (tracker report, sigil test, investigator checks) points at the killer's side, and several Town roles are out in the open. Stakes: Only one killing source is left, so exactly one death is likely each night and the bet must match it. A miss leaves the Fortune Teller stuck at one point while the game may end that same night. Target landscape: The claimed tracker, sigilist or investigator who exposed or tested the killer's side, versus the accused wolf or suspect, versus bystander claimed roles such as a roleblocked sentinel or unconfirmed healer. The basis is public claims and the day's vote record.
lessons.action: When one killer remains and a claimed power role has just driven the day's outcome (outed a wolf, tested the wolf, or led the vote), bet on that role as the killer's top threat, not on the accused or already-exposed suspect. A killer that is under suspicion usually survives the night, and the threat to it is the likelier victim.

lessons.situation: Early game (night 1 or 2), the Fortune Teller has no points yet and must pick a nightly death bet while wolves and a lone killer are all hunting. Day discussion produced a visible conflict or a prominent claimed power role. Information landscape: Mixed: some claims and night-one movement reports exist, but roles are unverified and votes were mostly abstentions, so the pick rests on behavioral reads. Stakes: No immediate parity pressure. The Fortune Teller needs two points in total, so each night's bet is a cheap, repeatable chance to score, and the self-bets guard against a later attack. Target landscape: Players who publicly claimed or acted as information roles, or who were just singled out by a night result or an open dispute, versus quiet players with no evidence either way. The choice rests on behavioral threat to the killers, not confirmed alignment.
lessons.action: With both self-bets still unspent and no points scored, bet on the player the killers most plausibly want dead tonight: an openly active, publicly claimed information role (such as a trailseer that just exposed someone) or a player the dead Trailseer's last follow pointed to. Name no role, since the death alone scores a point, and keep the self-bets for later nights.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is leaning toward eliminating you: three players have stated they would vote for you based on the visit, while another says the visit warrants scrutiny but is not conclusive. The shared basis is the claimed watch result, not independently verified evidence of your action.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five players remain; one elimination from parity at worst for the town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown. A single vote can flip which faction is winning, and the game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A further defense can reiterate that the claimed watch does not reveal your action, but the visit itself is already on the record and you have no role-based account to offer without inventing one. Redirecting suspicion would risk looking evasive. The imminent public vote is permanent; its outcome cannot be walked back.
query_dims.heat_now: High: three players have accused you and said they would vote for you, citing the claimed visit to the player killed by the Serial Killer. You acknowledged the visit but gave no role-based explanation.
query_dims.information_landscape: Limited and largely behavioral: the public record confirms the Serial Killer’s identity and a wolf attack saved by the Healer, while the visit evidence comes from an unverified Sentinel claim. A player was killed with their role concealed, so their side remains unknown. No public result establishes what your visit was for.
query_dims.my_position: You are the focus of the forming majority and are defending against it; you are not aligned with the likely vote.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Chanteuse, know your living packmate’s identity, and know your own blocks and the pack’s kills. Publicly, your role and packmate remain unrevealed. The claimed Sentinel’s account places you at the player who died to the Serial Killer; the claim does not identify your action, though you know the visit was your block.
query_dims.situation: With five players alive, the day-four vote centers on whether your unexplained visit to the player who died to the Serial Killer is enough to eliminate you. Three players favor your elimination, while the claimed Sentinel’s watch cannot distinguish a block from another action; the Serial Killer’s revealed role explains the other reported visitor but does not clear you.
