Target landscape: Players who voted against the true investigator or pushed an aggressive line versus the majority voters and a counter-claimant already confirmed as a liar; the basis is voting record and public behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: After a counter-claim or an elimination that exposes you, put your remaining check on a player whose daytime behavior links them to the exposed wolf, such as someone who voted against you or backed the counter-claimant, rather than on a player already confirmed or about to be removed. This produces a read that can be traced and carried forward even if you die.

query_dims.consensus_text: No consensus. Two abstain days with no lynch; the room is split into camps around the day 2 votes against player_4's accuser, player_10 and player_1, with no shared reading.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a wrong lynch is recoverable but each mistake brings the wolves nearer; the game cannot end on the next elimination.
query_dims.heat_now: Moderate and personal: player_8 voted me on day 2 and I have made no claim, so I am a low-information target rather than a focus of accusation.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel claim with a single visit fact, one denied visit, no confirmed deaths-to-role links beyond player_2 and player_6 (revealed by the Game Master), and no hard checks.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out: I am neither driving a lynch nor part of a majority, and I hold a private fortune teller role with no claim made.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 after two abstain days: a player claiming sentinel reported a night 1 watch on the dead trailseer showing only one visitor, and that visitor denies any role, while the accused sentinel refuses to name more; the village must decide whether to lynch on this single untested claim.
query_dims.target_landscape: Living players: player_3, player_4 (claims sentinel, watched dead player_2 on night 1 and reported only player_5 visiting), player_5 (denies role, accused by player_4), player_7, player_8, player_9 (claimed no role), player_10 (tied to a day 2 push by player_3 alone). Basis is mostly day 2 votes and one untested sentinel claim, no confirmed roles.

lessons.why: Written for a neutral FT already outed and facing a locked vote bloc; this seat has one stray day-2 vote against it and no accusation.
lessons.situation: Late in the game, the town's power roles are mostly confirmed or consistent with each other. The vote has narrowed to me versus one other unverified player, and I must choose between abstaining and voting the rival. Information landscape: Info-rich: role claims cover the town slots, saves and night results corroborate the town roles, and the public voting record is visible. The only open question is who among the unverified players is the lone killer or a wolf. Stakes: With few players left, one elimination changes the balance of power. My death ends my scoring chances, since a day vote never scores, so I must use my vote to split the count or push the real threat out. Consensus: The village is largely unified, on role-claim bookkeeping and corroborated night results, that the leftover unverified players are the problem. Neutral is treated as expendable. My position: holding out Heat: Extreme: several players, including confirmed town power roles, have declared votes against me because I am an expendable neutral once the town slots are claimed or corroborated. Target landscape: Two or three unverified players: me, an outed neutral fortune teller, and a rival with an unverified or contested claim (e.g. a vigilante or sentinel claimant suspected of being the lone killer). Every other living player holds a role corroborated by night events. The basis is process of elimination, not hard evidence on the rival.
lessons.action: When the room has already stacked elimination votes on you, cast your vote on the other leading suspect, the player with the least verified role or night results. An abstention lowers no one's count and can't force a tie, while a vote on the rival adds to a split or tie that could leave no one eliminated, and it pressures a plausible lone killer or wolf. If the votes against you are already a locked majority, the vote still goes to the rival rather than to nobody.

lessons.why: Needs a wolf about to be eliminated with a Trailseer case and a sigil result; here the board has one untested sentinel claim and eight alive, so the 'don't end the game before 2 points' logic is not live.
lessons.situation: The village is about to eliminate a wolf in an information-rich endgame where only one wolf would remain. Town can then win at night through a sigil strike or another kill. The fortune teller has not yet scored its second point. Information landscape: Rich. There is a prior Serial Killer elimination, night-one tracking testimony, and a sigil result, but no certainty about which evil is left. Stakes: Town is close to a win. One more evil removal leaves a lone wolf who can be killed that same night, and the game ends before the fortune teller scores. Your vote helps decide whether the game continues. Consensus: The village is building a majority against the tracked suspect on the strength of testimony and arguments. The agreement is moderately solid. My position: Aligned with the forming majority and reinforcing the case, which makes you a driver of the elimination. Heat: Low overall. The accused player may cast an isolated retaliatory vote at you, but the room is not suspicious of you. Target landscape: A suspected wolf, tracked or accused with an inconclusive sigil test, plus a claimed role under pressure from a quiet player. The suspected wolf is the main case, backed by daytime arguments and a Trailseer's testimony but no hard confirmation.
lessons.action: Before voting, count your points. If you have fewer than two and the leading candidate is a wolf whose removal would leave Town one elimination from winning, abstain if it is offered. If abstaining is not offered, vote for the least-supported candidate who is not a confirmed evil player, so the game runs long enough for your bets to score. A Town win ends the game before you can reach two points.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the game can end within one more elimination. A wrong lynch on the tied pair would leave three players and make the next night kill a near-decisive event, so the vote is costly to get wrong.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved on roles: no role is confirmed for any living player, the sentinel and trailseer claims are unverified, and the one private check (trailseer follow on night 4 showing player_7 visited no one) clears only one candidate. Town discussion relies on claims and deduction rather than announced results.
query_dims.situation: After a day 5 vote tied between two players, with no elimination, the village has no lynch; a sentinel claim (night 3 watch naming one visitor) conflicts with the accused player's denial, while the trailseer's follow results are private and only partly support the sentinel claim. Night 4 saw a healer save and a reanimated vigilante shot on the sentinel-claimant, and the pair of tied players is being argued over as the likely healer/necromancer pair.
query_dims.target_landscape: Two tied candidates from the day 5 vote: player_6 (claimed nothing publicly; accused of pushing the lynch and of being at player_2's door on night 4 by the trailseer-based reasoning) and player_1 (claimed nothing; was roleblocked night 3 and has a visitor on record from a sentinel claim). Neither has a confirmed role; the Trailseer's own follow results (player_6 visited no one on night 1, player_1 received a visit from player_5 on night 3) are private evidence only. Night 4's attack on the sentinel-claimant came through a dead vigilante, which is a reanimated kill, so the necromancer is the only living threat and the candidates are its possible bodies-of-interest.

lessons.why: Same decision (late game, whom to follow among unverified claimants) but it assumes a visit trace; against a Necromancer the trace is the dead body's name, so the advice cannot produce the 'decisive visit' it promises.
lessons.situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

lessons.why: Night-1 blind follow; this is night 5 with claims and results on the board.
lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

lessons.why: Needs a just-eliminated wolf and a confirmed investigator; neither exists here.
lessons.situation: A wolf was just eliminated by the vote, and the confirmed town investigator is the obvious target for wolf retaliation that night. The trailseer wants to preserve that investigator's last action in case they are killed. Information landscape: Info-rich: a wolf has been caught, the investigator is validated, and earlier night visits and claims are on record. Visit data on the likely victim is more valuable than a blind follow. Stakes: Losing the investigator without recovering their last check would remove a key information source. Seeing the investigator's visit, and getting it reported, can lead directly to the last wolf. Target landscape: The confirmed or strongly vetted info role facing retaliation, versus claimed protectors who were already attacked or saved, versus quiet unread players. The vetted role is the likeliest night victim and a natural way to find their last target.
lessons.action: When the trailseer's own role is likely to draw an attack, follow the player the wolves most want dead, such as the confirmed investigator who just exposed a wolf. If the target dies, the trailseer still learns whom they visited that night. That information can point suspicion at the visited player.

lessons.situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The Trailseer must pick a first follow target blindly, while the wolves and a lone killer may also pick arbitrary opening kills, including the Trailseer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no voting record, no night history, only baseline impressions from Day 1. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and evil far from parity, so no single follow is decisive. The value is in collecting a first concrete visit link before wagons and claims form, and the Trailseer may be killed before reporting it. Target landscape: Nine unrevealed other players with no claims, votes or behavioral deviations; any pick is an exploratory behavioral guess, so choose an unread player who does not stand out.
lessons.action: On the opening night with no claims or reads, follow one unread, low-profile player to get a concrete movement baseline. If the result names a door, keep it as a checkable link to cross-reference against other night results and later claims. If it shows no visits, treat that as weak information, because a wolf carrier whose victim was concealed leaves no trace, and the target may also be a passive role.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single elimination can end the game; a wrong vote is recoverable but each mis-elimination moves the evil side closer to parity.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible move now, such as a named accusation or a claimed night result, commits the speaker to a public role or result that can later be checked against deaths; a vote is permanent on the record, so a wrong vote cannot be withdrawn.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no verified investigation, sentinel, or trailseer results have been made public; the only hard fact is the revealed healer role and its night-one roleblock. Evidence is behavioral (voting patterns, abstentions, defenses of the lynched player).
query_dims.situation: Day 2 ends a lynch on a player who had stonewalled about a blocked night role; the revealed healer's roleblock is now public. The table is split between those who pushed the lynch and two abstainers, and no night result has been claimed publicly yet, so the next day's vote rests on behavior alone.
query_dims.target_landscape: Six surviving candidates: player_3, player_4, player_7, player_8, player_9, player_10 (the speaker is one of seven living). No living player has a revealed role. Player_5 was just lynched and revealed as healer, so its earlier roleblock is now public fact. Remaining candidates are judged only on behavior: who piled onto the lynch, who abstained, and who spoke on the blocked role.

lessons.why: Blind opening-kill advice (stab a quiet non-claimer, don't hunt a perfect target) still transfers to this night 2 board of pure behavioural reads, though it is written for night 1.
lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

lessons.why: Needs a claimed Investigator who has cleared the killer; no such claim exists.
lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.why: Needs a publicly saved, wolf-convicting investigator and a living healer; the healer was just lynched.
lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear village consensus is established in the current discussion. The only reported point is the claimant's account of a second consecutive roleblock; no shared target or evidence-based alignment is recorded.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five players are alive; the leading evil faction is 3 eliminations from parity, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a single elimination can be pivotal even though the stated distance to parity is 3.
query_dims.forward_exposure: You have made no public role claim or account of night actions. A visible claim or detailed night account would commit you to a story that could be challenged against public records; retracting it would be conspicuous. No specific visible move is currently established.
query_dims.heat_now: No current accusation or public scrutiny of you is recorded; your role and private actions remain undisclosed.
query_dims.information_landscape: Public evidence includes the revealed Healer's record confirming a prior save of the Investigator claimant, the revealed Illusionist's role, a concealed night-death role, and the claimant's unverified reports of repeated roleblocks. Your own identity and attacks are private. The current target decision is information-starved, with no confirmed result identifying a living suspect.
query_dims.my_position: You have not publicly expressed a position on the claim or a target, so you are neither visibly driving nor aligned with a stated majority.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the lone killer and that your attacks killed the player later revealed as Healer and the player whose role remains concealed; the public knows only the announced deaths and that a player claiming Investigator says they were roleblocked again. Your attack history and role are not publicly established.
query_dims.situation: With five players alive and no fresh public night outcome described for the current day, a player claiming Investigator reports a second consecutive roleblock, while you privately know your own lethal actions and remain unclaimed. The village has little current public basis to distinguish among the living targets, and your concealed private history is not part of its read.
query_dims.target_landscape: The vote can ultimately fall on any of the four other living players: one is a player claiming Investigator, with their repeated roleblock reports unverified, and the other three have no confirmed role or current evidence distinguishing them here. The remaining choices are largely behavior-based rather than supported by fresh public findings.

lessons.why: Written for a SK named by a Sentinel/Trailseer on day 2; nobody has accused this seat.
lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.why: Written for a SK the whole room is voting out; the seat has no heat.
lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.why: Accused-of-passivity scenario is absent, but the preventive half (give specific reads, engage so you are not the quiet default target) is usable in a day discussion now.
lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

query_dims.consensus_text: No public discussion or accusations have occurred, so there is no discernible village consensus.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine alive and five eliminations until the leading evil faction could win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown; the game cannot end within one more elimination, so this decision is not immediately terminal.
query_dims.heat_now: No suspicion or attention toward you is recorded; you have made no public claim or contribution yet.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the public record confirms two attacks on the concealed victim, but their role, side, and any will remain unknown; there are no public claims, accusations, or votes, and you have no private night information.
query_dims.my_position: No expressed position; you have not spoken, and no majority has formed.
query_dims.situation: On day 2, the village has nine players alive after the wolves and serial killer both attacked the same player on night 1; an illusionist concealed that player's role, leaving the village without a confirmed alignment or vote record to guide its first elimination decision.
query_dims.target_landscape: No elimination candidates or role claims have been publicly identified; the only known death is a player whose role was concealed, so their side and identity as a candidate remain unknown.

lessons.why: Needs a day-2 voting record and a claimed investigator's check being misquoted; the seat is at an opening turn with no votes or claims.
lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.
lessons.action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.

lessons.why: Four-player endgame with the speculator pressed to reveal; nine are alive.
lessons.situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.
lessons.action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.

lessons.why: Four alive, a vigilante demanding the speculator's role and conflicting tracker logs; none of that exists.
lessons.situation: With four players alive and one wolf left, a claimed vigilante demands the speculator's role while the claimed sentinel and claimed trailseer accuse each other over contradictory logs. Information landscape: Information-rich in confirmed dead roles, but the key conflict is between unverified claims, and a rules-confusion slip is being treated as proof. Stakes: At four alive with one wolf left, a wrong elimination likely hands the wolves the win. Pushing a mis-vote also exposes the speculator to a night shot. Consensus: The room leans toward whoever the credible shooter points at. It is tied up in the conflicting tracking logs and is pressuring the speculator for transparency. My position: Driving: pushing the accusation of one of the conflicting claimants to deflect heat. Heat: High: a credible claimed role singled the speculator out as a suspect for withholding its role all game. Target landscape: Two claimed roles, for example a sentinel and a trailseer, with logs that conflict, plus the speculator, who is being pressed for a role. The vigilante's shot gives it credibility, while the sentinel's and trailseer's results are unverified claims.
lessons.action: When a claimed role demands your role while two others trade accusations over conflicting logs, don't build the case on a rule-confusion or a thin data gap. Test the contradiction against the rules, for example whether a watch counts as a visit and who could have seen what. Back the elimination only if the mechanics actually prove a lie, and otherwise hold your vote for the player whose claim can't be explained.

lessons.situation: The morning after a night attack, with a save or a roleblock reported, a claim conflict erupts between rival investigator or healer claimants, or an unprompted visit report triggers a push on the reporter. The speculator is unpressured and has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced save or death, claimed night results, and rival claims whose contradictions can be tested against announced facts. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. No single vote flips the game yet, so the speculator should stay alive and gather evidence before committing its pick. Consensus: The village is converging on resolving the claim conflict, with attention on the contested claimants and not on quiet players. My position: With the majority, in a grounding, non-leading role. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the speculator, and the room's attention is on the claim conflict. Target landscape: Competing role claims (two investigators or two healers) and an unverified door-traffic or night-result report. Public announcements are the only verified anchor, and the rest is claim versus claim.
lessons.action: While no heat is on you and the room is split over competing claims, anchor your comments on facts the Game Master announced (a save, a death, a revealed role) and on what the rules allow. Stay neutral on the claim dispute, and use the quiet to see which side is gaining ground, since a Speculator that dies before picking loses.

query_dims.consensus_text: A clear majority is forming around eliminating the Healer claimant whose stated protection target was not the publicly saved player: four players have argued against that claimant, mainly because the rival account fits the save. The accused contests that this proves the rival's role, and no vote has yet occurred.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive, and it is four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town; the present vote matters but does not by itself decide which faction is winning.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible vote with the forming majority would align you with eliminating the claimant whose account does not explain the public save, without revealing your private attack history or role. It would create a public vote-record commitment, though your vote itself would not establish either Healer claim as true.
query_dims.heat_now: No one has accused you or challenged your behavior in the discussion; your night actions and Serial Killer role are not publicly attributed to you.
query_dims.information_landscape: The public has a confirmed Night 2 save from a Serial Killer attack, a revealed Sentinel and that Sentinel's Night 1 record, plus unverified Investigator and Trailseer claims. The save gives a concrete fit comparison between the Healer accounts but does not identify the Healer. The Night 1 victim's role remains concealed, leaving the game's information incomplete.
query_dims.my_position: You have not publicly stated a position, so you are presently uncommitted while a majority forms against one Healer claimant.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you made the Serial Killer attacks on the concealed victim on Night 1 and on the player publicly reported saved from a Serial Killer attack on Night 2. Publicly, the village knows those attack reports but not who made them. The save confirms a healer protected the target, not which of the two Healer claimants did so.
query_dims.situation: Before the Day 3 vote, two players claim the mutually exclusive Healer role after a public save of the claimed Investigator. One claimant says they protected the saved player; the other says they protected someone else. Several players favor eliminating the latter, while the claimant stresses that the save does not identify its source. You privately know you caused the Serial Killer attacks, including the attack that was stopped by the save, but no one has publicly connected those attacks to you.
query_dims.target_landscape: The main vote choices are the player claiming Healer whose account says they protected the saved player, and the competing Healer claimant who says they protected someone else. The save supports the first account's fit but does not prove that claimant's role; the second claimant's account is in tension with the save, not independently disproven. Other players include an unverified Investigator claimant and a claimed Trailseer whose reported follow is consistent with the Investigator claimant's roleblock account.

lessons.why: Written for a SK pinned by a Sentinel/Trailseer visit report with six-plus votes forming; here nobody has connected the attacks to the seat and the fight is between two Healer claimants.
lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single kill or vote ends the game; a concealed victim costs a revealed role the town would otherwise get, but the cost of spending a conceal now is recoverable while two conceals remain for later nights when a more valuable victim may be available.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Using a conceal on tonight's pack victim would hide that victim's role and trace from the town and commit the illusionist's own visit to the body; the role stays hidden until game end and the use cannot be taken back, while holding it preserves the option for a later night.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no night results have been publicly shared, the Investigator died without a public check, and the Fortune Teller died without any bets known to the town; the only firm facts are the two deaths and the abstain vote.
query_dims.situation: Night 2 approaches as the illusionist with two conceals left and the pack's kill still unassigned; the village has just abstained on day 2 with no hard leads, and the wolf partner is actively steering the room. The question is whether tonight's victim is worth a conceal, given that a revealed town role and its record would give the village concrete information.
query_dims.target_landscape: Eight living players on the board; no one has claimed a role publicly, and the two dead players are a Fortune Teller and an Investigator whose records were not publicly checked; no candidate has public evidence against them, so any pack target is chosen on behavior alone.

lessons.why: Exactly the seat's question (spend a conceal on tonight's victim with one or two left; prefer a victim whose role/will is still unknown); retrieved at score 0.881.
lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.why: Same decision (conceal or hold) but framed for night 1 with the partner carrying; the 'your own visit is still seen' point transfers, the night does not.
lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.why: Lone surviving illusionist with the chanteuse dead and an investigator driving suspicion; two wolves are alive.
lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack picks a quiet, unread first victim and you are the wolf who carries the kill. The risk is that the Trailseer or Sentinel catches your visit and gives Town a day-2 accusation against you. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day-1 vote, no claims, no confirmed roles, no night history. Only private wolf talk exists. Stakes: Early game with plenty of time. The main risk is losing a wolf early to a traced visit, which would cost the pack the endgame. A clean first night matters more than saving a charge. Forward exposure: Announces that an illusionist exists and spends one of two conceals if the victim dies. Your own visit leaves no trace, and the spent charge cannot be undone. If the victim survives, nothing is announced and the use is kept. Target landscape: Eight or nine unclaimed, unread players with no roles revealed. The target is picked from quiet behavior, not evidence, and could be a watcher, a tracker, or the night-immune lone killer.
lessons.action: When the carrier rotation makes you the carrier on night 1, carry the kill and use a conceal on the victim. A conceal on a victim you carried yourself leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer, and if the target turns out immune the use is kept.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single elimination can end the game, so the pick is not forced this turn, but a speculator that dies unpicked loses outright, so the pick must be made before a death becomes likely.

One night-kill record (player_9 investigator, night 2), one lynch record (vigilante, night 1 roleblock, night 2 held fire), public day-2 abstain vote and day-3 vote split, and unverified visit-direction requests with no result claims yet made publicly.
query_dims.situation: As the unpicked speculator, you face the day-3 aftermath: the town just lynched a vigilante, the discussion is now asking who received night results and who visited whom, and the village has no confirmed wolf. Dying without a pick loses, so the open question is whether the board is trending toward Town, the Wolves, or a lone killer strong enough to make a pick worthwhile now.
query_dims.target_landscape: Eight players alive; the decision is whether and when the speculator makes its one irreversible side pick, which must be chosen among Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or itself. Public role status: the day-3 vote eliminated a player revealed as a vigilante (claimed night-1 roleblock, held fire night 2); player_9 was revealed as an investigator killed night 2. Evidence basis: only the vote record and the claims about night 1; no confirmed wolf identity and no confirmed lone killer identity.

lessons.why: Same hold-or-pick decision, and its 'commit once evidence favours a side or you are likely to die' rule applies, but it is written for nights 1-2 and this is night 3 with a town power role just mis-lynched.
lessons.situation: Early game, night 1 or 2, with a discussion-only day 1 or an abstained day 2. At most one or two night deaths so far, and neither wolves nor the lone killer have been exposed. The speculator is still unpicked and has not been targeted. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil eliminations, only unverified claims and concealed or ambiguous bodies, and no momentum signal for any faction. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is no immediate pressure to lock in. The only cost of waiting is the risk of dying unpicked, which is low on night 1 and rises as killers act. Holding costs little and keeps the option open for an informed pick later. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self, or keep holding. All ten players are alive with no confirmed roles and no tested claims. Any pick would be a pure guess on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On nights 1-2, while no evil role has been confirmed eliminated and no claim has been tested, keep the one-time pick unspent. Reassess each night, and commit as soon as board evidence clearly favors one side or you suspect you are likely to be killed. Dying unpicked is a loss, but an uninformed early lock-in has no advantage, and the pick cannot be changed once made.

lessons.why: Needs an evil role confirmed eliminated with validated saves; the lynched vigilante is Town.
lessons.situation: Night 3 after Town's day vote eliminated a confirmed wolf or lone killer, with healer saves publicly verified. Town holds a large majority, but some killers remain. Past observations show the Town pick won when Town stayed disciplined and lost when Town later mis-eliminated its own power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: system-confirmed evil role reveals, a validated investigator claim, and announced healer saves. The remaining unknown is whether a wolf or killer is still hidden and how well Town will play. Stakes: Town leads, but a few mis-votes or kills could still flip the game, so the pick is only as good as Town's later play. Picking now removes the risk of dying unpicked, but it ties your win to Town's survival and avoiding errors. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self. After a confirmed evil elimination Town looks dominant, with validated investigator or healer claims and a numerical majority. Evil still has a wolf and possibly an unknown lone killer, and Town's later errors can still erase that lead.
lessons.action: Once the day vote has system-confirmed an evil elimination and the surviving power-role claims are validated, make the pick on that night instead of waiting longer. Choose Town only if the lone killer is confirmed gone or Town clearly outnumbers a single remaining wolf; if killers are still active with an uncertain Town lead, keep holding until one side is clearly ahead, unless you are likely to be killed that night.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive, and the leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this night is consequential but not a single-action swing.
query_dims.forward_exposure: The public abstention is permanent and commits no daytime target. The coordinated night actions are private: blocking a target or carrying out the kill would not publicly reveal the actor, but the block is spent for the night and a successful kill cannot be reversed.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information is limited and mostly claims: the Investigator claimant reports a Not suspicious check, the Sentinel claimant reports a visitor, and a follower’s account matches that route. These details do not verify the claimed roles or alignments. Publicly, the concealed victim was attacked by both wolves and the serial killer, but their role and side remain unknown. The Chanteuse privately knows the prior block did not affect its target; there is no night-immune-target result identifying the serial killer.
query_dims.situation: After a no-elimination day, the Chanteuse is coordinating a split night action with a living wolf partner: cancel the claimed Investigator’s possible check while the Chanteuse carries the pack kill against the claimed Sentinel. The two public information-role claims remain unverified, and the village abstained despite one vote against the player read as Not suspicious by the claimant.
query_dims.target_landscape: The pack’s current coordination favors blocking the unverified Investigator claimant, whose remaining checks are unknown, while the Chanteuse carries the kill against the unverified Sentinel claimant. The Investigator and Sentinel claims have no public confirmation; the visit accounts corroborate a route, not roles or alignment. The living partner supports this split. No attack on a night-immune player has identified the lone killer; the prior attack on the concealed victim resulted in a death, so that test was not used.

lessons.why: Same decision (block target on a mid-game night after day-2 claims, with a kill already chosen); the 'different player than the kill target, investigator first' rule is applied.
lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.why: Blind opening night; claims, a vote record and a night result exist.
lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.why: Needs a wolf partner killed by a confirmed vigilante; the partner is alive.

Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.

If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Stakes: Town has lost its healer protection but still has information roles; removing the investigator while blinding the tracker for a night shifts the information balance toward the wolves before parity pressure builds. Forward exposure: Blocking shows the village only that some blocker exists, if the blocked player speaks of it; nothing ties the block to you, and you can switch block targets nightly. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.
lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

You can switch targets each night, but a death by sigil cannot be undone. Target landscape: The claimed or suspected sigilist (2 sigils, possibly already spent), the kill target (a trailseer or sentinel who exposed a wolf visit), and other town info roles. Which player holds the sigil is deduced from public claims.

A blocked sigilist places nothing and makes no visit, so no sigil can strike you when you attack. If you cannot tell who the sigilist is, block the most likely candidate instead of the kill target.
