Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.why: Needs a sentinel/trailseer naming me as the only visitor to a night-1 victim; no such report is live on day 4.
lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.why: The advice to give specific reads each day so a claimant cannot single out the quiet player applies to a seat that passes in both the opening and proactive rounds with a vigilante pressing others, even though nobody has labelled it passive yet.
lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the next vote or kill cannot end the game, so a mistaken lynch is recoverable but each lost town member narrows the margin, and the unresolved abstain pattern means no information is being produced yet.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no public claims, no announced checks or watches, no verified night results; only the public death roles and the abstain tally exist.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 opened with no role claims after two night kills and an unanimous abstain vote; players are pressing each other to state night results, and the Trailseer holds a private follow of one living player whose visit could be cross-checked against tomorrow's morning report.
query_dims.target_landscape: Seven-to-eight living players with no public role claims; the only confirmed facts are the two night deaths (a fortune teller and an investigator, roles revealed) and an abstain-everywhere day 2 vote. No candidate has a public role status or verified evidence; every suspect is judged on behavior in discussion alone.

lessons.why: Same blind-follow decision with no claims, but it is night 2 after two deaths and a day vote, not night 1; the 'follow a quiet unvetted player, not one pressing you' advice is usable.
lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

lessons.why: Opening-night blind follow with all ten alive; stage differs (eight alive) but the null-result caution about concealed victims transfers.
lessons.situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The Trailseer must pick a first follow target blindly, while the wolves and a lone killer may also pick arbitrary opening kills, including the Trailseer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no voting record, no night history, only baseline impressions from Day 1. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and evil far from parity, so no single follow is decisive. The value is in collecting a first concrete visit link before wagons and claims form, and the Trailseer may be killed before reporting it. Target landscape: Nine unrevealed other players with no claims, votes or behavioral deviations; any pick is an exploratory behavioral guess, so choose an unread player who does not stand out.
lessons.action: On the opening night with no claims or reads, follow one unread, low-profile player to get a concrete movement baseline. If the result names a door, keep it as a checkable link to cross-reference against other night results and later claims. If it shows no visits, treat that as weak information, because a wolf carrier whose victim was concealed leaves no trace, and the target may also be a passive role.

lessons.why: Late game with a few suspects and claimed sigilist/vigilante holders; eight alive with no claims at all.
lessons.situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

lessons.situation: A wolf was just eliminated by the vote, and the confirmed town investigator is the obvious target for wolf retaliation that night. The trailseer wants to preserve that investigator's last action in case they are killed. Information landscape: Info-rich: a wolf has been caught, the investigator is validated, and earlier night visits and claims are on record. Visit data on the likely victim is more valuable than a blind follow. Stakes: Losing the investigator without recovering their last check would remove a key information source. Seeing the investigator's visit, and getting it reported, can lead directly to the last wolf. Target landscape: The confirmed or strongly vetted info role facing retaliation, versus claimed protectors who were already attacked or saved, versus quiet unread players. The vetted role is the likeliest night victim and a natural way to find their last target.
lessons.action: When the trailseer's own role is likely to draw an attack, follow the player the wolves most want dead, such as the confirmed investigator who just exposed a wolf. If the target dies, the trailseer still learns whom they visited that night. That information can point suspicion at the visited player.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six players are alive and the leading remaining evil faction is two eliminations from parity; one night result alone cannot end the game or flip the winning position, though it reduces the room for error.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved for predicting tonight's victim: public deaths confirm the Investigator, Trailseer, Sigilist, and Serial Killer are gone, and a healer save was announced on the claimed Sentinel on the previous night. There is no public evidence identifying the remaining wolves or establishing who will be attacked tonight.
query_dims.situation: After the Serial Killer was eliminated on day 3, six players remain, including you. The lone killer is gone, but the wolves' night attack remains a threat; no living player's role is publicly confirmed, and a claimed Sentinel is unverified. You must settle a death prediction against the option of spending a self-bet for protection.
query_dims.target_landscape: Tonight's bet can name any living player other than you, or use one of your two remaining self-bets to prevent an attack on you at the cost of scoring no points. The claimed Sentinel is unverified; the other living players have no publicly confirmed roles. There is little evidence to distinguish likely victims or predict their roles.

lessons.why: Three-player endgame against a necromancer; six players and no lone killer are alive.
lessons.situation: Last wolf voted out and three players left. A lone killer (the necromancer, who can attack through a reanimated body) wins by killing one more player, so the Fortune Teller is a live kill target and no other player's death is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead, the dead roles are confirmed, and the remaining Town sigilist is confirmed out of sigils. This makes the only remaining attacker and its available bodies clear. Stakes: The lone killer wins if anyone else dies tonight, so a bet that fails to cover your own life can end the game with the Fortune Teller short of two points. A self-bet keeps you alive for another night. Target landscape: The suspected necromancer (alive and holding a usable body, so unlikely to die), a confirmed sigilist with no sigils left (no threat), or a self-bet. Roles are confirmed from the graveyard, and nothing makes the suspect likely to die tonight.
lessons.action: With three alive and a lone killer that can attack, you are one of only two possible victims. If no other victim is predictable, spend a self-bet, because an attack on you fails that night. Don't bet on the suspected killer: a killer that is immune or about to win is unlikely to die, and a wrong bet leaves you open to the attack.

lessons.why: Same bet decision with the obvious victim publicly protected (the claimed sentinel was saved last night); but this lesson is for one remaining killer, here two wolves remain.
lessons.situation: Late game with the wolves dead or nearly dead and one killer left (serial killer, necromancer or last wolf). The Fortune Teller stands at 0-1 points and needs a death, and the most obvious target is publicly protected, so a bet on them fails to the save or the killer switches targets. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of the dead wolves are confirmed, claims and protection histories are public, and the surviving killer's identity or kill pattern is mostly known. Stakes: Few players remain and the game can end any night. Each night spent without scoring risks being voted out or the game finishing before the second point, so the bet must follow where the killer can actually kill, not just where it wants to. Target landscape: The investigator or leader shielded by a public healer claim, the claimed healer who is exposed, other claimed power roles (sigilist, sentinel, trailseer), and unconfirmed players. Hard evidence of who is protected, not behavior, drives the choice.
lessons.action: When the healer has publicly announced protecting the obvious top target (the confirmed or claimed investigator), place the bet on the next-most-valuable unshielded Town role the surviving killer must remove, such as the claimed healer or another power role. If the killer's last pick is predictable, name that role in the bet for the two-point payoff.

lessons.why: Three-player endgame tie; six alive.
lessons.situation: Three-player endgame tie between a confirmed Town power role, a suspected wolf and the Fortune Teller. The wolves need a kill to close the game, and the Fortune Teller needs points to win. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed by earlier night results and blocked actions, so the wolves' likely victim can be read from the board. Stakes: Each night is nearly decisive. A correct victim-and-role bet gives two points and wins the game for the Fortune Teller, while a miss wastes a night when the kill can end the game. Target landscape: A publicly confirmed Town role (e.g. a claimed vigilante whose shots were blocked), a suspected surviving wolf, or a self-bet. The Town player is the most likely kill target, backed by confirmed evidence from earlier nights and blocks rather than just behavior.
lessons.action: With three alive and a night kill that is predictable (a publicly confirmed Town role whose own actions are blocked or spent, with a wolf free to carry the kill), bet on that player to die and name their confirmed role. A correct victim plus role scores two points and can finish the win.

lessons.situation: After a day elimination or accusation, the remaining killer needs to silence the player who exposed it or holds a deadly tool against it. The Fortune Teller must choose between betting on the accused (who survives) and betting on the exposing claimant (who is attacked). Information landscape: Information-rich: a public claim or result (tracker report, sigil test, investigator checks) points at the killer's side, and several Town roles are out in the open. Stakes: Only one killing source is left, so exactly one death is likely each night and the bet must match it. A miss leaves the Fortune Teller stuck at one point while the game may end that same night. Target landscape: The claimed tracker, sigilist or investigator who exposed or tested the killer's side, versus the accused wolf or suspect, versus bystander claimed roles such as a roleblocked sentinel or unconfirmed healer. The basis is public claims and the day's vote record.
lessons.action: When one killer remains and a claimed power role has just driven the day's outcome (outed a wolf, tested the wolf, or led the vote), bet on that role as the killer's top threat, not on the accused or already-exposed suspect. A killer that is under suspicion usually survives the night, and the threat to it is the likelier victim.

lessons.situation: Night one after a discussion-only opening day. Several killers (wolves, and possibly a lone killer) will each attack someone, and no public mechanical constraint limits their choices. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigative findings, deaths, confirmed roles, or vote record exist. Stakes: Very low board pressure. A miss costs nothing but a night, and multiple attackers raise the chance that the chosen player dies. A hit on night one puts the win one successful bet away. Target landscape: All other living players, with no public claims, revealed alignments, or voting history to separate them. Any pick is close to a random draw among the candidates.
lessons.action: On a night with no evidence at all (no claims, no deaths, no votes), bet on any one quiet living player without naming a role, since the bet scores on any death by any cause. Keep both self-bets unspent for later nights when you may become a target.

lessons.situation: Early game (night 1 or 2), the Fortune Teller has no points yet and must pick a nightly death bet while wolves and a lone killer are all hunting. Day discussion produced a visible conflict or a prominent claimed power role. Information landscape: Mixed: some claims and night-one movement reports exist, but roles are unverified and votes were mostly abstentions, so the pick rests on behavioral reads. Stakes: No immediate parity pressure. The Fortune Teller needs two points in total, so each night's bet is a cheap, repeatable chance to score, and the self-bets guard against a later attack. Target landscape: Players who publicly claimed or acted as information roles, or who were just singled out by a night result or an open dispute, versus quiet players with no evidence either way. The choice rests on behavioral threat to the killers, not confirmed alignment.
lessons.action: With both self-bets still unspent and no points scored, bet on the player the killers most plausibly want dead tonight: an openly active, publicly claimed information role (such as a trailseer that just exposed someone) or a player the dead Trailseer's last follow pointed to. Name no role, since the death alone scores a point, and keep the self-bets for later nights.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the next single elimination does not end the game, so a misdirected block or kill is recoverable but each wasted night brings the wolves closer to parity.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible move tonight (a claim, a block declared, or a vote) would commit the chanteuse's standing in a village where the healer was just lynched and no claim has yet been tested; a public block cannot be retracted once the blocked player reports it.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no public result has been announced except the day 1 kill and the day 2 lynch. The only private information is the chanteuse's own block record and the pack's kill. No town claim has been checked against a death, so every candidate block target is unverified.
query_dims.situation: Night 2 for a chanteuse who blocked the healer on night 1 and whose pack has agreed on a quiet town player as the kill. The healer was lynched on day 2 after being blocked on night 1 and refusing to name their role, and the village is still waiting for a claimed sentinel or investigator result to test against tonight's deaths. The carrier rotates to a partner wolf, who has set the kill, so this night's block must be chosen to avoid the pack's victim while removing the most dangerous town night action.
query_dims.target_landscape: Town players alive: the quiet player the pack has settled on as the kill (no public role claim, no pushed read), the player who has been pressing for claimed results, and the player who has been voting with the majority. None of these has a verified public role; all judgments rest on behavior and vote pattern, not evidence.

lessons.why: Same decision (block target distinct from the pack kill) but the lesson's trigger is Town info roles having claimed with results on record; none has here.
lessons.situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.

lessons.why: Blind block choice with no claims is the same reasoning state, but this is night 2 with a death, a lynch and a blocked-healer history, not the opening night.
lessons.situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.

lessons.why: Needs a claimed investigator and trailseer with results and a pack-kill concealment plan; none exist.
lessons.situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles such as the healer and necromancer are confirmed, and the investigator and trailseer have public claims and results on record. Stakes: Town has lost its healer protection but still has information roles; removing the investigator while blinding the tracker for a night shifts the information balance toward the wolves before parity pressure builds. Forward exposure: Blocking shows the village only that some blocker exists, if the blocked player speaks of it; nothing ties the block to you, and you can switch block targets nightly. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.
lessons.action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.

lessons.situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.
lessons.action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.

lessons.situation: The chanteuse is the pack's carrier this night. A town sigilist is alive and has signaled traps, and the wolves want to kill a tracker or investigator who exposed them. Information landscape: Information-rich: day-2 claims by the trailseer, sentinel and sigilist show active town surveillance. Whether a sigil is already on a given wolf is unknown. Stakes: Dying to a sigil on the kill night loses a wolf and exposes the chanteuse. That leaves a lone illusionist against town, which is close to losing. Forward exposure: The block is a visit but it hides the sigilist's action. If the sigilist is not the one blocked, the sigil still strikes the carrier, kills you, and reveals the chanteuse. You can switch targets each night, but a death by sigil cannot be undone. Target landscape: The claimed or suspected sigilist (2 sigils, possibly already spent), the kill target (a trailseer or sentinel who exposed a wolf visit), and other town info roles. Which player holds the sigil is deduced from public claims.
lessons.action: If you will carry the pack kill and a sigilist has claimed or is likely active, use your block on the sigilist. A blocked sigilist places nothing and makes no visit, so no sigil can strike you when you attack. If you cannot tell who the sigilist is, block the most likely candidate instead of the kill target.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is split and no consensus has formed: the village is divided over whether player_9 or player_4 is the wolf-side party, with player_3 pushing on player_9, player_8 holding out on any vote without a second data point, and no shared read on the night 3 visit.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four alive with distance to parity 0 means the next elimination can end the game; a wrong lynch or any kill that leaves the remaining evil faction at parity hands it the win, so a single vote or kill here is decisive.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Admitting the night 3 visit to player_4 is already in the open room and cannot be retracted; any further specific claim about what I did or learned would commit me to a story that the remaining players can test against later public results, and would be hard to reverse.
query_dims.heat_now: Moderate and rising: my night 3 visit to player_4 is public through the sentinel's watch, and player_6 and player_9 are both pressing me on what I learned, so I am being asked directly to explain a visit I cannot explain without revealing my role.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved on the board: one unverified Suspicious read from a dead claimant, one sentinel watch result on the dead claimant showing two visitors, and several contested claims with no confirmed role among survivors.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out from the forming pressure on player_9, while standing in a contested middle position as a player with a visit to the dead player_4 on record.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the serial killer I privately know I killed player_2, player_10 and player_4, and that I visited player_4 on night 3; publicly I am one of four survivors whose visit to player_4 is on record through the sentinel's watch, while my role remains unknown to the village.
query_dims.situation: After a claimed investigator died at night with an untested Suspicious read on player_9 still open, the sentinel publicly reported that two players visited the dead claimant on night 3, one of whom is me, and player_9 pressed me to say what I learned from that visit while the village debated whether to vote on player_9.
query_dims.target_landscape: The surviving players are player_3 (claiming sentinel, with a watch result on player_4 showing two visitors), player_6 (me), player_8 (abstaining twice, asking pointed questions), and player_9 (accused on a night 2 Suspicious read from the dead claimed investigator player_4). Only player_4's claim and the sentinel's watch are on record; no role among survivors is confirmed by elimination.

lessons.why: A sentinel's result puts the SK at a night victim's door and the SK must vote; advice to vote a rival suspect with competing evidence rather than lone-vote the accuser is exactly usable (here the dead claimant's Suspicious read on player_9).
lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six alive with two more eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong elimination would leave the village one step closer to parity, so the vigilante's remaining shots are valuable but a shot on an unverified target would be costly and could not be undone.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Publicly firing a shot would reveal the vigilante role and commit the agent to a target; a shot cannot be taken back, and a miss or a town kill would be irreversible, while holding fire keeps the role hidden.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only role-specific evidence is one untested follow chain from a trailseer claim, the sentinel's will (one watch, no visitors), and the healer's protection record; no investigator, sentinel, or healer result is live.
query_dims.situation: Day 3, after the village lynched a player revealed as the healer on a mostly unanimous vote, the two remaining accusers are the self-described trailseer and a quiet player who has been voting against them, while the vigilante holds two shots and has no verified lead against any living player.
query_dims.target_landscape: Six living players; the public trailseer claim (player_3) names a night-1 visit to the sentinel that is untested and matches no confirmed record; the sentinel's will shows it watched player_9 and saw no one; no living player has a confirmed role or a verified night result.

lessons.why: Same decision (hold fire or shoot) with no verified lead; the situation text itself says 'Information-starved', and the Do (hold for a lead that names someone) is directly usable.
lessons.situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
lessons.action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.

lessons.why: Same shoot-or-hold decision after a Town mis-lynch, but the lesson requires a player exposed by hard evidence; here the only lead is an untested trailseer claim.
lessons.situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.
lessons.action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is broadly cautious and has not aligned on an elimination target. Speakers agree that the reported visit alone does not implicate the visited player, and the discussion is seeking additional night information.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; no single elimination here can end the game, though the early loss of two confirmed Town information roles makes the limited evidence base consequential.
query_dims.forward_exposure: You have publicly asked whether the questioned player’s night action resolved. This commits you only to seeking clarification, not to a role claim or accusation; the question can be left without further commitment.
query_dims.heat_now: No one has accused you or challenged your account; your public question has drawn no expressed suspicion so far.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information is limited: two Town roles and the two night attackers are publicly confirmed, but night actions are private. The Sentinel’s visitor result is a player claim, not a Game Master announcement; no further private result has been publicly substantiated.
query_dims.my_position: You are contributing a question within the cautious discussion, not driving an accusation or opposing a formed majority.
query_dims.public_private_text: You know privately that your pack killed the revealed Investigator and that your block on the questioned player succeeded. Publicly, the confirmed night deaths were the Investigator killed by wolves and the Trailseer killed by the Serial Killer. The Sentinel’s unverified account says the dead Trailseer visited another player; the public discussion treats that as compatible with a follow action, not proof of guilt.
query_dims.situation: On day 2, after the wolves’ night kill revealed an Investigator and the Serial Killer’s attack revealed a Trailseer, the Sentinel claimant reported that the dead Trailseer visited a living player. The group regards this as consistent with a follow action rather than incriminating evidence, while a separate question about whether another player’s action resolved has produced no confirmed result.
query_dims.target_landscape: No specific elimination target has emerged. The dead Investigator and Trailseer are system-confirmed Town roles; the living players’ roles are otherwise unknown or, for the Sentinel claimant, unverified. The only concrete visitor evidence is the Sentinel claimant’s account, which fits the Trailseer’s possible follow action and does not establish wrongdoing by the visited player.

lessons.why: No trailseer has exposed the chanteuse; the trailseer is dead and the room is not pressing the seat.
lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.
lessons.action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.

lessons.why: The wolf partner is not accused.
lessons.situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

lessons.why: Day-2 vote in an info-poor game where the room is cautious and has no target; the chanteuse is the one tempted toward an elimination vote on a quiet unaccused player, which is what the seat did (player_4, the sigilist).
lessons.situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.
lessons.action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear direction. The discussion treats the claimed Sentinel's result cautiously and is seeking additional information; no vote target has been established.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and the leading evil faction needs four eliminations to reach parity; a single vote or kill cannot end the game, though an unsupported elimination could still cost the village a scarce player.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: no one has accused or singled you out in the discussion.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved, with two public Night 1 deaths and revealed roles, but no wills or private results publicly verified. The Sentinel claim is unverified, and its reported visit is compatible with the Trailseer's role.
query_dims.my_position: Not driving and not visibly aligned with a forming majority; you have not stated a position in the discussion.
query_dims.situation: On the first voting day, a claimed Sentinel reported that the player revealed as Trailseer visited the watched player on Night 1. The room recognizes this could be the Trailseer's ordinary follow action, so the result neither implicates the watched player nor identifies who killed the Trailseer; no competing concrete lead has surfaced.
query_dims.target_landscape: No elimination candidate has emerged. The living player claiming Sentinel is unverified; their account that the revealed Trailseer visited the watched player is consistent with that role's follow action, but does not identify an attacker.

lessons.why: Endgame about a last wolf and a nearly-won Town; this is day 2 with eight alive.
lessons.situation: The village is about to eliminate a wolf in an information-rich endgame where only one wolf would remain. Town can then win at night through a sigil strike or another kill. The fortune teller has not yet scored its second point. Information landscape: Rich. There is a prior Serial Killer elimination, night-one tracking testimony, and a sigil result, but no certainty about which evil is left. Stakes: Town is close to a win. One more evil removal leaves a lone wolf who can be killed that same night, and the game ends before the fortune teller scores. Your vote helps decide whether the game continues. Consensus: The village is building a majority against the tracked suspect on the strength of testimony and arguments. The agreement is moderately solid. My position: Aligned with the forming majority and reinforcing the case, which makes you a driver of the elimination. Heat: Low overall. The accused player may cast an isolated retaliatory vote at you, but the room is not suspicious of you. Target landscape: A suspected wolf, tracked or accused with an inconclusive sigil test, plus a claimed role under pressure from a quiet player. The suspected wolf is the main case, backed by daytime arguments and a Trailseer's testimony but no hard confirmation.
lessons.action: Before voting, count your points. If you have fewer than two and the leading candidate is a wolf whose removal would leave Town one elimination from winning, abstain if it is offered. If abstaining is not offered, vote for the least-supported candidate who is not a confirmed evil player, so the game runs long enough for your bets to score. A Town win ends the game before you can reach two points.

lessons.why: Late game with the seat stacked against; this is day 2 and nobody is pressing the seat.
lessons.situation: Late in the game, the town's power roles are mostly confirmed or consistent with each other. The vote has narrowed to me versus one other unverified player, and I must choose between abstaining and voting the rival. Information landscape: Info-rich: role claims cover the town slots, saves and night results corroborate the town roles, and the public voting record is visible. The only open question is who among the unverified players is the lone killer or a wolf. Stakes: With few players left, one elimination changes the balance of power. My death ends my scoring chances, since a day vote never scores, so I must use my vote to split the count or push the real threat out. Consensus: The village is largely unified, on role-claim bookkeeping and corroborated night results, that the leftover unverified players are the problem. Neutral is treated as expendable. My position: holding out Heat: Extreme: several players, including confirmed town power roles, have declared votes against me because I am an expendable neutral once the town slots are claimed or corroborated. Target landscape: Two or three unverified players: me, an outed neutral fortune teller, and a rival with an unverified or contested claim (e.g. a vigilante or sentinel claimant suspected of being the lone killer). Every other living player holds a role corroborated by night events. The basis is process of elimination, not hard evidence on the rival.
lessons.action: When the room has already stacked elimination votes on you, cast your vote on the other leading suspect, the player with the least verified role or night results. An abstention lowers no one's count and can't force a tie, while a vote on the rival adds to a split or tie that could leave no one eliminated, and it pressures a plausible lone killer or wolf. If the votes against you are already a locked majority, the vote still goes to the rival rather than to nobody.

query_dims.consensus_text: No village consensus has formed; the room is fragmented after the sentinel lynch, with the sigilist claim being the only fresh public statement and no shared target emerging.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single elimination ends the game, so a wrong lynch is recoverable but each mistake shortens the margin toward a wolf or necromancer win.
query_dims.heat_now: Low on me: I have made no claims and have no accusations aimed at me; my only public exposure is the night bets which have scored once and missed twice.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only tested reports are the dead sentinel's night 1 watch, now unverifiable, and the sigilist's unverified claim; no living player has a confirmed result to share.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out, with no stated position against any forming consensus and making no claim.
query_dims.situation: Day 4 with five players alive after a sentinel lynch and two night kills of town-side roles. A player claiming sigilist says their sigil struck the chanteuse last night and is holding the last sigil for a clear attacker, while the wolves' remaining members are still hidden and no vote has been held since the day 3 lynch.
query_dims.target_landscape: Five living players: player_3, player_8, player_9 (claims sigilist, sigil placed on a dead chanteuse), player_10, and me (fortune teller, unrevealed). Public role status: dead are trailseer, vigilante, sentinel, chanteuse, investigator; no living player has a verified role except the sigilist claim, which is unconfirmed by any announcement and only a single claim. Evidence basis is mostly day-2 vote history and the dead sentinel's night 1 claim, which is now dead-end.

lessons.why: Same low-profile FT posture (agree with a claim, add one modest point) but written for an early day; this is day 4 with five alive and a necromancer.
lessons.situation: An early day after a night kill, with no wolf-kill leads or checks revealed. One investigative claimant has reported a non-visit result and the village is just starting to interpret night movements. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single dead player and one claimed no-visit result, with no investigative checks, caught lies or voting record to go on. Stakes: Early game with plenty of cushion; no single vote or kill flips the game. The aim is to stay alive for more night bets while adding no suspicion, since there is little to gain from pushing a read now. Consensus: Calm and undirected. Players echo each other's observations, with no accusation forming and a leaning toward abstaining. My position: With the majority. Echoing and refining shared observations, not driving. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the fortune teller. Target landscape: A claimed trailseer or similar reporter clears one quiet player. The other living players have unknown roles and no concrete leads, so there is no basis yet for a behavioral accusation.
lessons.action: When the day opens with little evidence and just one or two claims, agree with the claim and add one modest logical observation, such as which roles a given report cannot cover. Then let others speak, without proposing a target, so the discussion stays calm and you stay unnoticed.

lessons.why: Discussion of visit reports with a calm FT; the reports here are from dead watchers, so 'restate what each claimant reported' has little to work on.
lessons.situation: A day discussion in which night deaths have produced visit reports from claimed trailseer or sentinel players. Those reports point at an accused player or create competing leads, and the fortune teller has no heat and is still working toward two prediction points. Information landscape: Mixed but mostly information-rich: announced deaths and roles, plus claimed visit reports that conflict or are contested. Reports are claims, not announcements, so they can be checked against how the rules treat concealed victims. Stakes: The board is mid-game and not at the brink; one wrong day-vote hurts Town but does not end the game. The fortune teller's own win depends on surviving nights to score points, so staying unnoticed matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is engaged and fairly aligned on dissecting the visit reports. There is no firm lean yet, or it is forming around the accused visitor. It rests on claimed results rather than announced facts. My position: With the majority, not driving. Contributing a summary but taking no hard stance. Heat: None. No one is suspecting or questioning the fortune teller, who is a neutral with no side and reads Not suspicious. Target landscape: Several living players with unverified role claims and visit reports from a claimed trailseer or sentinel; the accused deny or counter-claim. The basis is claimed night results and explanations, not confirmed facts.
lessons.action: With zero heat and no role claim of your own, stay in the analytical middle: restate what each investigative claimant reported, ask the accused to explain their visits, and point out which claims conflict. Hold back from committing to one target until the explanations come in, so you stay a low-profile voter while the village's own evidence does the work.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four players remain, and the leading evil faction is two eliminations from parity at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a single death or vote can sharply change the winning position; concealing a victim could also withhold a role and will that might help the village identify the remaining wolf.
query_dims.forward_exposure: The pack's victim and any resulting death or save will be publicly reported. Using the remaining conceal would hide a dead victim's role and Town will, but would reveal that an illusionist conceal was used; it is irreversible once the body is concealed. No attack on a night-immune player has identified the Serial Killer through my private results; the Serial Killer was instead publicly eliminated on day 3.
query_dims.information_landscape: The board has substantial confirmed history: the Investigator and Trailseer died night 1, the claimed Sentinel's watched visits are unverified private-result claims, a wolf attack on that claimant was publicly saved night 2, and the Serial Killer and Chanteuse were publicly revealed on elimination. The night 3 victim's role and will remain hidden from everyone but me. There is no result from an attack on an immune player identifying the Serial Killer; that killer's elimination is public. The remaining candidates' roles and the purpose of their actions are largely unknown, so the present target choice is information-starved.
query_dims.situation: After the Chanteuse was eliminated and revealed as a wolf, I am the sole surviving wolf among four players, with the Serial Killer already eliminated. I must choose a night victim and whether to spend my final conceal; a successful kill leaves three alive, making the next elimination especially consequential. The previous concealed victim's role remains unknown to the village, though I privately learned they were the Fortune Teller.
query_dims.target_landscape: The living candidates are the player claiming Sentinel, whose two claimed watches are spent; the player who voted with the majority to eliminate the Chanteuse; and the player who also voted to eliminate the Chanteuse and was saved from the wolves on night 2. Their roles are otherwise unconfirmed. A death could reveal a Town role and will, while concealing it would deny the village that information. The Chanteuse is dead, so there is no living wolf partner to coordinate with; I am tonight's carrier.

lessons.why: The lone surviving illusionist with the chanteuse dead, carrying the kill and deciding where to spend the last conceal: the same decision and dynamic.
lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.why: One conceal left and a choice whether this victim justifies it: the same decision; Do (save it for an unknown role) is directly usable.
lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.why: Night-1 opening kill; this is night 4 with four alive.
lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack picks a quiet, unread first victim and you are the wolf who carries the kill. The risk is that the Trailseer or Sentinel catches your visit and gives Town a day-2 accusation against you. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day-1 vote, no claims, no confirmed roles, no night history. Only private wolf talk exists. Stakes: Early game with plenty of time. The main risk is losing a wolf early to a traced visit, which would cost the pack the endgame. A clean first night matters more than saving a charge. Forward exposure: Announces that an illusionist exists and spends one of two conceals if the victim dies. Your own visit leaves no trace, and the spent charge cannot be undone. If the victim survives, nothing is announced and the use is kept. Target landscape: Eight or nine unclaimed, unread players with no roles revealed. The target is picked from quiet behavior, not evidence, and could be a watcher, a tracker, or the night-immune lone killer.
lessons.action: When the carrier rotation makes you the carrier on night 1, carry the kill and use a conceal on the victim. A conceal on a victim you carried yourself leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer, and if the target turns out immune the use is kept.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive; the leading evil faction is 5 eliminations from parity at worst for the town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown. At worst for the town, the game can end within one more elimination, so a single death may decide whether the board remains playable; the effect of any particular target’s removal on the endgame is unclear without their role.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A night kill is not publicly attributed to its killer, but the victim and that the attack came from the Serial Killer are announced if the target can be killed at night. The death is irreversible; no particular endgame advantage is established without knowing the target’s role or faction.
query_dims.information_landscape: The Illusionist’s elimination and the Night 2 Sentinel record are system-confirmed. The public save confirms an attack on the claimed Investigator and that the Healer protected them, but not who protected them. The Healer, Investigator, and Trailseer claims are not role-confirmed; the Night 1 concealed death leaves that player’s role and faction unknown. The Serial Killer privately knows their own attacks and that the Night 2 target survived because of a healer save. Information is limited and asymmetric.
query_dims.situation: After the village eliminated a player revealed as the Illusionist, the surviving Serial Killer faces a concealed-role board and a night-kill choice among seven living players. Public discussion has centered on conflicting Healer claims: one claimant’s protection account fits the announced save, while the other says they protected someone else. The other role claims and private night results remain unverified.
query_dims.target_landscape: The living candidates include a claimed Healer whose account fits the public save but whose role is unverified, a claimed Investigator with an unverified Not suspicious result, a claimed Trailseer with an unverified follow result, and other living players with no publicly established roles. The recently eliminated Illusionist’s revealed role confirms one wolf is gone, but the side of the player whose role was concealed on Night 1 remains unknown.

lessons.why: Claimed investigator just publicly saved by the healer and the SK must pick a night target: the same decision; the Do (aim at a different, unprotected player) was applied.
lessons.situation: A trusted claimed investigator, already confirmed by a wolf flip and publicly saved by the healer the previous night, is the town's obvious leader. The lone killer must pick a night target among several town power roles while the healer is known to be alive. Information landscape: Information-rich. A wolf flip corroborates the investigator, and the Game Master has announced a healer save on that exact player. Voting records and role claims are public, so the healer's likely pattern is visible. Stakes: Few players remain, so each wasted night lets the town hold its voting majority and reach a vote against you. A failed kill costs a whole night of progress toward the point where at most one other player remains. Forward exposure: The kill is a secret night action that reveals nothing about you if it succeeds, and a failed kill only shows a healer save. Choosing a different target is fully reversible each night, while repeating an obvious target commits you to another probable save. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator is the likely protection target. The alternatives are the claimed sentinel, other unconfirmed power roles, and quiet townies whose roles are unconfirmed and who are less likely to be guarded. Priority is judged on role value and on how predictable the healer's protection is, not on how loud a player is.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other town leader was just publicly saved by the healer, or just outed a wolf and is the obvious protection target, aim the night kill at a different high-value or quiet player the healer is unlikely to cover. This could be the claimed sentinel or another unprotected power role. The healer cannot protect the same player as the obvious pick and also everyone else, and a failed kill only reconfirms the healer and keeps the town bloc intact.

lessons.why: Needs an investigator who cleared the SK and singled out a suspect; none here.
lessons.situation: After a mid-game day vote that ended in abstain or an indecisive result, a claimed Investigator has singled out a suspect. The Investigator's result on you is favorable, so you are not suspected. Wolves are still alive and the room is split. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a voting record, and at least one Investigator result that clears you. All of it is unverified except revealed deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several players left, so one kill does not decide the game. Removing a wolf shrinks the pack and keeps town attention off you, while a misread victim leaves you exposed in the next vote. Forward exposure: The kill shows an active lone killer but not who it is, and it cannot be undone. If the victim is a wolf, it boosts the Investigator's credibility and your clearance. If the victim is a lone accuser, the revealed role and the earlier vote can cast you as retaliating. Target landscape: The player the claimed Investigator targeted, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claiming information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). The first has the strongest evidence basis, since it rests on a claimed check and a vote. A lone accuser who voted against you is a behavioral target only.
lessons.action: On a night after a vote, if a claimed Investigator has publicly singled out and voted against a specific player and has already cleared you, stab that player. A wolf death confirms the Investigator's credibility and keeps the room focused on the surviving wolf instead of you. If that player is instead a lone accuser who voted against you, weigh the retaliation read before stabbing.

lessons.why: Opening-night blind kill; this is night 3.
lessons.situation: Opening night of a ten-player game. Nobody has spoken a read, no one has died, and you must choose a first victim blind while wolves also kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wills, no voting record, no claims and no night results. Stakes: Early game with a full table, so no single kill is decisive. The risk is being named by a Sentinel who watched the victim, but with nine candidates the chance of that is modest. Killing a power role such as Sentinel or Vigilante meaningfully weakens town. Forward exposure: The visit cannot be taken back. A Sentinel watching the victim would see your name, and the morning report shows an active lone killer. The wolves' own kill makes two bodies, which muddies attribution. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all quiet, with no claims, no behavioral reads and no voting record. Any of them could be an information role, protected, or watched. The choice rests on nothing but a guess.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, votes or reads, accept that any visit can be seen and stab one quiet, non-claiming player to start the body count. Do not spend effort hunting for a perfect target, because no information exists to separate them. Either outcome is acceptable: a town power role dies, or the kill gives the room a second killer to chase.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is substantially aligned against you: all three other living players have accused you or stated they are voting for you. The stated case combines the Suspicious result with the unresolved contradiction between the Healer claims; absence of a public save does not resolve that contradiction.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four players are alive, and the leading evil faction is two eliminations from winning at worst for the town, because a concealed body’s side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this vote is a swing decision with potentially immediate endgame consequences.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Maintaining the Healer claim commits you to a role claim that conflicts with another player’s account of protecting the same target on night two. That commitment is already public and cannot be withdrawn without a credibility cost; further explanation could add claims that are difficult to verify.
query_dims.heat_now: High: three of the other living players have accused you and said they are voting for you. Their stated basis is the claimed investigator’s Suspicious result and the incompatible Healer claims; no public event directly confirms either Healer account.
query_dims.information_landscape: There is some discriminating public history: the investigator claimant’s earlier Suspicious result matched a revealed Illusionist, and the Trailseer’s revealed will establishes what the followed player visited, not who visited them. The current Suspicious check and both Healer accounts remain private claims, with no public save or other direct confirmation; evidence is mixed rather than conclusive.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out against the forming consensus: you maintain the Healer claim while acknowledging that the check is evidence against you and that the competing protection claims cannot both be true.
