query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Necromancer and know the night actions you made through dead players’ bodies. Publicly, you have claimed Healer; the village has no confirmation of that claim. The public read includes a Suspicious check from a claimant whose earlier Suspicious result was corroborated by an eliminated player’s revealed role.
query_dims.situation: A player claiming Investigator, whose earlier Suspicious finding was corroborated when the accused was revealed as an Illusionist, now reports a Suspicious check on the claimed Healer. The claimed Healer and another player both say they protected the same target on night two; no save was announced, and the revealed Trailseer’s follow only showed that the target visited no one. The other living players are aligned in accusing the claimed Healer.
query_dims.target_landscape: The immediate vote centers on the claimed Healer with the Suspicious result versus the player making the competing Healer claim. The investigator’s earlier result was strongly supported by a revealed role; the current result is a private claim. Neither Healer claim is publicly confirmed, and the fourth living player has claimed Sigilist without public verification.

lessons.why: Endgame vote at four alive with the necromancer cornered by claimed town players: the Do (vote the other contested claimant rather than counter-accuse the room's side) is what the seat did.
lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

lessons.why: Mid-game nine-alive vote split over a tracker report; this is four alive.
lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

lessons.why: Same 'room converging on me, split with a rival rather than lone-vote the accuser' logic, but the exposure is a Suspicious check and rival healer claim, not an impossible body-derived result.
lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear village consensus. One player weakly favors the agent based on the unexplained Day 2 vote; that player has withdrawn the vote as a strong argument. Others are probing the claimed Investigator’s blocked actions, without converging on a target.

query_dims.heat_now: Low: the agent is the tentative target of a weak vote preference because the revealed Trailseer voted for the agent on Day 2. No one has presented independent evidence against the agent, and the claimed Investigator’s result, if true, is Not suspicious.

Confirmed facts include the dead Sentinel’s and Trailseer’s roles and wills, the former Illusionist’s revealed role, the healer save on the claimed Investigator, and the public vote records. The Investigator claim and its results are not independently verified; the body concealed on Night 1 remains unknown, and there is no confirmed current alignment result.
query_dims.my_position: Under mild pressure but not a settled majority target; the agent has not advanced a competing elimination case in today’s discussion.
query_dims.situation: With five alive, the village is trying to choose an elimination despite little actionable information: a claimed Investigator reports two consecutive roleblocks and one earlier Not-suspicious result on the agent, while the only stated case against the agent is the revealed Trailseer’s unexplained Day 2 vote. The former Illusionist was eliminated, but a wolf and possibly the lone killer remain.
query_dims.target_landscape: The live elimination discussion centers weakly on the player who favored eliminating the agent on Day 2, based only on that vote; the claimed Investigator says that player read Not suspicious, which rules out wolf suspicion if true but does not exclude the lone killer. The claimed Investigator’s two blocked checks are unverified. No other clear candidate is established.

lessons.why: Requires four alive, the serial killer dead and the speculator's Town pick made; here five alive, the SK may be alive.
lessons.situation: Final-wolf vote at four alive: the village must eliminate the last wolf now or face parity at night, and the Speculator is one of the two unverified players. Information landscape: Information-rich: the dead Investigator's will clears one player, the Sigilist's abilities are logged and spent, and the lone killer is confirmed dead. Stakes: Eliminating the last wolf wins immediately for Town and for a Town pick, while a miss leaves three alive with parity at night. Consensus: Two confirmed Town players treat the vote as a choice between the two unverified players and are open to a clear case. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the cleared players. Heat: Exposed: the remaining suspect openly pushes to eliminate the agent based on a quiet record, and the confirmed Town players see it as a binary choice. Target landscape: Two unverified players, the Speculator and one suspect who survived earlier scrutiny, among four alive. The other two are cleared or confirmed Town, by a dead Investigator's will and spent, logged abilities. The suspect's push on the Speculator is behavioral, while the confirmed Town players are the deciding votes.
lessons.action: When four are alive, one wolf remains, and the Speculator has picked Town, join the cleared Town players in eliminating the one unverified suspect rather than the other. Ignore the suspect's counter-accusation of you when it rests only on a quiet record, because eliminating the last wolf ends the game with a Town win and your pick wins.

lessons.why: Requires four alive, one wolf left and the SK dead; not this board.
lessons.situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.
lessons.action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.

lessons.why: Late-game vote where the speculator is mildly accused, but it is written for four alive with one step from evil parity; five alive here.
lessons.situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.
lessons.action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.

lessons.situation: The speculator has already picked a side (Town) and sits in a split or deadlocked day vote where its single vote can decide a tie or prevent a bad elimination of a claimed Town role. Both wolves and a lone killer may still be alive. Information landscape: Moderate and muddled: night kills, a hidden role, conflicting role claims and night-result claims, but no confirmed wolf or killer. Mostly unverified claims plus voting records. Stakes: With about six players alive and two killing factions active, one vote can decide an elimination or block a Town loss. A mistaken Town elimination moves evil toward parity and weakens the Town side the speculator picked. Consensus: The village is scattered or split into near-equal camps with no single dominant target; the push is based on muddled claims and behavioral reads. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none; nobody has directed accusations at the speculator, and its speech has been neutral. Target landscape: Several candidates split the room: claimed Town power roles (healer, trailseer, sigilist, vigilante) versus an unconfirmed quiet or counter-accusing player. The evidence is partly claims and conflicting timelines, partly behavior and past votes, with no confirmed wolf.
lessons.action: When you have already picked Town and the day vote is split among several candidates, cast your vote sincerely on the unconfirmed player whose behavior or claims look most evil. Prefer the candidate whose claims conflict with other players' reports over a claimed Town power role. Your vote can swing a split or tie, so use it to stop a Town-aligned elimination and to remove the likeliest killer, which keeps Town the winning side you picked.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive. The leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown; nevertheless, the board can end within one more elimination at worst for the town. The pick’s end-of-game effect is unclear until the winning side is known; choosing now locks in that side, while dying unpicked loses.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information is mixed but incomplete: the Illusionist’s elimination is system-confirmed, and the public record confirms a Serial Killer attack was stopped by a healer save. The first night’s victim remains role-concealed; remaining role claims and night accounts are not independently verified, and there is no public evidence establishing the current count or identity of the surviving evil roles.
query_dims.situation: After the village unanimously eliminated a player revealed as the Illusionist, the board has fewer known wolves but still includes an unresolved concealed death and an unverified claim to be the Investigator. You face the one-time choice of which side you expect to win while the surviving evil balance and the concealed player’s side remain uncertain; choosing a side only helps if that side wins, while delaying risks dying before picking.
query_dims.target_landscape: Your one-time pick is still unspent; the candidates are Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or yourself. The eliminated player was revealed as an Illusionist, but the other concealed night-death’s side remains unknown, and no public evidence identifies the surviving members of any side. The pick is announced without revealing who made it; dying before choosing means you lose.

lessons.why: Same decision (pick now or hold) on night 3 right after a confirmed wolf elimination with a healer save public; the Do asks whether killers remain active, which is the live question.
lessons.situation: Night 3 after Town's day vote eliminated a confirmed wolf or lone killer, with healer saves publicly verified. Town holds a large majority, but some killers remain. Past observations show the Town pick won when Town stayed disciplined and lost when Town later mis-eliminated its own power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: system-confirmed evil role reveals, a validated investigator claim, and announced healer saves. The remaining unknown is whether a wolf or killer is still hidden and how well Town will play. Stakes: Town leads, but a few mis-votes or kills could still flip the game, so the pick is only as good as Town's later play. Picking now removes the risk of dying unpicked, but it ties your win to Town's survival and avoiding errors. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self. After a confirmed evil elimination Town looks dominant, with validated investigator or healer claims and a numerical majority. Evil still has a wolf and possibly an unknown lone killer, and Town's later errors can still erase that lead.
lessons.action: Once the day vote has system-confirmed an evil elimination and the surviving power-role claims are validated, make the pick on that night instead of waiting longer. Choose Town only if the lone killer is confirmed gone or Town clearly outnumbers a single remaining wolf; if killers are still active with an uncertain Town lead, keep holding until one side is clearly ahead, unless you are likely to be killed that night.

lessons.why: Early nights 1-2 with all ten alive; this is night 3 with seven alive.

The speculator is still unpicked and has not been targeted. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil eliminations, only unverified claims and concealed or ambiguous bodies, and no momentum signal for any faction. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is no immediate pressure to lock in. The only cost of waiting is the risk of dying unpicked, which is low on night 1 and rises as killers act. Holding costs little and keeps the option open for an informed pick later. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self, or keep holding. All ten players are alive with no confirmed roles and no tested claims. Any pick would be a pure guess on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On nights 1-2, while no evil role has been confirmed eliminated and no claim has been tested, keep the one-time pick unspent. Reassess each night, and commit as soon as board evidence clearly favors one side or you suspect you are likely to be killed. Dying unpicked is a loss, but an uninformed early lock-in has no advantage, and the pick cannot be changed once made.

The village abstained on day 2 with one lone accusation (player_9 against player_8) and no claims yet. The board is information-starved, and the day 2 vote suggests the living players are not converging on any target. Dying unpicked would be a loss for me, so the timing of my single pick is the live decision, with the board still too unclear to tell which side is trending.

Candidates are all nine other living players, none with a public role claim or public evidence; the sole public signal is player_9's lone accusation of player_8, which rests on no shown evidence. Dying unpicked is a loss, but an uninformed early lock-in has no advantage, and the pick cannot be changed once made.

Stakes: Town leads, but a few mis-votes or kills could still flip the game, so the pick is only as good as Town's later play. Choose Town only if the lone killer is confirmed gone or Town clearly outnumbers a single remaining wolf; if killers are still active with an uncertain Town lead, keep holding until one side is clearly ahead, unless you are likely to be killed that night.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is unsettled and fragmented, with no shared read; discussion is centered on demanding that player_5 name a role, and no coalition has formed.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a wrong vote is recoverable but costly, and no single vote or kill can end the game this day.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible claim about my night or any push against another player commits me to a checkable account; a Sentinel or Trailseer naming me would turn the visit into a public test, and a denial would be hard to reverse.
query_dims.heat_now: Low to moderate: player_5 has drawn several pointed demands and a light low-confidence vote lean from player_10, but I have not been named by anyone with a result.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no verified night results, no revealed Town wills beyond role reveals, and only claims about blocks and unnamed roles.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out from any forming consensus, since none exists yet; I am engaging with checkable points to avoid being the passive default vote.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the serial killer, I privately know I killed player_2 on night 1, while the public record shows only that a speculator was stabbed by the serial killer; the village now knows the killer is alive and unnamed, and I have publicly said nothing about my own night, which is the gap I must keep hidden.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 after a night in which a speculator was killed by the serial killer and a trailseer died to the wolves, with a blocked player_5 refusing to name their role while several players press for a vote on that basis.
query_dims.target_landscape: Eight alive, all unclaimed on the public record except player_5 who says a night role was blocked without naming it; the accusations so far rest on behavior and unverified blocked-role claims rather than any result.

lessons.why: Needs a sentinel/trailseer result already placing the SK at the night-1 victim's door; nobody has accused the SK.
lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after Night 1. A Sentinel or Trailseer reported seeing the Serial Killer visit the person who died to the lone-killer kill. I deflected with a fake claim or a denial, and the table is piling onto me. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Night 1 body and role reveal are confirmed, and an investigative visit report ties me to the victim. There are one or two other claimed night results, and my counter-story is unverified. Stakes: I am the lone killer and can only be removed by a daytime vote. Being voted out ends my game with many players still alive, so surviving this vote is the whole objective. One vote cannot change the outcome by itself, but a lone vote on the accuser adds nothing to my survival. Consensus: Near-unanimous against me. Town and wolves both treat the visit report as a hard lead, and only a neutral abstains or sits out. My position: Holding out alone against a forming bloc of six or more votes. Heat: Maximum. A claimed watch or follow result places me at the exact victim of the Night 1 kill, and both Town and wolves see me as the obvious vote. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser or a counter-claimant locks me into a one-for-one duel with a credible Town info or power role, which I cannot reverse once votes are public. Voting for a different rival suspect commits me to less and lets me move along with other voters. Target landscape: Three kinds of candidate: me, the accuser (a Sentinel or Trailseer whose report fits the Night 1 death), and a rival suspect named by another result (for example someone tracked visiting a wolf victim or the Investigator). The accuser's report matches the body, while the rival's evidence is thinner but still gives voters another name. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly the Sentinel's or Trailseer's report places me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim has not held.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer result has put you at the victim's door and the room is lining up on you, cast your vote on the one rival suspect with competing evidence that other voters might join. Do not cast a lone vote on your accuser, and do not defend a fake claim by attacking a credible info role. Voters spread across suspects, or abstaining, can deny anyone the plurality, and a tie or abstain majority means no one is eliminated. Your night kill is the only way you win, so surviving the vote matters more than winning the argument.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single night or vote can end the game; the board is far from decisive, which means a watch spent early is recoverable but each of my two watches is a finite resource that cannot be reloaded.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no night results, no claims, no recorded discussion. The only public data is the day 2 vote record and the day 1 quiet night. Any watch is the first real evidence on the board.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 ended in an abstain: the village voted to abstain with one lone accusation against a single player that nobody joined, and no claims or discussion have been recorded. As the Sentinel, I hold both watches unspent and must decide whether to spend one tonight on a player who is a likely victim or a suspect, knowing that a watch shows who visited that player and never reveals my own visit.
query_dims.target_landscape: Nine living players with no public role claims and no night results yet; the only public action so far is one vote from a player against another on day 2 that drew no support, and the village abstained. Everyone's role status is unverified, so candidates rest on no evidence beyond silence and one lone accusation.

lessons.why: Target-selection advice (watch a door likely to be visited, not a hostile or quiet one) transfers, but the lesson is for the last watch and this seat holds both.
lessons.situation: Mid-game, with the first watch already spent and one watch left. The Sentinel is deciding whether to use it on a personal adversary or hold it for a higher-value door. Every watch is a visit, and the Sentinel is not told of its own visit. Information landscape: Still thin: the Night 1 result is the main hard fact, plus a few public claims and one vote record. There are no confirmed wolf identities, so targeting rests on likely attack paths and not on proof. Stakes: The last watch is the Sentinel's final hard evidence, and once it is spent the role has nothing left to do at night. Spending it on a low-traffic door gave nothing in the cluster, so a likely-attack target improves the chance of a usable visitor list. Target landscape: A handful of living players: a prominent claimed or confirmed Town role, a player who has accused you, and quiet unverified players. Favor the one most likely to be attacked or visited, based on public claims or revealed roles, over one picked because they are hostile to you.
lessons.action: Save the last watch for a night when you can name a door that is likely to be attacked or visited, such as a prominent claimed role or a player the wolves or killer plausibly want dead. A watch on a vocal accuser or a quiet bystander tends to return a zero-visitor result, and a watch is spent whether or not it shows anything.

lessons.why: Night 1/2 blind watch, no claims, no deaths, two watches in hand: the same decision; spend one on a quiet unclaimed player and keep the other (followed).
lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. The Sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two watches blind or hold both. The Night 1 kill, a possible roleblock and the lone killer's attack can all land the same night, so the result may be lost, show nothing, or catch a key visitor. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no night results, no claims and no voting record. Only opening-round chatter exists. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive, so one blind watch is a cheap bet. Results across the cluster varied: zero visitors, a visit from the healer or trailseer, a multi-visitor cluster, and the serial killer caught at the door. The cost is that the Sentinel itself may be killed or blocked that night and the result lost, so only one of the two charges should be committed. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes or role flips. Every door is equally unknown, so choose a quiet, unpressured player on pure behavior, since there is no evidence to separate them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims, deaths or reads, spend one of the two watches on a quiet, unclaimed player and keep the second for later. A watch can catch the killer's visit or reveal who is acting at night, and the visitor list is the only hard evidence a Sentinel can gather before Day 2. Pick a target the pack or the lone killer might plausibly hit, not a loud player who is likely to draw heat.

lessons.why: Late-midgame with conflicting claims and one watch left; none of that exists.
lessons.situation: Late-midgame night after an abstain or tied vote. Conflicting role claims are on the board and you hold one watch left. You must decide whose door to watch, knowing results come only from visitors to that player. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, vote records and some prior night results, but nothing is verified. Alignments of the candidates are unconfirmed, and visit data exists only for whoever you watch. Stakes: Town can still afford a mistake, but this is the last watch, so a wasted use leaves no visitor-tracking for the rest of the game. A watch that exposes a visit pattern or kill trace can settle a claim fight before wolves reach parity. Target landscape: The choice is between a contested claimant (e.g. counter-claimed investigator or sigilist) under heavy suspicion, the obvious wolf-priority targets (claimed investigator, healer, trailseer), a quiet player from a tied vote, or an investigator-cleared player. The claim conflicts are public, but none of the candidates is verified. Only the contested claimant or the likely kill target is likely to draw visits.
lessons.action: With your last watch, pick the player most likely to receive a visit tonight. That means a contested or heavily accused claimant whose claim other roles can verify or attack, or the likely wolf kill target. A watch on a quiet suspect or an already-cleared player usually returns "no visitors", because attackers visit their victims, not themselves.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is leaning toward eliminating you: the claimed Sigilist and unclaimed player openly support that vote, and the Investigator has framed you as a likely target. The Healer claim dispute and absence of an explicit Investigator vote leave the alignment short of confirmed unanimity.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: With four alive, it is two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so this vote is a swing decision with an immediate endgame risk.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Maintaining the Healer claim and directing attention toward the unclaimed player commits you to a public identity and accusation that are difficult to retract. Revealing your Necromancer role or the concealed victim’s role would expose private information and your earlier attacks; the current Healer claim has not disclosed that information.
query_dims.heat_now: High: the claimed Investigator reports a Suspicious read on you, and the claimed Sigilist and unclaimed player are explicitly voting for you. The Investigator has credibility from the earlier read that matched the revealed Illusionist.
query_dims.information_landscape: There is substantial public mechanical evidence: the Illusionist and Vigilante were revealed, the Trailseer’s will was read, and two deaths were announced as reanimated attacks. The concealed night-2 victim’s role is unavailable publicly. Current role and result claims, including the competing protection accounts and the new Suspicious read, are not independently verified; the earlier Investigator claim has strong support from the Illusionist reveal.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out against the forming vote against you; you maintain the Healer claim and point to the unclaimed player’s account as a competing issue.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Necromancer: you attacked through the revealed Illusionist’s body on night 2, killing the player whose role was concealed, and through the revealed Vigilante’s body on night 3, killing the Trailseer. Publicly, the village knows those deaths were made by reanimated abilities, but the night-2 victim’s role remains concealed. The claimed Investigator’s Suspicious read on you and the competing Healer claims are public claims, not verified role facts.
query_dims.situation: At four alive, a claimed Investigator’s Suspicious result puts the Healer claimant under strong elimination pressure, while a second player disputes the Healer’s account of a night-2 protection. The conflict is especially consequential because two prior deaths were publicly attributed to reanimated attacks, but the private identity of the Necromancer and the concealed night-2 victim’s role remain unknown to the village.
query_dims.target_landscape: The immediate vote landscape centers on you, whom a claimed Investigator says read Suspicious and who claims Healer; the Investigator claimant, whose earlier Suspicious result against the revealed Illusionist has strong public support; a player claiming Sigilist without public confirmation; and an unclaimed player who says they protected the Investigator on night 2. The claimed Healer’s night-2 protection claim conflicts with that last account, but neither protection claim has public confirmation.

lessons.why: The seat is pressed at four alive and told to give a specific role claim; it already holds a Healer claim, so the advice helps defend the claim but 'stalling' is not the problem (and the lesson says pick an unused town role, which the contested Healer is not).
lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Two town power roles have claimed, their results back each other up, and the necromancer is pushed to state a role or be voted out. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed roles of the dead, public vote history, claimed night results and spent abilities leave very little room to bluff. Stakes: One elimination vote decides the game. If the necromancer is voted out it loses outright, and a failed claim leaves no later day to repair it. Consensus: The few remaining players are converging on a bloc of cross-verifying town claims, with the unclaimed or contradicted player as the obvious elimination. My position: Holding out alone against a forming two-player bloc. Heat: High to critical. Claimed town roles are demanding my claim, or I am the odd player out after their results cleared each other. Forward exposure: A role claim commits me to a night history that the claimed town roles can check against their own results and spent abilities. A claim that fails the check is nearly irreversible, but staying silent is already read as guilt in a small endgame. Target landscape: The claimed power roles (vigilante, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist) and any unclaimed player. Their claims are partly corroborated by revealed deaths and spent abilities, so each can be tested against the record. Public vs private: Privately a lone killer who has been attacking through a dead player's body, while publicly needing to pass as an ordinary town power role under direct claim demands.
lessons.action: When pressed to claim at the final three or four, give a specific role claim instead of stalling. Pick a still-living town role that no revealed death or other claim has already used, and tell a night story that fits every claimed result and the visit rules. For example, a Sentinel is never told of its own watch, and a Trailseer's follow is a visit others can cross-check.

lessons.why: Needs a sentinel report that has already confirmed a necromancer; none has.
lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

lessons.why: A standing do-not-quote-body-derived-results constraint applies to a necromancer who is speaking, but the seat has no result it needs to quote.
lessons.situation: After a night attack or save, the necromancer holds results gathered through a dead town role and wants to redirect suspicion onto the visitors. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: the dead role's death is on record, so the room can tell which living roles could have produced such a result. Stakes: My win needs the room kept off me for many more days, so losing the cover of a hidden identity costs far more than anything the leaked result could gain. Consensus: The village is unsettled after a night attack and save, with no fixed target. The living roles are still working out what the visits mean. My position: Not yet in conflict, but I would be holding out alone if I spoke up with the hidden result. Heat: Zero before sharing. It would jump to universal accusation if I quoted the body-derived result. Forward exposure: Stating a result that only the dead role could have produced points straight at the necromancer, and the room cannot unsee it. A read built on public evidence can be dropped without penalty. Target landscape: The players whose visits I learned about (claimed healer, other claimants) are the targets, but the only support is a hidden source. Public evidence such as claim overlaps is available to use instead. Public vs private: Privately I hold a night result obtained through a dead role, such as who visited a door. Publicly, no living player holds that role, so quoting the result shows I am the necromancer.
lessons.action: If a dead player's ability gave you night information, steer suspicion only through reasons the room can see: public claims, votes, and contradictions between players. Do not quote the body-derived result, such as sentinel visitor names, when no living role could explain how you got it. Only a living claimed role could plausibly share such a result, and you cannot back that claim.

lessons.situation: A claimed information role accuses a player based on a night result, the accused disputes it, and the necromancer is tempted to step in and challenge the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead role with a concealed role, a specific claimed tracking report, and mechanical counter-claims from the accused. All of it is still unverified. Stakes: The board has many living players, so every public commitment matters for the endgame. A defense that turns out wrong leaves a damaging record, while a vote with the majority costs nothing. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on the accused, driven by a concrete claimed report that the claimant has already defended against objections. My position: Holding out, if I contest the lead. Better to move to the majority side. Heat: Low to none. Attention is on the accused player and the claimant, not on me. Forward exposure: Publicly challenging a claimed information lead puts my name on the record against it, and that record cannot be undone if the target flips evil. Joining the consensus costs little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: The accused player denies the charge and argues mechanics. The claimed trailseer, or other power-role claimant, gives a specific sighting. The evidence for the claimant is stronger than the accused's counter-argument. Public vs private: Publicly the room is split between an accused player and a claimed power role with a concrete report. Privately I am the lone killer with no stake in either side's survival, so I can choose the least risky alignment.
lessons.action: When a living claimant's report (for example a trailseer's) already has the room converging on an accused player, go along with that lead and voice a short read that matches it. If you doubt the report, ask a neutral question about it rather than staking your name on a mechanics rebuttal. The accused may flip, and a record of defending them marks you as their ally.

lessons.situation: Final three or four players. I must choose whom to push, either the pair that verifies each other or the one claimant whose story stands alone. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed results can be cross-checked against spent abilities, revealed deaths and visit mechanics. Stakes: With so few players, one vote swings the game. A failed push at a verified player hands the bloc a unanimous vote against me. Consensus: The remaining town claims align with each other on the basis of verified results and leave me as the outlier. My position: Trying to swing the votes of a bloc that already trusts each other. Heat: High. My earlier claim or evasion has drawn suspicion, and the table is looking for the odd player out. Forward exposure: Attacking a cross-verified player forces a binary vote against me if the attack fails, and it cannot be taken back. Targeting an uncorroborated claim keeps a fallback and splits the room. Target landscape: A cross-verified pair of town roles versus an unverified claimant, a spent claimant, or the unclaimed player. The evidence is the claimed results against the visit record, not tone. Public vs private: I know which claims are false and which are genuine, but publicly I must present myself as a town member reasoning from the record. Attacking a verified claim contradicts what the table has already confirmed.
lessons.action: In the endgame, aim the accusation at the claimant whose story the record cannot corroborate, such as a vigilante who held bullets or a claim with no verifying partner. Do not attack a pair whose night results already cross-verify. If two claims check each other out, give your own consistent claim and call for a vote on the unverified player or the unclaimed player.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room shows a tentative lean toward voting for one of the two reported visitors, with two speakers explicitly favoring that candidate. The other visitor is acknowledged as sharing the reported visit and vote against the Sigilist; there is no settled consensus.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive and three eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; this decision does not decide the game with one elimination, so its immediate outcome is consequential but not an immediate parity flip.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible defense of either visitor could align you with them and draw attention to your position; naming the pack's attack or claiming wolf-related knowledge would expose information only the pack has. You have made no public night-action claim, so staying unclaimed preserves that separation; no visible move is committed yet.
query_dims.heat_now: No one has publicly accused or scrutinized you in today's discussion; your role and night actions remain unclaimed.
query_dims.information_landscape: Public evidence includes the revealed roles of the Investigator, Trailseer, and Sigilist; the announced wolf attack and healer save; a Sentinel claim and visitor report; and the public day-two votes. The visitor report is unverified and does not identify actions. You privately know the pack's targets and that the saved player was its target, but the room does not know that source-specific information.
query_dims.my_position: You have not publicly stated a position in the current discussion, so you are neither visibly driving nor holding out from its tentative lean.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know the wolves attacked the publicly announced saved player, and that the healer saved them. Publicly, a player claiming Sentinel reports that two visitors went to the player later killed by the Serial Killer; this does not establish either visitor's role or action. Your knowledge of the pack's attack is not public.
query_dims.situation: A player claiming Sentinel reports two visits to the player later revealed as the Sigilist, while the discussion is narrowing toward one of those visitors because of their vote and reported visit. The other visitor points out that the same evidence implicates them too, leaving behavior and shared circumstantial evidence rather than a role-confirming result.
query_dims.target_landscape: The leading vote suggestion is against an unclaimed player who both voted to eliminate the player later revealed as the Sigilist and is named in the Sentinel claimant's visitor report. The other reported visitor also voted to eliminate that Sigilist, so the visit evidence applies to both; neither visit establishes an attack. The player claiming Sentinel has no publicly verified role or result.

lessons.why: Needs a dead wolf partner and a tracking report or shared votes pointing at the seat; the seat is not accused.
lessons.situation: After a night death (concealed body) and a wolf partner or lone killer revealed dead, the village revisits earlier evidence (a tracking report, shared votes with the dead wolf) pointing at me, and my deflections so far have been technical or flattering rather than substantive. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, permanent day-two vote records, and an uncontested dead-player tracking report all sit on the public record. Stakes: Few players remain, so a wrong vote today can end the wolves or hand the game to the remaining killer; losing the last wolf here is effectively losing the game. Consensus: The village is aligned and converging on me, based on permanent vote records and a dead player's uncontested report rather than on mood. My position: Holding out against a majority that has lined up on me. Heat: High to critical: the room has an uncontested record tying me to a wolf, and the wolf partner or lone killer is already dead. Forward exposure: Any defense commits me to a story that the permanent voting record and the dead players' testimony can check; a hollow or evasive one can't be walked back once the room labels it wolf distancing. Target landscape: Me as the carryover suspect, backed by public evidence (tracking report, voting overlap with a revealed dead wolf), versus vague alternative leads with little evidence behind them. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kills, the concealed body and my partner's actions; publicly the room has uncontested records (a tracking report, shared votes with a dead wolf) pointing at me, and I have no sincere answer to them.
lessons.action: When the room is already fixed on public evidence tying you to a wolf act (a tracking report, a shared vote with a dead wolf), answer that specific evidence head-on with a concrete, checkable alternative explanation, and put forward a specific alternative suspect with reasons. Don't spend your turn on technicalities or on praising a town claimant, because a defense that leaves the damaging record unanswered and offers no other lead leaves you as the obvious vote.

lessons.why: Needs the wolf partner revealed and dead; the partner is alive.
lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been revealed and killed. You are pressured over a lone vote against a dead Town player, while a Town player's result (a non-triggering sigil) is available as a defense. Information landscape: Moderate: public voting records and a privately held Town result that can be used to clear you, but no hard role confirmations on the quiet alternative suspect. Stakes: Each vote now decides whether the last wolf survives. Moving even a couple of swing voters off you keeps the wolf team alive into the final few players. Consensus: The village is split. Some players press you over the vote record, while players holding a clearing result and neutral voters are open to another suspect. My position: holding out Heat: High. Players cite your isolated vote against a now-dead player as the basis for suspicion. Forward exposure: Citing a Town player's result ties you to a non-attacking story that you cannot take back, and later tracking evidence could break it. The alternative-suspect push can be adjusted as new information arrives. Target landscape: Candidates are you, under pressure from the vote record, and a quiet player with no confirmed role who was targeted by the dead wolf. Suspicion of the quiet player is behavioral, while the case against you is the vote record. Public vs private: Privately you are an active wolf, but the partner carried the kill that night, so a Town result such as an un-triggered sigil looks exculpatory. The room reads that result as evidence you are not the killer.
lessons.action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Use only what the rules show: the sigil not triggering means only that you did not attack on that night, and it does not clear you of being a wolf. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.

lessons.why: Needs a trailseer report placing the illusionist at a concealed victim's door; none.
lessons.situation: A trailseer claims to have seen the illusionist visit a player who died that night with a hidden role, and the illusionist has to answer in daytime discussion. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed death with a hidden role plus a direct tracking report that matches what the illusionist actually did. Stakes: An elimination of the illusionist here leaves the surviving wolf alone and closer to losing, so avoid a flat denial that the room can disprove. Consensus: The majority takes the tracker's findings at face value; only a couple of players are confused about how concealment affects visits. My position: opposing the forming consensus Heat: Critical; directly accused of visiting a murder victim on the night they died. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits you to calling the trailseer a liar and rules out any later switch to a benign visiting claim. A benign-visit explanation stays open and can be adjusted if the town pushes back. Target landscape: The accused visitor (you) against the single claimed tracker; the town has no competing account of the night, so the report counts as hard eyewitness evidence. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the reported visit is true, because it concealed the body, while publicly it insists it never left home.
lessons.action: When a trailseer or sentinel report places you at the door of a victim whose role was hidden, do not flatly deny the visit. Offer a benign reason for being out that night (for example, a claim of a visiting town role, or that you checked on that player), and stress that the report only shows a visit, not who attacked. Do not claim that illusionist concealment makes the report invalid: if you were not the carrier, your own visit to hide the body is still seen, and a flat denial against a tracker report the town trusts loses you the room.

lessons.situation: A claimed watcher reports a visitor at the dead wolf partner's door, and the accused denies it while the village weighs the two stories. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed dead wolf, a watcher's claim about its visitors, and a supporting investigator result. Stakes: Removing the lone killer is necessary before wolves can win and costs the pack nothing, while staying unscrutinized keeps the illusionist alive for the endgame. Consensus: Town converges on the accused and the vote is nearly unanimous. My position: with majority Heat: None: no one has linked the illusionist to the kill or questioned its behavior. Forward exposure: Backing the watcher commits the illusionist to treating that claimant as credible later, though that is easy to revisit if the watcher is contradicted. Target landscape: The accused visitor, who claims town and denies the visit, versus the claimed watcher whose report is plausible given the dead wolf. The basis is a watch result, not behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows its partner was killed by an outside night killer, so the accused visitor is probably that killer, and the public read matches this.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is already dead and a claimed sentinel or other watcher accuses an outside killer, back the watcher's report and press the accused to explain their visit. This helps the town remove the lone killer without any suspicion falling on you. Keep your wording the same as the rest of the village's.

lessons.situation: A sentinel or trailseer publicly lists the illusionist among several visitors to one player, creating a risk of an investigation trap. Information landscape: Fairly rich in visit data from several claimed watchers, but nothing is verified by deaths and the data converges on an odd target. Stakes: A single named-visitor result could expose the pack on day 2; defusing it keeps both wolves alive and the vote at abstain. Consensus: The village treats the multi-visit pile-up as a puzzle and has no single suspect, so it leans toward abstaining. My position: with majority Heat: Moderate: explicitly named by a sentinel as a visitor, diluted by other claimants reporting the same visits. Forward exposure: Admitting a visit commits the illusionist to being a visiting role in later claims, and it is only partly reversible. Avoiding a specific role claim keeps flexibility. Target landscape: The quiet visited player and the other visitors defending their own overlapping actions. All are unverified claimants, and the evidence is visit lists rather than behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the visit was the wolf kill or another wolf action, whereas the town sees an inexplicable convergence of visits on one quiet player.
lessons.action: When a claimed watch or tracking result names your partner or you as a visitor, acknowledge only the visit that cannot be disproved. Frame it as a casual check-in and point the room at the strangest part of the data, such as several players visiting the same target. This keeps your claim consistent with the visits other players can report while avoiding a specific role claim.

lessons.situation: A claiming tracker names me as a visitor to the night-one victim while a separate dual-claim conflict dominates the room. Information landscape: Information-rich: two investigative claims with direct visit reports on both night deaths, plus a hard counterclaim. Stakes: A named wolf-side visitor who survives today by deflection but leaves the accusation unresolved; it can return at the next vote and cost a wolf while the pack still needs several eliminations. Consensus: The room is split and distracted by a bigger role-claim dispute, so it can be redirected but has not cleared me. My position: With majority; I am following the room's focus on the other conflict while deflecting from my own accusation. Heat: High; named by a claimed tracker as a visitor to the night victim, though partly diluted by another player caught at a different body. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits me to calling the reporter a liar without any role alibi; it is reversible only by building a story later, and if the reporter survives or is validated it brings me down. Target landscape: The claiming tracker who named me, a rival dispute (conflicting claims of the same role) in the room, and myself; the reports are unverified but the tracker's claim is accurate. Public vs private: Privately I know the report is accurate because I carried out the kill, while publicly the room is split over a different dispute and can be pointed away from me.
lessons.action: When a claimed tracker or watcher reports you at a victim's door, do not rely on a bare denial: pair it with a coherent counter-story, such as a plausible role claim with a believable alibi. Use any competing role conflict in the room to draw attention off yourself, but keep the counter-story ready so the report cannot resurface later.

lessons.situation: A claimed watcher or tracker reports visits to a player who survived or died, and I (a wolf-side illusionist) am among the visitors named or about to be exposed. Information landscape: Information-rich: visit reports, an attack that was thwarted or a body, and several role claims on the table, though none verified. Stakes: Mid-game with a wolf exposed by a visit report; a single failed explanation risks a vote on me, while a convincing cover keeps the wolf pack on course toward parity. Consensus: The room is information-rich and willing to act on visit reports, but has not settled on who is lying; it accepts any claim that plausibly explains the visits. My position: Driving; I set the narrative right after the report by claiming first and redirecting focus. Heat: High; named as a visitor at a sensitive door by a claimed night-information role on the exact night of the event. Forward exposure: A fake role claim locks me in publicly and guarantees a collision if the genuine role-holder is alive; it is hard to retract, but it buys immediate safety and can set up removing the real role-holder. Target landscape: The unverified observer who reported visits, the genuine role-holder whose action matches my claim, and the surviving target; the observer's claim is unverified while my cover story is plausible. Public vs private: Privately I know the visit was a wolf action (kill attempt or ability use), but publicly the visit must be framed as a Town role's action to explain being seen.
lessons.action: When an unverified watcher or follower reports your visit at a victim's or target's door and you are exposed, immediately claim a Town role whose action explains that visit (e.g. Healer protecting the target), and tie it to the night's outcome. If the claim fits the report and the room accepts it, steer the town toward the player who raised the report, and plan the later collision with the real role-holder.

lessons.situation: Early day with several town investigative or tracking roles revealing night results and comparing them. Quiet players are being identified, and the illusionist wolf holds private knowledge of the pack's kill that the public lacks. Information landscape: Mostly claims and tracking logs with no confirmed alignments, so alignment information is thin while movement information is rich enough to cross-check. Stakes: Early game with many town players alive, so no single vote decides the game. Surviving the night without becoming the tracking focus matters more than steering the vote. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around reviewing claims and leaning toward abstaining or questioning quiet players. The basis is claimed night results, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out by saying nothing while the room coordinates claims and compares notes. Heat: Low at the start, but it climbs quickly once claimants point out a player who has not contributed. Forward exposure: Speaking commits me to words that can later be checked against tracking logs. Any slip that references an unannounced event reveals wolf knowledge and cannot be undone. Staying silent is also hard to reverse once I have been named as the silent player. Target landscape: The room has no specific execution target. Claimed investigative and protective roles are cross-referencing visits, and inactive players are the easiest candidates for suspicion, based on behavior rather than evidence. Public vs private: The town is assembling tracking logs and assuming a quiet first night or a mere victim, while I privately know the wolves' kill hit a night-immune target and what each wolf did. The public read has no hint of that unannounced failed kill.
lessons.action: When several town investigative roles are comparing notes on an early day, give a brief, low-content contribution in your own voice. Echo the shared tracking facts or ask a neutral question about a claim, and never mention the unannounced failed kill or the immune target. Total silence invites a call-out and a night of scrutiny from the Sentinel and Trailseer, while a short on-topic remark keeps you out of the 'silent player' bucket without exposing wolf knowledge.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.

lessons.situation: Day two with several town investigative and protective claims surfacing, a night death that flipped information, and the room absorbed in checking one claimant. The illusionist wolf knows about an unannounced immune target. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims, with three town role claims and a dead trailseer's visit reported, but nothing confirms wolf alignment. Stakes: Mid-early game; the pack still has room, but one revealed slip about the immune target would expose a wolf and tilt the count toward town. Consensus: The town is coalescing around abstaining and picking apart one claimant's lack of results, based on claimed night results. My position: Staying out of the main debate and moving with the room, ready to join it. Heat: Low. Reported town information frames me as an innocent subject of night information, and attention sits elsewhere. Forward exposure: Accusing the immune player would require explaining how I know about an unannounced failed kill, instantly revealing wolf knowledge and being irreversible. A mild on-topic comment commits me to little and can be revised later. Target landscape: The room is scrutinizing a newly claimed role with thin results and accepting a cleared target. The immune player is publicly unverified and not under pressure. lessons.situation: A claimed investigator reports a suspicious result on the illusionist, or counter-claims against a real investigator, and the village treats it as a binary choice that favors the accuser. Information landscape: Information-rich: a specific investigative report, town deductions that verify it, and sometimes an announced save, leaving little room for an unsupported denial. Stakes: Losing the illusionist halves the wolf pack and leaves the partner alone against a village that has already shown it can work out the mechanics, so the day's speech should protect the partner's standing first. Consensus: Near-unanimous and fast: town members are checking the mechanics themselves and agree that only a wolf fits the result. Naming an alternative target keeps a fallback and keeps your partner out of the fight. Target landscape: The accuser is a lone claimed information role with no rival claimant. The only other candidates are quiet or unclaimed players, and the accuser's report is hard evidence while your counter is behavioral. lessons.action: When a claimed investigator names you suspicious and the room can verify that only a wolf could read that way, skip the "fabricated check" argument and the counter-claim. Instead pair a brief, calm denial with a concrete alternative suspect (an unexplained claimant, a quiet player, a vote pattern), and say nothing that ties or defends your partner. If the room is still locked on you, spend your remaining speech turns pulling suspicion off your partner and onto that alternative rather than winning the duel.

lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. lessons.why: Early day 2 abstention; not the board.

It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.why: A claimed investigator has a Suspicious result on the illusionist and calls for a vote; the Do (vote the accuser, keep the partner with the majority, push for a close split if the evidence is only a claim) was followed.
lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. lessons.situation: The agent is the illusionist on a final day vote. A dead partner or a night trace links the agent to the wolf team, and the village is converging on eliminating the agent. Target landscape: The choices are the agent's own wagon, the vocal accuser (an investigator or trailseer-type claimant), and a quieter or claimed player with few votes. The case against the agent rests on hard evidence (vote record, dead-role reveal, tracking report). The accuser is backed by the room, so attacking the accuser gains nothing. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the dead partner, the concealed kill, and the accuser's evidence are all real. Publicly the town reads the linked vote record or tracking trace as decisive proof of guilt.
lessons.action: When the room has locked onto you from a vote record or a dead teammate's trace, put your ballot on the same alternate target your living wolf partner is using, preferably one who already has some votes. Do not cast a lone retaliatory vote on the loudest accuser. Only a combined bloc on one plausible alternative can split the room or force a tie, which means no elimination. If you are the last wolf, put your vote on the non-accuser who already has traction.

Consensus: The room is information-rich and willing to act on visit reports, but has not settled on who is lying; it accepts any claim that plausibly explains the visits. My position: Driving; I set the narrative right after the report by claiming first and redirecting focus. Heat: High; named as a visitor at a sensitive door by a claimed night-information role on the exact night of the event. Forward exposure: A fake role claim locks me in publicly and guarantees a collision if the genuine role-holder is alive; it is hard to retract, but it buys immediate safety and can set up removing the real role-holder. Target landscape: The unverified observer who reported visits, the genuine role-holder whose action matches my claim, and the surviving target; the observer's claim is unverified while my cover story is plausible. Public vs private: Privately I know the visit was a wolf action (kill attempt or ability use), but publicly the visit must be framed as a Town role's action to explain being seen.

If the claim fits the report and the room accepts it, steer the town toward the player who raised the report, and plan the later collision with the real role-holder.

Target landscape: The accused visitor, who claims town and denies the visit, versus the claimed watcher whose report is plausible given the dead wolf. The basis is a watch result, not behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows its partner was killed by an outside night killer, so the accused visitor is probably that killer, and the public read matches this.

This helps the town remove the lone killer without any suspicion falling on you. Keep your wording the same as the rest of the village's.

Naming an alternative target keeps a fallback and keeps your partner out of the fight. Target landscape: The accuser is a lone claimed information role with no rival claimant. The only other candidates are quiet or unclaimed players, and the accuser's report is hard evidence while your counter is behavioral. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the accusing investigator's check is accurate, while publicly the only option offered is to call it false, which the room can test against the rules.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator names you suspicious and the room can verify that only a wolf could read that way, skip the "fabricated check" argument and the counter-claim. Instead pair a brief, calm denial with a concrete alternative suspect (an unexplained claimant, a quiet player, a vote pattern), and say nothing that ties or defends your partner. If the room is still locked on you, spend your remaining speech turns pulling suspicion off your partner and onto that alternative rather than winning the duel.

lessons.situation: A trailseer claims to have seen the illusionist visit a player who died that night with a hidden role, and the illusionist has to answer in daytime discussion. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed death with a hidden role plus a direct tracking report that matches what the illusionist actually did. Stakes: An elimination of the illusionist here leaves the surviving wolf alone and closer to losing, so avoid a flat denial that the room can disprove. Consensus: The majority takes the tracker's findings at face value; only a couple of players are confused about how concealment affects visits. My position: opposing the forming consensus Heat: Critical; directly accused of visiting a murder victim on the night they died. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits you to calling the trailseer a liar and rules out any later switch to a benign visiting claim. A benign-visit explanation stays open and can be adjusted if the town pushes back. Target landscape: The accused visitor (you) against the single claimed tracker; the town has no competing account of the night, so the report counts as hard eyewitness evidence. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the reported visit is true, because it concealed the body, while publicly it insists it never left home.
lessons.action: When a trailseer or sentinel report places you at the door of a victim whose role was hidden, do not flatly deny the visit. Offer a benign reason for being out that night (for example, a claim of a visiting town role, or that you checked on that player), and stress that the report only shows a visit, not who attacked. Do not claim that illusionist concealment makes the report invalid: if you were not the carrier, your own visit to hide the body is still seen, and a flat denial against a tracker report the town trusts loses you the room.

lessons.situation: A sentinel or trailseer publicly lists the illusionist among several visitors to one player, creating a risk of an investigation trap. Information landscape: Fairly rich in visit data from several claimed watchers, but nothing is verified by deaths and the data converges on an odd target. Stakes: A single named-visitor result could expose the pack on day 2; defusing it keeps both wolves alive and the vote at abstain. Consensus: The village treats the multi-visit pile-up as a puzzle and has no single suspect, so it leans toward abstaining.
