My position: with majority Heat: Moderate: explicitly named by a sentinel as a visitor, diluted by other claimants reporting the same visits. Forward exposure: Admitting a visit commits the illusionist to being a visiting role in later claims, and it is only partly reversible. Avoiding a specific role claim keeps flexibility. Target landscape: The quiet visited player and the other visitors defending their own overlapping actions. All are unverified claimants, and the evidence is visit lists rather than behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the visit was the wolf kill or another wolf action, whereas the town sees an inexplicable convergence of visits on one quiet player.
lessons.action: When a claimed watch or tracking result names your partner or you as a visitor, acknowledge only the visit that cannot be disproved. Frame it as a casual check-in and point the room at the strangest part of the data, such as several players visiting the same target. This keeps your claim consistent with the visits other players can report while avoiding a specific role claim.

lessons.situation: A claiming tracker names me as a visitor to the night-one victim while a separate dual-claim conflict dominates the room. Information landscape: Information-rich: two investigative claims with direct visit reports on both night deaths, plus a hard counterclaim. Stakes: A named wolf-side visitor who survives today by deflection but leaves the accusation unresolved; it can return at the next vote and cost a wolf while the pack still needs several eliminations. Consensus: The room is split and distracted by a bigger role-claim dispute, so it can be redirected but has not cleared me. My position: With majority; I am following the room's focus on the other conflict while deflecting from my own accusation. Heat: High; named by a claimed tracker as a visitor to the night victim, though partly diluted by another player caught at a different body. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits me to calling the reporter a liar without any role alibi; it is reversible only by building a story later, and if the reporter survives or is validated it brings me down. Target landscape: The claiming tracker who named me, a rival dispute (conflicting claims of the same role) in the room, and myself; the reports are unverified but the tracker's claim is accurate. Public vs private: Privately I know the report is accurate because I carried out the kill, while publicly the room is split over a different dispute and can be pointed away from me.
lessons.action: When a claimed tracker or watcher reports you at a victim's door, do not rely on a bare denial: pair it with a coherent counter-story, such as a plausible role claim with a believable alibi. Use any competing role conflict in the room to draw attention off yourself, but keep the counter-story ready so the report cannot resurface later.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the remaining evil faction can win, and the game can end within one more elimination; a wrong lynch now leaves the village one loss from a wolf-side outcome, so the next vote is high-cost.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a firm night result to share. Public evidence is limited to the night 3 record (a player struck by a sigil and killed by a reanimated vigilante, the investigator's day 2 check) and the claims of the living players, which are unverified.
query_dims.situation: Four players remain alive after the day 4 vote eliminated a player revealed as the necromancer. The village is weighing a sigilist claim that is consistent with the night 3 record, while two unclaimed players are being pressed for what they did, and the remaining evil roles are believed to be the illusionist and fortune teller, both still hidden.
query_dims.target_landscape: Three living players: player_1 (abstained both days, no claimed role, no night result), player_9 (claims sigilist, sigil placed on a player who was struck down on night 3, consistent with the record), and player_10 (claims no result, voted to abstain today, pressed others to explain their votes). Public role status: no living player has a confirmed role; player_9's sigil claim is claimed with partial public support, while player_1 and player_10 are unclaimed.

lessons.why: Lone killer is already dead (necromancer voted out), so the 'protect against the lone killer' premise is gone.
lessons.situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.

lessons.why: Same decision (healer picks among claimed power roles after a killer is voted out, one wolf left) but only one claimed role exists and its result is unverified, not the 'verified result' the advice needs.
lessons.situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.
lessons.action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.

lessons.why: Healer protecting a power role the killers want dead is the same decision, but the corroborating evidence it keys on (a validated investigator) is absent.
lessons.situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, after a confirmed wolf elimination. The healer has publicly revealed their role and prior protection and is likely the next kill. A necromancer is also active and attacking through dead bodies. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed illusionist elimination validated the trailseer's report, and the morning announcements show an active necromancer attacking through bodies. Stakes: Late-mid game with few players left, so each save or loss shifts the balance sharply. Keeping a power role alive through a strike matters even though the exposed healer will probably die that night. Target landscape: Other living players, mainly two claimed power roles (a sentinel you previously protected and a trailseer whose report just led to an elimination). Both have public standing, and the choice rests on the attack pattern and prior protection rather than certainty.
lessons.action: When you are publicly exposed and expect to be attacked, spend the night protecting the claimed power role that has shown real value or already drawn an attack, such as a sentinel you protected before while a necromancer is striking through bodies. Keep that player covered on consecutive nights if the attacker's pattern still points at them, because a save blanks the strike and keeps their ability in play even if you die afterward.

lessons.situation: Early night (night 2) after a public information-role claim, with the wolves (and possibly a lone killer) choosing their kill and the town's key information source an obvious target. Information landscape: Mostly unverified claims with few or no confirmed flips or wills, sometimes partly confirmed by a correct elimination; the claimant's visibility is the main evidence, and the healer has no hard read on which claim is real. Stakes: Losing the lead information role this early strips the town of checks before any roles are confirmed, while a save wastes the wolves' kill and keeps the town's lead intact; the board is not yet at parity, so one lost key role hurts but is not decisive. Target landscape: Several claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and quiet unclaimed players; the investigator who cleared the healer or whose check was validated is the most prominent unverified-or-confirmed target, versus a sentinel or trailseer with less impact.
lessons.action: On the night after a claimed investigator, sentinel or other information role has become the town's most visible information source, protect that claimant, since the wolves most likely attack the player who is verified or clearing others. If two claimants compete, protect the one whose results are most useful to the town (an investigator who has cleared you, or one whose check was confirmed by an elimination) over a less-pressing claimant.

lessons.situation: The previous night's protected key claimant was attacked and saved, and the town debates whether the wolves will repeat the attack or hunt elsewhere, possibly with an impostor claiming credit for the save. Information landscape: Information-rich: a public save announcement, an eliminated wolf or necromancer role revealed, and known claims about visitors; the healer knows their own protection record, others only have claims. Stakes: Two consecutive successful saves deny the wolves back-to-back kills, preserving the town's majority and its leading voice; wasting the night on a lower-value target risks losing the key claimant for no gain. Target landscape: The confirmed or leading investigator who just survived an attack, versus other claimants (sigilist, sentinel) and quiet players with no sign of being targeted; the investigator's survival and wolf persistence are the basis, not behavior reads.
lessons.action: If your protected target survived an attack last night and remains the town's key confirmed information role or leader, protect them again, because wolves usually persist against the most threatening claimant. Switch the protection only if new evidence shows the wolves have moved to a different, more valuable target.

lessons.situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The healer must pick a protect target for the pack's first kill with no prior results, and the wolves may kill the healer instead. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, no checks, no votes and no claims, only brief introductory remarks. Stakes: Early game with a full board, so a single night's protection will not decide the game. Losing the healer early removes protection from Night 2 onward, but the blind target cannot be improved with the information available. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public claims, no verified roles and no vote record. The only basis is thin Day 1 behavior, so the pick is speculative.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, protect one engaged, neutral-baseline player rather than stalling over the choice, since there is no evidence to rank candidates and you cannot protect yourself. Treat the night as a free baseline visit: if the morning shows a save or a death, that is the first real data for choosing Night 2 targets.

lessons.situation: The healer has repeated the same protection across nights or announced it publicly, and the claimed target's ability is spent or its threat to the killer has faded. The killer can avoid the telegraphed target and hit the healer or an active role instead. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are publicly claimed, and spent abilities (sentinel watches, investigator checks) have been stated openly. The killer's choices are visible only through morning outcomes. Stakes: Losing the healer, or an active investigator, with one killer left lets the killer avoid saves from then on. A predictable protection pattern risks giving up the night's save and the healer itself. Target landscape: The previously protected player (claimed investigator or spent sentinel) versus other live claimed utility roles with active abilities; assessed from public claims about spent abilities and from the killer's past target choices.
lessons.action: If you have publicly named your protect target, or have guarded the same player for consecutive nights, change targets. A killer who reads the pattern can skip the guarded player and attack you or an unguarded role, so an unpredictable pick keeps both your protection and your own life in play. Skip a target whose ability is spent or whose threat is gone (a sentinel with no watches, an investigator with no checks), and guard the live information role the killer most wants removed.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: With 9 alive and 5 eliminations until the leading evil faction could win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown, the board is not at immediate parity. The game cannot end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this pick is not a one-elimination swing; the end-of-game consequence of choosing now rather than later is unclear from the current record.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved for choosing a winning side: the dead player’s role and will remain concealed, and the claimed night results are not verified. The Sentinel and Trailseer accounts corroborate a visit route, but not either claimant’s role or anyone’s alignment; the Investigator’s Not suspicious claim about you does not distinguish you from most non-wolves.
query_dims.situation: After a concealed night-one death attributed to both wolves and the serial killer, day two ended in a broad abstention; one player’s vote to eliminate the concealed victim’s seat was the sole dissent. The unverified Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer claims have not produced a confirmed alignment, leaving your one-time side pick open amid an unresolved board.
query_dims.target_landscape: The side choice is among Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or yourself. Your Speculator role and unmade pick are privately known to you; publicly, the claimed Investigator’s Not suspicious read on you is unverified and compatible with your role. No public evidence clearly favors one side.

lessons.why: Needs a confirmed evil elimination and validated claims; none exist on this board.
lessons.situation: Night 3 after Town's day vote eliminated a confirmed wolf or lone killer, with healer saves publicly verified. Town holds a large majority, but some killers remain. Past observations show the Town pick won when Town stayed disciplined and lost when Town later mis-eliminated its own power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: system-confirmed evil role reveals, a validated investigator claim, and announced healer saves. The remaining unknown is whether a wolf or killer is still hidden and how well Town will play. Stakes: Town leads, but a few mis-votes or kills could still flip the game, so the pick is only as good as Town's later play. Picking now removes the risk of dying unpicked, but it ties your win to Town's survival and avoiding errors. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self. After a confirmed evil elimination Town looks dominant, with validated investigator or healer claims and a numerical majority. Evil still has a wolf and possibly an unknown lone killer, and Town's later errors can still erase that lead.
lessons.action: Once the day vote has system-confirmed an evil elimination and the surviving power-role claims are validated, make the pick on that night instead of waiting longer. Choose Town only if the lone killer is confirmed gone or Town clearly outnumbers a single remaining wolf; if killers are still active with an uncertain Town lead, keep holding until one side is clearly ahead, unless you are likely to be killed that night.

lessons.why: Night 2, day 2 ended in abstention, no confirmed evil, speculator unpicked: exactly the case, and the advice (hold) is usable now.
lessons.situation: Early game, night 1 or 2, with a discussion-only day 1 or an abstained day 2. At most one or two night deaths so far, and neither wolves nor the lone killer have been exposed. The speculator is still unpicked and has not been targeted. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil eliminations, only unverified claims and concealed or ambiguous bodies, and no momentum signal for any faction. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is no immediate pressure to lock in. The only cost of waiting is the risk of dying unpicked, which is low on night 1 and rises as killers act. Holding costs little and keeps the option open for an informed pick later. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self, or keep holding. All ten players are alive with no confirmed roles and no tested claims. Any pick would be a pure guess on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On nights 1-2, while no evil role has been confirmed eliminated and no claim has been tested, keep the one-time pick unspent. Reassess each night, and commit as soon as board evidence clearly favors one side or you suspect you are likely to be killed. Dying unpicked is a loss, but an uninformed early lock-in has no advantage, and the pick cannot be changed once made.

query_dims.consensus_text: No public discussion or accusations have been recorded today, so there is no clear village consensus or stated basis for one.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive, and it is five eliminations until the leading remaining evil faction could win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so a single result is not immediately decisive.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible push or vote today could establish a public position and invite scrutiny of its reasoning; with no public accusations or claims yet, that commitment is still reversible through later discussion, though the vote record will be permanent.
query_dims.heat_now: No suspicion directed at you is recorded in the available public discussion. Your private pack discussion and block are not public.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the public has a wolf-kill announcement but no identity of the victim's role or will, and no public claims or accusations today. You privately know your block succeeded, but that does not establish the blocked player's role.
query_dims.my_position: No public position relative to a consensus is established; no consensus has formed in the recorded discussion.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know the pack killed a player whose role was concealed, and that your block stopped one player's action last night. Publicly, the village knows only that the wolves killed someone and an illusionist hid the role; the blocked player's experience is private to them.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 begins after the wolves killed a player whose role and will were concealed by an illusionist. The village has no revealed role or will from that death, and today's discussion has not yet produced an accusation or competing public reads.
query_dims.target_landscape: No living candidate has been publicly raised as a target yet. The dead player's role remains unknown to the village, and there is no announced role-based evidence distinguishing any of the nine living players.

lessons.why: Written for a chanteuse whose partner was just exposed and killed; here no partner is exposed and nothing is claimed.
lessons.situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.
lessons.action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.

lessons.why: Final-three wolf endgame; this is a day-2 opening with nine alive.
lessons.situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.

lessons.why: Needs a dead partner and a stumbling claimant; neither exists on day 2.
lessons.situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.
lessons.action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.

lessons.situation: The endgame has 3-4 players left, you are the last wolf, and an unconfirmed player is pushing a case built on your voting record. A claimed Town role's result could clear the swing player and make them an ally. Information landscape: Information-rich: full public voting records, a claimed trailseer result, and a dead player's final vote are all available. These details can be used to rebut the accuser. Stakes: One vote or one night kill decides the game: winning this vote brings the wolves to parity at the next kill, while losing it eliminates the last wolf. Consensus: The room is split with no majority. Everyone is working from public vote history and one or two claimed results, and one swing player is deciding whom to believe. My position: Driving a counter-narrative to form a defensive voting coalition with the swing player. Heat: High: the accuser has laid out your voting record and tied you to a dead wolf on a key mis-elimination. Forward exposure: Answering the accuser head-on commits you to a specific story about your old vote and to a coalition with one other player. If the swing player sides with the accuser, you are voted out right away and cannot undo it. If the swing player sides with you, you can win the vote or at least split the room. Target landscape: A field of three or four: the vocal accuser citing voting records, a claimed Town role whose claim has some support (such as a cleared visit report), and possibly another claimed role. The case against you rests on past votes, evidence rather than behavior; the case against the accuser rests on behavior and on the dead players' positions. Public vs private: Privately you are the last wolf who drove the earlier kills and mis-eliminations, while publicly you pose as an innocent Town player who made an honest deduction alongside the room.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf in a tiny endgame (3-4 alive) and are accused with hard evidence like voting records, answer the accusation directly. Reframe your past vote as a reasonable reaction to the situation, then cite a result or vote from a still-living or already-dead Town player that undercuts the accuser. Aim to win over the swing Town player; if they are not yet persuaded, shift your pitch to the accuser's inconsistencies and to the accuser as the likelier wolf.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator has outed your wolf partner with a suspicious check, or a true investigator is dueling the partner's counterclaim. The room is forming an elimination consensus while you are unsuspected. Information landscape: Moderately to highly informative. There are role claims, a check report, and possibly sentinel or healer-save evidence that backs the investigator, so the town has concrete leads. Stakes: The partner is likely lost, so the wolf side's survival now depends on you staying unsuspected. Staying uncorrelated with the partner is worth more than a failed rescue that could expose you next. Consensus: The village is converging quickly on eliminating the accused partner. Its basis is the investigator's report and supporting mechanical logic from other town roles, and the room is largely ignoring pleas to slow down. My position: holding out Heat: Low to none. You are not named, but speaking up for the accused partner would put you in the spotlight. Forward exposure: Any defense of the partner is permanent on the record and becomes an associative link once the partner flips wolf, and it cannot be undone. Silence or neutral talk commits you to nothing and leaves later options open. Target landscape: The candidates are the accused wolf partner and the claimed investigator, possibly with a counterclaimer. The room is deciding on the strength of check reports and mechanical deductions, such as a healer save or ruling out other roles, rather than on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you know the accused partner is a wolf and the accusing investigator is accurate or at least credible. Publicly the room is still debating the check, and you have no suspicion on you.
lessons.action: When a credible investigator accusation or counterclaim is pulling the room against your wolf partner, stay out of the partner's defense: do not urge caution, vouch for them, or advocate for them. Keep your day talk short and about other players, or stay silent, so nothing visibly ties you to the partner and the room's attention stays on the duel. If you must speak, give only neutral points that would still stand if the partner flipped wolf.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear consensus yet; the room has not formed a view on who to target because no accusations have been made in discussion.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single mistaken or wrongly-directed vote is recoverable at this count but would spend one of the four margins that remain.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible move on day 2 (accusing, defending, or voting) commits you to a public stance that later night results may contradict; a vote is public and permanent, so a wrong-direction vote cannot be withdrawn.
query_dims.heat_now: Low; no one has accused you and the public record contains no link between you and the night kills.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: two role reveals and no claims, checks, watches, or votes yet exist publicly, so every later accusation will rest on behavior rather than evidence.
query_dims.my_position: Unanchored; neither driving a vote nor aligned with a forming majority.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the serial killer, you privately know you killed player_5 on night 1, the fortune teller, while the public only knows a player was stabbed and revealed as a fortune teller; the village reads the kill as a wolf-or-lone-killer mystery with no suspect yet.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 opens with eight players alive after a fortune teller and an investigator were killed on night 1, and no one has yet claimed a role or made an accusation. You are a lone killer whose kill is hidden from the public and must blend in without drawing attention while the village starts looking for suspects.
query_dims.target_landscape: Eight living players with no claims surfaced yet and no hard evidence against anyone; the only public information is the two revealed deaths, a fortune teller and an investigator, which gives no basis yet to rank candidates.

lessons.why: Keyed on a Sentinel/Trailseer report naming the SK as visitor; no report has been made at this opening.
lessons.situation: On Day 2 discussion, a claimed Sentinel (and often a Trailseer) reports that the Serial Killer visited the Night 1 kill victim. The Serial Killer must survive the vote that follows. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's role is revealed, and visit results from the Sentinel and Trailseer are in play. Other information such as Investigator clears is also public, which makes any blanket denial easy to contradict. Stakes: I am the likely vote target and a Day 2 elimination ends my game outright. The room's attention is the only thing I can change this day, so I need to split it between suspects, not hand it a clean one-on-one verdict. Consensus: The village is converging fast on the named visitor, since the direct visit report and my uncorroborated denial point the same way. Both the town and the wolves have reason to remove the Serial Killer. My position: holding out Heat: Maximum heat: I am explicitly named as the only visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, by a claimed investigative role. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a fake unique-role claim commits me to a binary truth clash that a living real role holder or a corroborating report can settle at once, and I cannot retreat from it. A claim-free reframe that spreads attention across several suspects stays reversible and does not lock me into any one story. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, whose report is direct visit evidence, and other living players with partial results or only behavioral reads. A fabricated role claim invites a counter-claim from the real holder. The best alternative target is someone with a concrete, checkable inconsistency, not a player I simply accuse as a liar. Public vs private: Privately I know the Sentinel's report is accurate and the visit was my own kill. Publicly the room is treating the report as a claim that has to be weighed against my answer.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel names you as the sole visitor to the Night 1 victim, answer that a visit shows only presence, not an attack, and that any Town visiting role would leave the same trace. Then move the room off the you-versus-Sentinel duel onto a second concrete suspect, using a Trailseer or Investigator result or a vote-record inconsistency, and ask for those results to be cross-checked. Do not stake yourself on a flat denial or on a unique role whose real holder can counter-claim, because either one gives the room a single hard contradiction to vote on.

lessons.why: Late game, about five alive, room united against the SK; this is day 2 with eight alive and no heat.
lessons.situation: Late in the game with few players left, a claimed power role or a vote-record case has pointed the room at me. Wolves and town both want me gone, and I have to survive the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, and claimed results and vote records are on the table. Anything I say can be checked against them. Stakes: With about five players alive, one lost vote ends my win condition. If I survive, the wolves and I will keep trading kills. Splitting the room is worth more than winning an argument. Consensus: The room is nearly united against me, resting either on a mechanical result from a claimed role or on a shared view that I contributed little. Wolves and town are voting together. My position: Holding out against the room's consensus, with little support. Heat: High to extreme: I am the main target, accused through a role result or through passivity and a dead wolf's vote. Forward exposure: A concrete, checkable case against another player commits me to a read that the next reveal can confirm or refute. It is reversible if I tie it to public votes and claims, and it gives the room a second option besides me. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other unconfirmed players, usually a surviving wolf. Several town and wolf roles are already revealed or dead. The case against me rests on a hard result or on behavior, and the alternative suspect has a thinner record. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and the pressure on me comes from a mechanical result or a pattern of passivity. Publicly I appear as an outsider the room can safely vote out.
lessons.action: When the room turns on you, spend your turn building a concrete case against the best alternative suspect, usually a surviving wolf, using only public facts such as their vote record, who they pushed, and who they protected. Name the specific contradiction and ask the room to weigh it against you. Aim to split the vote or draw a second target, since a daytime vote is the only way you can be removed.

lessons.why: The generic advice (give specific reads each day, engage early) is usable on day 2 even though the trigger (a claimant labelling the seat passive) is absent.
lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, a claimed role points at me because I have been quiet and received that wolf's vote. The room is split between me and one other suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a few claimed results exist, and there is a vote record, but nothing proves who I am. Stakes: With the vote split close to even, my own heat decides which suspect goes. Showing early engagement keeps me out of the spot where one extra vote eliminates me. Consensus: The room is still forming. A claimed role has named me, and the other candidate has offsetting suspicion on them, so the vote is close. My position: Holding out, with no allies. Heat: Moderate to high: I am accused of passivity and linked to a dead wolf's vote, with no hard evidence against me. Forward exposure: Specific early reads commit me to positions, but they are low-risk and reversible if I tie them to the public record. Staying passive and explaining it away commits me to nothing, which makes me the default vote when the room needs a target. Target landscape: The room has few confirmed players and several unaccounted ones. A claimed role is steering attention toward whoever has contributed least or drawn a dead wolf's vote. This is a judgment on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer with no town role to protect. Publicly I look quiet and uncommitted, which makes me an easy target for any claimant needing a suspect.
lessons.action: From the early days, give specific reads each day, referencing votes and claims, and engage with what other players say, so I am not the quiet player a claimed role can single out. If a role claimant has already labeled me passive, answer with a specific read on someone else instead of explaining my silence.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is split on the lynch target between player_2 and player_6: one accuser presses for a clean vote on player_2 and the other accused player points to the accuser's day 4 vote and your vote slip; no shared evidence exists for either.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Three alive with a single elimination able to end the game: a wrong lynch leaves two living players where the evil side may already equal or outnumber the others, so the day vote is decisive.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Pushing a lynch on player_2 or defending yourself in a 3-player day commits you to a visible position; a vote on player_2 that goes wrong or a reversal of your earlier day 4 vote slip would be recorded permanently in the vote history and cannot be undone.
query_dims.heat_now: Moderate: player_6 has openly pushed for a clean lynch on player_2 and the day 4 tie vote record and your own misstatement of the vote target ('player_8' instead of 'player_9' for player_2 accusation) are on the public record, creating a credibility question against you.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a verified night result or claim; the only public evidence is vote history (day 3, day 4 tie) and the public record of the concealed player_10 role.
query_dims.my_position: Holding a position close to the accuser of player_2 on the vote, with the outcome dependent on the one accused player who has no claim.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately you are the illusionist and know your pack partner (the chanteuse, still alive and unrevealed) and that player_10's concealed role was a sigilist; publicly the village only knows player_10's role is hidden, and you present as a town-aligned player with no night result to share.
query_dims.situation: A three-player day where player_6 demands a clean lynch on player_2 after a day 4 tie, while player_2 counters by pointing to player_9's day 4 vote slip; the accused player_2 has no claim, and each remaining player is accusing another on vote history alone.
query_dims.target_landscape: Three living players: player_2 (no claim, abstained days 2 and split votes, voted by player_6 and accused by player_9), player_6 (accuser of player_2, voted player_2 on day 4, had a wolf-channel role in earlier kills), and yourself. Player_2's suspicion rests on vote behavior and abstains only, with no claim or night result.

lessons.why: Day-2 abstain-consensus scenario; this is a three-player day 5 lynch.
lessons.situation: Nine or so players are alive on early day 2 with no hard leads. The village converges on abstaining, while the packmate breaks away to push an unsupported elimination and the illusionist is tempted to join them. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable claims, such as no-visit trail results, non-suspicious checks or a dead role, and no confirmed evil alignment. Stakes: Wolves are far from parity, so no single vote decides the game, but a visible wolf-wolf voting link can lose it later. Staying hidden is worth more than a speculative elimination attempt. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in leaning toward abstaining, because there are no guilty leads and the day is read as an information-poor start. My position: holding out Heat: None or low; the illusionist has taken part neutrally in discussion and is not under suspicion, so it has nothing to gain from a risky vote. Forward exposure: A lone elimination vote beside the packmate is public and permanent. It ties the illusionist's record to the packmate's agenda, so any later death or reveal of the packmate exposes the illusionist, and it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Unclaimed or quiet players with no accusations or hard evidence against them, or a claimed info role, versus simply joining the majority abstain; none of the targets has an evidence-based case. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the packmate's role and that any target they push is unsupported, while the town sees an information-poor day where abstaining is the natural, safe consensus.
lessons.action: When the room is abstaining on an information-starved day and you are an unsuspected illusionist, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain) instead of pairing with your packmate on a lone elimination vote. If the packmate already broke away, still abstain; a failed push only leaves a permanent public record linking two wolves, and that record becomes fatal evidence once either one is revealed.

lessons.why: Needs a claimed investigator/trailseer with hard evidence accusing the seat; no such accuser exists.
lessons.situation: A claimed investigator or trailseer has accused me with hard evidence on day 2 or later. The vote is a duel between me and the accuser, and the town is consolidating against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed night results, visits corroborated by other claimants, and public vote records. My fabricated defense is contradicted by that evidence. Stakes: My own elimination is likely, but the endgame depends on keeping my partner unlinked. Losing both wolves in two days ends the game, so the priority is protecting my partner's cover. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on eliminating me, on the strength of the accuser's report and corroborating claims from the sentinel, trailseer or sigilist. My position: Holding out in a small minority against a near-unanimous town, with my wolf partner as the only possible ally. Heat: Critical to extreme. A specific hard report (a suspicious check, a sighting at the victim's door, or a duplicate investigator claim) names me, and others have corroborated it. Forward exposure: A counter-vote on the accuser is irreversible and commits me to a 1v1 credibility duel. If I lose, my illusionist role is revealed, and any partner who voted with me is implicated by the public record. Target landscape: The claimed investigator or trailseer with a direct check or sighting against me, versus deflecting onto inactive or neutral players with no evidence against them. The accuser has setup legitimacy or corroboration; my defense rests on a fabrication. Public vs private: Publicly the room accepts the accuser's report or sighting that places me at the scene. Privately I know I am the illusionist and my partner is the chanteuse, so the accusation is true or close to it and I must not tie my partner to my vote.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or trailseer with hard evidence has you as the primary target and the room is consolidating against you, cast your own vote on that single accuser to stay consistent with your counter-claim. Keep your wolf partner's vote with the majority, and don't have them join yours, because public permanent votes link whoever votes with a flipped wolf. If the accuser's evidence is only their own claim, push for a close split, since a tight tally keeps suspicion off your partner.

lessons.why: Day-2 advice about not voting against an info claimant; the info claimants are already dead.
lessons.situation: On day 2 with no guilty results, the village coalesces around abstaining. The illusionist is tempted to cast an isolated vote against a claimed info role that the wolves want gone. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims and a negative tracking result, with no proof about anyone's alignment. Stakes: A failed lone vote removes no one and only adds a traceable record. The wolves can remove the claimant at night instead, so the vote adds exposure and little else. Consensus: Nearly the whole village favors abstaining and waiting for more information, with no coalition behind any elimination. My position: holding out Heat: Low; a claimed result such as 'visited no one' leaves the illusionist relatively safe until it votes in a way that stands out. Forward exposure: Voting against a claimed info role who is then killed, possibly with the role concealed, permanently ties the illusionist's record to that death. Town will cite it on later days, and it cannot be walked back. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer or other info role who reported on the illusionist, versus joining the room in abstaining; the claimant has no evidence against them, only the wolves' private interest. Public vs private: The illusionist privately knows the claimant is a threat to the wolf team and is likely a night-kill target, while the public consensus prefers waiting and gathering information.
lessons.action: When the village is abstaining and you are unsuspected, do not vote against an information-role claimant (such as a trailseer or sentinel) whom the wolves intend to kill that night; abstain with the room. A vote against a player who dies concealed that night becomes a permanent link that town can use to condemn you.

lessons.situation: The agent is the illusionist on a final day vote. A dead partner or a night trace links the agent to the wolf team, and the village is converging on eliminating the agent. The agent's only visible lever is its own ballot. Information landscape: Information-rich. It contains a revealed dead wolf, a claimed investigator or trailseer result, permanent voting records, and a concealed night death that cannot clear the agent. Stakes: If the agent is eliminated, the wolf side is wiped out or reduced to one wolf, and the lone killer is left as the remaining evil. The wolves are several eliminations from parity, so the pack can afford only a vote that actually splits the room. Consensus: Near-unanimous, resting on concrete evidence: a revealed chanteuse, a vote record, and a claimed check or tracking report. There is little disagreement to exploit. My position: Holding out alone against a unified majority. Heat: Maximum. The whole room names the agent, based on the Day 2 vote pairing with the revealed dead wolf or on a trailseer trace. Forward exposure: The final vote is public, permanent and irreversible. A lone vote on an accuser confirms isolation and commits the agent to a stance that cannot affect the outcome. Joining a shared alternate target at least keeps a path to a tie. Target landscape: The choices are the agent's own wagon, the vocal accuser (an investigator or trailseer-type claimant), and a quieter or claimed player with few votes. The case against the agent rests on hard evidence (vote record, dead-role reveal, tracking report). The accuser is backed by the room, so attacking the accuser gains nothing. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the dead partner, the concealed kill, and the accuser's evidence are all real. Publicly the town reads the linked vote record or tracking trace as decisive proof of guilt.
lessons.action: When the room has locked onto you from a vote record or a dead teammate's trace, put your ballot on the same alternate target your living wolf partner is using, preferably one who already has some votes. Do not cast a lone retaliatory vote on the loudest accuser. Only a combined bloc on one plausible alternative can split the room or force a tie, which means no elimination. If you are the last wolf, put your vote on the non-accuser who already has traction.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; one more elimination leaves three alive, and a wolf-side kill tonight would bring the count to three, where a further loss could end the game, so a wrong bet costs a point and a self-bet attempt spent on a non-attacked night is lost for good.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed roles among survivors, one sigilist claim with consistent record support, one investigator Not suspicious read on player_3 from night 2, and only behavioral reads on player_10. Night results for the surviving players are mostly unshared.
query_dims.situation: Night 4 is approaching with four players alive after a necromancer was voted out on day 4. As the fortune teller, you must bet on who dies tonight and decide whether to spend one of your two self-bets, while the remaining wolves and the lone killer are still unidentified among the three survivors and the discussion is split over whether the sigilist's claim is credible.
query_dims.target_landscape: Three living players: player_3 (publicly accused on day 2 by a dead player, admitted no real evidence, checked Not suspicious by a now-dead investigator on night 2), player_9 (claims sigilist, placed a sigil that struck a player on night 3, a claim consistent with the public record), and player_10 (evasive about their night results, the target of the day 4 elimination vote that failed to pass). Role status is unverified claim for player_9 and no public role for the others.

lessons.why: Premise is a live necromancer with three alive; the necromancer was just voted out and the wolf is the remaining killer.
lessons.situation: Last wolf voted out and three players left. A lone killer (the necromancer, who can attack through a reanimated body) wins by killing one more player, so the Fortune Teller is a live kill target and no other player's death is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead, the dead roles are confirmed, and the remaining Town sigilist is confirmed out of sigils. This makes the only remaining attacker and its available bodies clear. Stakes: The lone killer wins if anyone else dies tonight, so a bet that fails to cover your own life can end the game with the Fortune Teller short of two points. A self-bet keeps you alive for another night. Target landscape: The suspected necromancer (alive and holding a usable body, so unlikely to die), a confirmed sigilist with no sigils left (no threat), or a self-bet. Roles are confirmed from the graveyard, and nothing makes the suspect likely to die tonight.
lessons.action: With three alive and a lone killer that can attack, you are one of only two possible victims. If no other victim is predictable, spend a self-bet, because an attack on you fails that night. Don't bet on the suspected killer: a killer that is immune or about to win is unlikely to die, and a wrong bet leaves you open to the attack.

lessons.why: Needs a publicly announced healer shield on the obvious target; none exists.
lessons.situation: Late game with the wolves dead or nearly dead and one killer left (serial killer, necromancer or last wolf). The Fortune Teller stands at 0-1 points and needs a death, and the most obvious target is publicly protected, so a bet on them fails to the save or the killer switches targets. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of the dead wolves are confirmed, claims and protection histories are public, and the surviving killer's identity or kill pattern is mostly known. Stakes: Few players remain and the game can end any night. Each night spent without scoring risks being voted out or the game finishing before the second point, so the bet must follow where the killer can actually kill, not just where it wants to. Target landscape: The investigator or leader shielded by a public healer claim, the claimed healer who is exposed, other claimed power roles (sigilist, sentinel, trailseer), and unconfirmed players. Hard evidence of who is protected, not behavior, drives the choice.
lessons.action: When the healer has publicly announced protecting the obvious top target (the confirmed or claimed investigator), place the bet on the next-most-valuable unshielded Town role the surviving killer must remove, such as the claimed healer or another power role. If the killer's last pick is predictable, name that role in the bet for the two-point payoff.

lessons.why: Same decision (FT bet in a small endgame with a wolf free to kill), but it requires a publicly confirmed Town role with spent actions, which the seat does not have.
lessons.situation: Three-player endgame tie between a confirmed Town power role, a suspected wolf and the Fortune Teller. The wolves need a kill to close the game, and the Fortune Teller needs points to win. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed by earlier night results and blocked actions, so the wolves' likely victim can be read from the board. Stakes: Each night is nearly decisive. A correct victim-and-role bet gives two points and wins the game for the Fortune Teller, while a miss wastes a night when the kill can end the game. Target landscape: A publicly confirmed Town role (e.g. a claimed vigilante whose shots were blocked), a suspected surviving wolf, or a self-bet. The Town player is the most likely kill target, backed by confirmed evidence from earlier nights and blocks rather than just behavior.
lessons.action: With three alive and a night kill that is predictable (a publicly confirmed Town role whose own actions are blocked or spent, with a wolf free to carry the kill), bet on that player to die and name their confirmed role. A correct victim plus role scores two points and can finish the win.

lessons.situation: After a day elimination or accusation, the remaining killer needs to silence the player who exposed it or holds a deadly tool against it. The Fortune Teller must choose between betting on the accused (who survives) and betting on the exposing claimant (who is attacked). Information landscape: Information-rich: a public claim or result (tracker report, sigil test, investigator checks) points at the killer's side, and several Town roles are out in the open. Stakes: Only one killing source is left, so exactly one death is likely each night and the bet must match it. A miss leaves the Fortune Teller stuck at one point while the game may end that same night. Target landscape: The claimed tracker, sigilist or investigator who exposed or tested the killer's side, versus the accused wolf or suspect, versus bystander claimed roles such as a roleblocked sentinel or unconfirmed healer. The basis is public claims and the day's vote record.
lessons.action: When one killer remains and a claimed power role has just driven the day's outcome (outed a wolf, tested the wolf, or led the vote), bet on that role as the killer's top threat, not on the accused or already-exposed suspect. A killer that is under suspicion usually survives the night, and the threat to it is the likelier victim.

lessons.situation: Early game (night 1 or 2), the Fortune Teller has no points yet and must pick a nightly death bet while wolves and a lone killer are all hunting. Day discussion produced a visible conflict or a prominent claimed power role. Information landscape: Mixed: some claims and night-one movement reports exist, but roles are unverified and votes were mostly abstentions, so the pick rests on behavioral reads. Stakes: No immediate parity pressure. The Fortune Teller needs two points in total, so each night's bet is a cheap, repeatable chance to score, and the self-bets guard against a later attack. Target landscape: Players who publicly claimed or acted as information roles, or who were just singled out by a night result or an open dispute, versus quiet players with no evidence either way. The choice rests on behavioral threat to the killers, not confirmed alignment.
lessons.action: With both self-bets still unspent and no points scored, bet on the player the killers most plausibly want dead tonight: an openly active, publicly claimed information role (such as a trailseer that just exposed someone) or a player the dead Trailseer's last follow pointed to. Name no role, since the death alone scores a point, and keep the self-bets for later nights.

lessons.situation: Night one after a discussion-only opening day. Several killers (wolves, and possibly a lone killer) will each attack someone, and no public mechanical constraint limits their choices. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigative findings, deaths, confirmed roles, or vote record exist. Stakes: Very low board pressure. A miss costs nothing but a night, and multiple attackers raise the chance that the chosen player dies. A hit on night one puts the win one successful bet away. Target landscape: All other living players, with no public claims, revealed alignments, or voting history to separate them. Any pick is close to a random draw among the candidates.
lessons.action: On a night with no evidence at all (no claims, no deaths, no votes), bet on any one quiet living player without naming a role, since the bet scores on any death by any cause. Keep both self-bets unspent for later nights when you may become a target.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is leaning toward eliminating you: the Investigator claimant's result has strong public support from the earlier reveal, and the remaining claimant has explicitly said they would vote for you. The fourth survivor's position is not stated, so unanimity is not established.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four players remain; the leading evil faction is two eliminations from parity, at worst for the town because a concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this vote is a swing decision. The end-of-game consequence of this particular vote is unclear from the record; immediately, eliminating you removes one living player.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Your Healer claim is already public and commits you to a role whose protection history cannot be verified from nights with no public save. Continuing to defend that account keeps your Necromancer role and reanimated attacks concealed for now, but leaves you exposed to the corroborated Investigator claim; retracting it would make the deception visible and is not readily reversible.
query_dims.heat_now: High: the player claiming Investigator reports a Suspicious result on you, and their earlier Suspicious result was borne out when the accused was revealed as the Illusionist. The claimed Healer defense has no public save corroborating it.
query_dims.information_landscape: Public information includes revealed roles and town wills, the revealed Illusionist, and the Investigator claimant's previously corroborated result. The current Suspicious result and your claimed protections are private-action reports without independent public confirmation. The concealed roles of two night victims leave some faction composition uncertain.
query_dims.my_position: You are the accused and are defending yourself against the forming vote; you are not driving the consensus.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Necromancer and that your reanimated attacks killed two players; you also know the concealed role of one of those victims was the Chanteuse. Publicly, your role and those actions are unknown. The public sees a player claiming Investigator whose earlier Suspicious result was corroborated by the revealed Illusionist, now reporting you Suspicious, while you claim Healer.
query_dims.situation: A player claiming Investigator, whose earlier Suspicious result was corroborated by an Illusionist reveal, now reports you Suspicious. You answer with a Healer claim and say your protections produced no public save; another survivor favors voting you, so the verified-looking private-result claim is driving an endgame vote against your concealed identity.
query_dims.target_landscape: The immediate vote centers on you, a claimed Healer now read Suspicious by a player claiming Investigator with a previously corroborated result. The Investigator is a strong-evidence claim, not system-confirmed; the other two survivors have no role status established here. The public basis against you is the result and the lack of a public save, while your own knowledge confirms the result is consistent with your role and actions.

lessons.why: Written for a necromancer watching another player being accused; here the seat is the accused.
lessons.situation: A claimed information role accuses a player based on a night result, the accused disputes it, and the necromancer is tempted to step in and challenge the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead role with a concealed role, a specific claimed tracking report, and mechanical counter-claims from the accused. All of it is still unverified. Stakes: The board has many living players, so every public commitment matters for the endgame. A defense that turns out wrong leaves a damaging record, while a vote with the majority costs nothing. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on the accused, driven by a concrete claimed report that the claimant has already defended against objections. My position: Holding out, if I contest the lead. Better to move to the majority side. Heat: Low to none. Attention is on the accused player and the claimant, not on me. Forward exposure: Publicly challenging a claimed information lead puts my name on the record against it, and that record cannot be undone if the target flips evil. Joining the consensus costs little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: The accused player denies the charge and argues mechanics. The claimed trailseer, or other power-role claimant, gives a specific sighting. The evidence for the claimant is stronger than the accused's counter-argument. Public vs private: Publicly the room is split between an accused player and a claimed power role with a concrete report. Privately I am the lone killer with no stake in either side's survival, so I can choose the least risky alignment.
lessons.action: When a living claimant's report (for example a trailseer's) already has the room converging on an accused player, go along with that lead and voice a short read that matches it. If you doubt the report, ask a neutral question about it rather than staking your name on a mechanics rebuttal. The accused may flip, and a record of defending them marks you as their ally.

lessons.why: Final four, necromancer under direct claim pressure, advice to keep one consistent claim against the visit rules is usable.
lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Two town power roles have claimed, their results back each other up, and the necromancer is pushed to state a role or be voted out. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed roles of the dead, public vote history, claimed night results and spent abilities leave very little room to bluff. Stakes: One elimination vote decides the game. If the necromancer is voted out it loses outright, and a failed claim leaves no later day to repair it. Consensus: The few remaining players are converging on a bloc of cross-verifying town claims, with the unclaimed or contradicted player as the obvious elimination. My position: Holding out alone against a forming two-player bloc. Heat: High to critical. Claimed town roles are demanding my claim, or I am the odd player out after their results cleared each other. Forward exposure: A role claim commits me to a night history that the claimed town roles can check against their own results and spent abilities. A claim that fails the check is nearly irreversible, but staying silent is already read as guilt in a small endgame. Target landscape: The claimed power roles (vigilante, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist) and any unclaimed player. Their claims are partly corroborated by revealed deaths and spent abilities, so each can be tested against the record. Public vs private: Privately a lone killer who has been attacking through a dead player's body, while publicly needing to pass as an ordinary town power role under direct claim demands.
lessons.action: When pressed to claim at the final three or four, give a specific role claim instead of stalling. Pick a still-living town role that no revealed death or other claim has already used, and tell a night story that fits every claimed result and the visit rules. For example, a Sentinel is never told of its own watch, and a Trailseer's follow is a visit others can cross-check.

lessons.why: Final four, choosing whom to push, with an unverified player to aim at: same decision and dynamic.
lessons.situation: Final three or four players. I must choose whom to push, either the pair that verifies each other or the one claimant whose story stands alone. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed results can be cross-checked against spent abilities, revealed deaths and visit mechanics. Stakes: With so few players, one vote swings the game. A failed push at a verified player hands the bloc a unanimous vote against me. Consensus: The remaining town claims align with each other on the basis of verified results and leave me as the outlier. My position: Trying to swing the votes of a bloc that already trusts each other. Heat: High. My earlier claim or evasion has drawn suspicion, and the table is looking for the odd player out. Forward exposure: Attacking a cross-verified player forces a binary vote against me if the attack fails, and it cannot be taken back. Targeting an uncorroborated claim keeps a fallback and splits the room. Target landscape: A cross-verified pair of town roles versus an unverified claimant, a spent claimant, or the unclaimed player. The evidence is the claimed results against the visit record, not tone. Public vs private: I know which claims are false and which are genuine, but publicly I must present myself as a town member reasoning from the record. Attacking a verified claim contradicts what the table has already confirmed.
lessons.action: In the endgame, aim the accusation at the claimant whose story the record cannot corroborate, such as a vigilante who held bullets or a claim with no verifying partner. Do not attack a pair whose night results already cross-verify. If two claims check each other out, give your own consistent claim and call for a vote on the unverified player or the unclaimed player.

lessons.situation: After a night attack or save, the necromancer holds results gathered through a dead town role and wants to redirect suspicion onto the visitors. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: the dead role's death is on record, so the room can tell which living roles could have produced such a result. Stakes: My win needs the room kept off me for many more days, so losing the cover of a hidden identity costs far more than anything the leaked result could gain. Consensus: The village is unsettled after a night attack and save, with no fixed target. The living roles are still working out what the visits mean. My position: Not yet in conflict, but I would be holding out alone if I spoke up with the hidden result. Heat: Zero before sharing. It would jump to universal accusation if I quoted the body-derived result. Forward exposure: Stating a result that only the dead role could have produced points straight at the necromancer, and the room cannot unsee it. A read built on public evidence can be dropped without penalty. Target landscape: The players whose visits I learned about (claimed healer, other claimants) are the targets, but the only support is a hidden source. Public evidence such as claim overlaps is available to use instead. Public vs private: Privately I hold a night result obtained through a dead role, such as who visited a door. Publicly, no living player holds that role, so quoting the result shows I am the necromancer.
lessons.action: If a dead player's ability gave you night information, steer suspicion only through reasons the room can see: public claims, votes, and contradictions between players. Do not quote the body-derived result, such as sentinel visitor names, when no living role could explain how you got it. Only a living claimed role could plausibly share such a result, and you cannot back that claim.

lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown, six eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a single result or elimination can be decisive despite that worst-case parity distance.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-rich relative to the prior day: the Illusionist's revealed role supports your private Night 1 result, while the Sentinel claim and roleblock claim are unverified. The concealed night-death role remains unknown; no check result on another living player is available yet.
query_dims.situation: After the player you checked was eliminated and revealed as the Illusionist, your Night 1 Suspicious result gained strong public support. You have one check remaining, and the current night presents a choice among the seven other living players for gathering further alignment information.
query_dims.target_landscape: The seven other living players are possible check targets. One claimed Sentinel and reported seeing no visitors at their target; another claimed to have been roleblocked. The other living players have no public role confirmation here. Your previous Suspicious result was supported when its target was eliminated and revealed as the Illusionist; the other night-killed player's role remains concealed.

lessons.why: Night 1 advice; the seat is on night 2 with one check already spent.
lessons.situation: Night 1 after a discussion-only Day 1. The Investigator holds both checks and must choose between holding them and probing an unread player blind. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no claims, no votes, no night results. Stakes: Early board with no pressure, so no single check is decisive. But the Investigator may die before a banked check is ever used, and any early read, whether it finds a wolf or clears an ally, compounds into later votes. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, flips or behavioral tells. Pick a quiet, non-prominent player at random, since nothing separates them.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no leads, spend one check on a quiet, unclaimed player instead of banking both. An early Suspicious finds a wolf, and a Not suspicious gives you a baseline read. Treat a clean result as clearing only wolves: the Serial Killer and neutrals also read Not suspicious, and a Necromancer reads that way on any night it does not attack.

lessons.why: Keyed on an abstained day 2 with both checks left; this day ended in an elimination and one check remains.
lessons.situation: Day 2 ended in an abstain after multiple night deaths, with two killing factions active and only soft, unverified role claims on the table; the Investigator still has both checks. Information landscape: Information-starved: the claims are unverifiable and no alignments are confirmed, so any read has to come from behavior. Stakes: With two killing factions active and no hard leads, the village needs at least one verified collaborator; an early check on a central voice yields a lasting anchor even if the investigator dies. Target landscape: Unverified claimants, quiet players, and an analytical non-claimant who is actively evaluating claims; no one has confirmed alignment, and behavior is the only basis for choosing.
lessons.action: If the night has no hard lead, use a check on an active, influential player who has not claimed a role and is shaping the vote, to build a verified anchor among the central voices. A Not suspicious read clears a wolf or town member but does not clear a lone killer, so treat the anchor as likely town rather than certain.

lessons.why: Right decision (last check after a wolf flip, pick by day-2 vote behaviour) but the key premise, vote outliers, is absent.
lessons.situation: After the Day 2 vote and a Day 1 or 2 reveal, the voting record shows a few players splitting from the room: defending an eliminated wolf, or pushing to eliminate the Investigator without evidence. One wolf (or the pack's remainder) is likely hiding among them, and the Investigator has one check left. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed wolf or sentinel death is on the record, plus public vote tallies showing clear outliers. No private proof yet, so the final check converts behavioral suspicion into a result. Stakes: The pack is already thinned and one check remains, so the last check is the Investigator's final chance to confirm a wolf. A correct hit can lead to eliminating the remaining wolves and winning, while a wasted check leaves Town without direction. Target landscape: Seven or so living players, with roles of the dead revealed.
