query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single wrong sigil or lynch is recoverable but each sigil spent without a strike removes one of only two remaining traps, and a wrong target would leave the wolves or serial killer free to act at no cost.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Placing a sigil on a player is a visible visit-commitment that spends one of two sigils permanently; it only reveals itself as a trap if the target attacks, and a sigil on a non-attacker returns only 'no effect', which would narrow suspicion without spending the other sigil's worth of information.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no investigator or sentinel result has been announced, the only verified fact is the night-one block on the lynched healer, and day-two accusations rest on behavior and claims rather than results.
query_dims.situation: As the sigilist with two sigils, you face a night where the pack or the serial killer will likely attack one of the six remaining players, and a sigil placed on whoever attacks will strike that attacker. The village lynched a healer who claimed a blocked role without naming it, so no one is publicly verified as a night actor; the question is whether a sigil spent on a behaviorally suspicious player would catch a wolf or a serial killer attacking.
query_dims.target_landscape: Seven alive: the surviving players are player_3, player_4, player_6, player_8, player_9, player_10 and you. No one has a public role claim tied to tonight's kill. Public role status: player_1 (trailseer) and player_2 (speculator) dead by night, player_5 (healer) lynched and revealed. The remaining players' roles are unknown; the only evidence is behavioral: player_10 pressed the lynch on player_5, player_8 and player_9 abstained, and player_5 claimed a blocked role without naming it.

lessons.why: Same spend-or-hold decision and 'if no suspect plausibly carries, keep the sigil' applies, but the premise (earlier sigils hit non-attackers, carrier timing) is missing.
lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.why: Same decision after an abstain/split day, but the advice requires a concrete lead the seat lacks.
lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

lessons.why: Requires visit lists to pick between attacker and protector; the seat has none.
lessons.situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.

lessons.why: Hold both sigils when there are no leads: right advice, but written for night 1 and this is night 2 with three deaths.
lessons.situation: Opening night, ten players alive, day one was discussion only with no vote or deaths. The sigilist must decide between placing a sigil on a blind guess and keeping the charges. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no role claims, no voting records, no visit histories to separate likely attackers from passive roles. Stakes: Early board with a large margin before any faction can win. Nothing is forcing a spend, and each of the two charges is worth more on a night with a real lead than on a coin-flip target. Forward exposure: Holding reveals nothing and commits nothing, and the charge stays available. Placing is irreversible, spends one of two charges, and is a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unvetted: no claims, no votes, no night results. Any target is a pure guess, and most players, including investigative, protective and passive roles, will not attack.
lessons.action: On night one, when there are no deaths, claims, votes or visit data, keep both sigils and place none. A sigil only does anything if its target attacks that night, and a blind pick usually lands on a non-attacker (several observations show it striking nothing and spending a charge). Hold the charges until a night when a specific suspect is likely to attack.

query_dims.consensus_text: The discussion is strongly aligned around eliminating the accused, mainly because several players accept the claimed Night 1 Suspicious result as a strong lead. The reasoning is not independent confirmation: the result remains private and unverified.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive, and it is 5 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. A single vote or kill does not flip which faction is winning, and the game cannot end within one more elimination.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Your public support for eliminating the accused commits you to the village’s current test of the claimed result; your public vote will be permanent. It does not reveal your role, and you can later change your stated assessment, but not the vote record.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: no one has accused you. You asked the claimant about remaining checks and said the accused was the clearest target, which makes your position visible but has not drawn suspicion.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved, with one specific but unverified private-result claim, an unverified roleblock account with no result, and an empty watch result that does not identify anyone. The concealed Night 1 victim's role and will are unavailable, leaving the public alignment evidence limited.
query_dims.my_position: With the forming majority: you have publicly described the accused as the clearest target if the village votes.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Necromancer and that you took no action on Night 1. Publicly, your role and private knowledge are unknown; the discussion centers on an unverified Investigator claim of a Suspicious result.
query_dims.situation: A player claiming Investigator says a Night 1 check found the accused Suspicious, and most speakers favor eliminating the accused despite the result being unverifiable before the flip. The accused denies the allegation and emphasizes that the votes rely on one private claim rather than independent evidence.
query_dims.target_landscape: The accused player is the immediate elimination candidate based on an unverified Investigator claim of a Night 1 Suspicious result and their denial. The claimant is a possible later subject of scrutiny if the accused is revealed not to be a wolf. The blocked-action claimant and the player with an empty watch result provide no direct alignment evidence.

lessons.why: Seat is not exposed; nobody is voting against it.
lessons.situation: After my revealed information mechanically exposed me as acting through a dead body, the claimed investigator rallied the village to eliminate me. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role announcement combined with my own claimed result is hard evidence of my identity. Stakes: Elimination is near-certain this vote, and it would end the lone-killer run. Any survival chance depends on splitting the vote, so a plausible alternative target matters more than revenge. Consensus: The room is overwhelmingly aligned, seven of nine, on voting me out, based on the hard mechanical contradiction. My position: Holding out alone against the room consensus. Heat: Critical. The room recognizes that my report is impossible for anyone but the Necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the trusted accuser confirms total antagonism and leaves no way back. A vote on a visitor to the accuser keeps a doubt open and is more plausible. Target landscape: The accuser is a claimed investigator who is widely trusted after surviving an attack. The two visitors at the accuser's door are the only alternative targets. The accuser's case rests on hard mechanics, while the visitor case is only a possibility. Public vs private: I privately used a dead role's body and know my claimed result is only possible for a Necromancer. The village has correctly worked this out and trusts my accuser.
lessons.action: If your claimed result has been shown to be mechanically impossible and the room is converging on you, cast your vote on one of the alternative suspects (for example a visitor at your accuser's door) while pressing that case aloud, instead of a bare retaliatory vote on your accuser. A lone vote on the accuser adds no allies and gives the room nothing to doubt. Even a thin alternative case makes the vote count as a counter-narrative that might split the room.

lessons.why: Day vote with a contested claim and the necromancer choosing a side while hiding; the advice (follow the rules-consistent majority) is what the seat did, but the room here is near-unanimous, not split 5-4.
lessons.situation: Day vote with a contested accusation. A claimed tracker or watcher placed an unconfirmed player at a victim's door, and the accused denied it and called the report mechanically impossible. A Necromancer must choose a side while hiding its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple role claims, a concealed night death, and public voting records. All of it is claims, though, not announced fact. Stakes: The board is mid-game with nine alive. Every vote matters for the Necromancer's long run toward last-two. A wrong public stance costs credibility, and surviving to night is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is split fairly evenly, about 5-4, over whether the claimant or the accused is credible. Several claims are in play and a night death has a concealed role. My position: Holding out in the minority on the split, against the side that ended up winning. Heat: Low. I am seen as an ordinary town voice arguing mechanics, with no one pushing me as a suspect. Forward exposure: A vote against an investigative claimant is public and permanent, and it looks bad if the claimant's accused is revealed as a wolf. It cannot be reversed after the vote. A vote with the rules-consistent majority commits me to little. Target landscape: The choice is between a claimed information role (Trailseer, Sentinel or Investigator) whose report is a claim only, and the player they accuse, who denies it and disputes the mechanics. Neither is confirmed. The evidence is the claim's consistency with the rules versus the accused's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I am the Necromancer who wants dead wolf or role bodies available for night use. Publicly I am only an ordinary town participant arguing a mechanics dispute, and my minority vote can look anti-information once the accused flips.
lessons.action: When you are low-heat in an information-rich vote split between an information claimant and the player they accuse, test the claimant's report against the written visit and concealment rules first. Then vote with the side those rules support, which is usually the majority, instead of a dissenting vote. A lone or minority vote against a claimant is permanent on the record, and staying alive and unsuspected keeps your night body-use available.

lessons.why: Endgame 3-4 alive with the necromancer cornered; nine alive.
lessons.situation: An endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. The necromancer is cornered by claimed town players after killing at night, and a counter-vote on a town claimant led to an immediate two-vote elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, claims are cross-checkable, and the vote record is public, so a false or absent claim stands out. Stakes: One vote decides whether I live. With so few players, a 2-vote majority ends the game for me, and each day I survive keeps my win condition (at most one other alive) reachable. Consensus: The town players are coordinated and aligned, using revealed dead roles and each other's claims, and I am isolated from that alignment. My position: holding out against the group, so I am the outlier whom two matching votes can eliminate. Heat: Very high. Claimed town players are pressing me directly for staying unclaimed, or have cross-checked claims that corner me. Forward exposure: The final vote is public and irreversible. A vote against a claimed town role aligns me with no one and gives the accusers a clean two-vote majority on me, while a vote on the other unclaimed player at least puts me on the majority side. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town roles (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) and the other unrevealed player. The claims rest on cross-checked night results and revealed bodies; the unrevealed player is judged mostly on behavior. Public vs private: I know I am the necromancer, and all I have publicly is an unclaimed or thinly defended profile. The town and any surviving wolf read me as a suspect, or at least as one of two unclaimed players who must step forward.
lessons.action: With 3-4 players left and my own name in danger, put my vote on the player the claimed town members are most likely to target, such as the other unclaimed or unverified player, instead of counter-accusing a claimed town member. A vote against the room's likely majority leaves me on the short end of a 2-vote lynch. If the table is already locked against me, spend the last words on creating a split between two accusers rather than defending myself.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and the leading evil faction needs four eliminations to reach parity; this is not a swing decision, and one mistaken sigil expenditure is costly but does not make the game end within one more elimination.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden, irreversible expenditure of one sigil and creates a visit; if the target attacks, the strike may be publicly revealed through a sigil death, but the original attack still resolves unless separately stopped.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the Investigator and Trailseer were revealed dead, and the Sentinel result is an unverified claim that identifies a visit but not an attacker. No surviving player has provided confirmed evidence identifying a likely attacker.
query_dims.situation: After the village abstained on a three-vote push to eliminate the Sigilist, the night action decision is whether to spend a sigil despite having no identified attacker. The unverified Sentinel claim says the revealed Trailseer visited a player, a result compatible with the Trailseer's follow action and not evidence of an attack.
query_dims.target_landscape: The options are the living players: one unverified Sentinel claimant whose account is consistent with the revealed Trailseer's role, and other living players with no publicly confirmed attacker status. There is no evidence-based attacker identification; any target choice rests on behavior or a guess about who may attack tonight.

lessons.why: Wants visit lists after an attack/save; the seat has only an unverified Sentinel claim.
lessons.situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.

lessons.why: Sigil decision with a wolf alive, but it presumes narrowed suspects and earlier non-attacker hits.
lessons.situation: The town is mid-game with at least one wolf alive. The sigilist must choose between a sigil on a guessed attacker and holding, and several earlier sigils hit non-attackers. Information landscape: Partial information from investigator clears, healer saves and trailseer trails. The wolf pool is narrowed but nobody is confirmed, and carrier timing is unknown. Stakes: Each sigil is half of the role's night capability. A wasted sigil on a non-attacker gives no strike and no protection, while a hit on the carrier would kill a wolf. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a hidden visit that is spent whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. It stays unannounced unless the target attacks and is struck. Target landscape: Unverified suspects, a quiet player who pushed a vote, a cleared investigator, and a healer-protected sentinel. Suspicion rests mostly on behavior, with only partial evidence from checks and trails.
lessons.action: While a wolf is still alive, put the sigil on the suspect whose seat turn it is to carry the pack's kill, since the carrier is the only wolf who visits for the kill. Prefer a suspect with attack evidence over a quiet or cleared player. If no suspect plausibly carries that night, keep the sigil.

lessons.why: Day 2 ended in an abstain after a push on the seat, two charges, behavioural leads: exact match, and its advice is 'wait for a concrete lead'.
lessons.situation: Day two ended in an abstain or split vote, with competing accusations and a quiet or contested suspect. Both a wolf pack and a second killer may be active, and the sigilist has two charges and some behavioral leads. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: split votes, unverified role claims, and a few night-one visit results. No confirmed alignments, so any target is a probabilistic read. Stakes: With multiple killers alive each night, one well-placed sigil that strikes an attacker could remove a threat. A spend that comes back as "no effect" is a charge lost with no confirmation of anything. Forward exposure: Placing is an irreversible spend of one charge and a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. A "no effect" report does not clear the target, so it leaves the suspicion open. Target landscape: Candidates include a player who drew minority votes, the players who pushed the vote, a silent player, and claimed information roles. Evidence is behavioral and unverified, and several of these players may use non-attack abilities such as checks or blocks.
lessons.action: Once there is a concrete lead after day two, place a sigil on the player most likely to carry a kill that night: a suspect drawn from vote pushes, tracker or sentinel reads, or a silent player. If the result is "no effect", treat it as inconclusive, because it fits both a target who did not attack and a target protected by night immunity; it clears nobody. Do not read it as exoneration.

lessons.situation: Opening night, ten players alive, day one was discussion only with no vote or deaths. The sigilist must decide between placing a sigil on a blind guess and keeping the charges. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no deaths, no role claims, no voting records, no visit histories to separate likely attackers from passive roles. Stakes: Early board with a large margin before any faction can win. Nothing is forcing a spend, and each of the two charges is worth more on a night with a real lead than on a coin-flip target. Forward exposure: Holding reveals nothing and commits nothing, and the charge stays available. Placing is irreversible, spends one of two charges, and is a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could see. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unvetted: no claims, no votes, no night results. Any target is a pure guess, and most players, including investigative, protective and passive roles, will not attack.
lessons.action: On night one, when there are no deaths, claims, votes or visit data, keep both sigils and place none. A sigil only does anything if its target attacks that night, and a blind pick usually lands on a non-attacker (several observations show it striking nothing and spending a charge). Hold the charges until a night when a specific suspect is likely to attack.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the wolves can win, so a single kill does not end the game but each town loss narrows the margin; a concealed body costs one of the two remaining conceals and removes a future role reveal from the town, which matters while three more eliminations are needed for a wolf win.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Spending a conceal on tonight's pack victim hides the body's role and blocks the town from learning it, and commits the illusionist to one of only two remaining hides; the carrier's visit to the victim also disappears from watchers, which may protect the pack's trace but cannot be undone once used.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved for the town: the only hard night result is a dead sentinel's untestable watch on a dead trailseer, and two dead town roles' records are already public. The illusionist holds private knowledge of the pack's target and the carrier identity; no living town player has a verified night result.
query_dims.situation: As the illusionist with two conceals left and a wolf partner who is carrying tonight's kill, the pack has chosen a victim among the seven living players, and the illusionist must decide whether that victim's revealed role and record would be worth hiding from the town. Earlier, the sentinel was lynched on a visit claim about the partner, which cannot be tested, and the town is now voting among remaining suspects while the partner has voted for another player.
query_dims.target_landscape: Tonight's pack target is a player whose role is not yet known to the illusionist's side; the illusionist privately knows only the pack's kill and that the carrier is the other wolf. Public role status of the victim is unknown until morning. The wolves' remaining living members are the illusionist and one partner, with no public claims among the town tied to a verified result.

lessons.why: Written for the lone surviving illusionist; the seat has a living wolf partner.
lessons.situation: The lone surviving illusionist, with the chanteuse dead and the town holding confirmed deaths and claimed results, must carry the night kill and choose where to spend the last conceal. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed by sigil or lynch, a claimed investigator with results, a sentinel with shared logs, and public voting records already pointing at the wolf. Stakes: A single wolf is close to parity, but one more wrong move or lynch ends it. Removing the investigator's findings buys a night but does not stop a vote already forming on you. Forward exposure: Carrying and concealing leaves no visit trace at the victim's door, but it uses up your last conceal and leaves you the only wolf. The victim's role is hidden, which signals an illusionist is alive and acting. The conceal cannot be undone and does not erase prior voting records. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who has cleared players or found a wolf, the sentinel with watch logs, a confirmed or suspected sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. Information-bearing claimed roles are the priority over quiet players.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with your final conceal, carry the kill on the town's main information role (the investigator or the role whose results are driving suspicion) and hide the body. This keeps the role, will and attack trace off the record, and a carrier that conceals leaves no trace at that door. It does not erase day-vote history, so plan to survive the next vote on other grounds.

lessons.why: Partner carries and the seat decides whether to conceal, but written for night 1; night-3 board differs.
lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack kills a quiet unread player, and the partner (for example the Chanteuse) carries while you decide whether to conceal. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no confirmed alignments, no history of visits or votes. Stakes: Two charges for the whole game. Spending one early buys partner cover and private role knowledge. Holding both keeps them for later, more decisive nights. Forward exposure: Uses one conceal, announces an illusionist's presence, and your own hiding visit can still be seen by a watcher on the victim. If the victim survives, the use is kept and every visit to the victim is seen. Target landscape: Unclaimed, unread players with no public roles, chosen by behavior. The victim could be any role, including a night-immune one.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner carries the night-1 kill, spend one conceal on the victim if you want the partner's visit hidden from a watching Sentinel or following Trailseer and want to learn the victim's role privately. If you would rather stay unseen yourself, hold both charges, because your own visit to hide the body is still seen by a watcher.

lessons.why: Deciding whether this kill justifies a conceal, advice: spend it on a victim whose role and will are still unknown. Exact decision.
lessons.situation: You have one or two conceals left and are deciding whether the current kill justifies spending one. The pack may be exposed to sigil traps, a rival killer or a day-vote link to the victim. Information landscape: Information-rich: the victim's claims, the sigilist's or sentinel's reports and the voting records are already public. These can validate the victim's information even if the role is hidden. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, so each remaining conceal is a scarce asset. Wasting one on a victim whose role is already known, or while the carrier is at risk, leaves the pack without cover for a later decisive kill. Forward exposure: Spending the final charge leaves you with no concealment for later kills. The conceal does nothing against a sigil strike on the carrier, against a partner killed that night, or against the day vote record that ties you to the victim. If the victim is saved, the use is kept. Target landscape: A publicly claimed town role that has already told its story, against an unclaimed or unconfirmed player whose role and will would still be new information. The claimed role gains little from hiding, while an unknown role's will might expose the pack.
lessons.action: Save the last conceal for a victim whose role and will are still unknown or whose death would otherwise confirm a town result. Do not spend it on a role that has already publicly claimed and been linked to the pack's night work. Before committing, check that your partner's carry is not exposed to a sigil or to a kill by another killer.

lessons.situation: Night 1: the pack picks a quiet, unread first victim and you are the wolf who carries the kill. The risk is that the Trailseer or Sentinel catches your visit and gives Town a day-2 accusation against you. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day-1 vote, no claims, no confirmed roles, no night history. Only private wolf talk exists. Stakes: Early game with plenty of time. The main risk is losing a wolf early to a traced visit, which would cost the pack the endgame. A clean first night matters more than saving a charge. Forward exposure: Announces that an illusionist exists and spends one of two conceals if the victim dies. Your own visit leaves no trace, and the spent charge cannot be undone. If the victim survives, nothing is announced and the use is kept. Target landscape: Eight or nine unclaimed, unread players with no roles revealed. The target is picked from quiet behavior, not evidence, and could be a watcher, a tracker, or the night-immune lone killer.
lessons.action: When the carrier rotation makes you the carrier on night 1, carry the kill and use a conceal on the victim. A conceal on a victim you carried yourself leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer, and if the target turns out immune the use is kept.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear direction: the discussion has not formed an accusation or aligned around a candidate. The only shared point is that the Sentinel claimant's reported visit does not by itself implicate the visited player.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; a single vote or kill cannot flip which faction is winning, though the early information vacuum makes the next death and any resulting evidence consequential.
query_dims.heat_now: No suspicion or accusation is directed at you in the discussion so far; your Fortune Teller role and zero points are private.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the Night 1 deaths and roles are confirmed, but there are no public wills or verified living-player results. The Sentinel's visit report is an unverified claim, and even if accurate it does not identify the attacker.
query_dims.my_position: Not driving or holding out against a consensus; you have not publicly taken a position.
query_dims.situation: After the wolves killed a revealed Investigator and the Serial Killer killed a revealed Trailseer on Night 1, a player claiming Sentinel said the Trailseer visited another survivor. A second speaker noted that this could have been the Trailseer's follow action and does not establish who attacked them. The room has no current vote target, leaving the next likely death and your own exposure uncertain.
query_dims.target_landscape: No elimination candidates have been publicly advanced. The Sentinel claim is unverified; the dead Investigator and Trailseer were role-revealed by the game master.

lessons.why: Early day after a night kill with one claimant; advice is to agree with the claim, add a modest observation, name no target.
lessons.situation: An early day after a night kill, with no wolf-kill leads or checks revealed. One investigative claimant has reported a non-visit result and the village is just starting to interpret night movements. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single dead player and one claimed no-visit result, with no investigative checks, caught lies or voting record to go on. Stakes: Early game with plenty of cushion; no single vote or kill flips the game. The aim is to stay alive for more night bets while adding no suspicion, since there is little to gain from pushing a read now. Consensus: Calm and undirected. Players echo each other's observations, with no accusation forming and a leaning toward abstaining. My position: With the majority. Echoing and refining shared observations, not driving. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the fortune teller. Target landscape: A claimed trailseer or similar reporter clears one quiet player. The other living players have unknown roles and no concrete leads, so there is no basis yet for a behavioral accusation.
lessons.action: When the day opens with little evidence and just one or two claims, agree with the claim and add one modest logical observation, such as which roles a given report cannot cover. Then let others speak, without proposing a target, so the discussion stays calm and you stay unnoticed.

lessons.why: Same day-discussion posture, but premise (competing visit reports, an accused player) is only partly present.
lessons.situation: A day discussion in which night deaths have produced visit reports from claimed trailseer or sentinel players. Those reports point at an accused player or create competing leads, and the fortune teller has no heat and is still working toward two prediction points. Information landscape: Mixed but mostly information-rich: announced deaths and roles, plus claimed visit reports that conflict or are contested. Reports are claims, not announcements, so they can be checked against how the rules treat concealed victims. Stakes: The board is mid-game and not at the brink; one wrong day-vote hurts Town but does not end the game. The fortune teller's own win depends on surviving nights to score points, so staying unnoticed matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is engaged and fairly aligned on dissecting the visit reports. There is no firm lean yet, or it is forming around the accused visitor. It rests on claimed results rather than announced facts. My position: With the majority, not driving. Contributing a summary but taking no hard stance. Heat: None. No one is suspecting or questioning the fortune teller, who is a neutral with no side and reads Not suspicious. Target landscape: Several living players with unverified role claims and visit reports from a claimed trailseer or sentinel; the accused deny or counter-claim. The basis is claimed night results and explanations, not confirmed facts.
lessons.action: With zero heat and no role claim of your own, stay in the analytical middle: restate what each investigative claimant reported, ask the accused to explain their visits, and point out which claims conflict. Hold back from committing to one target until the explanations come in, so you stay a low-profile voter while the village's own evidence does the work.

query_dims.consensus_text: The village is divided on the day 3 sentinel claim and the day 2 abstain pattern, with no clear majority on any living target yet.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single result can end the game next; a wrong lynch costs a town player but is recoverable, while your own exposure would remove your ability to strike unseen.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Claiming any role or citing a night result only a dead role could produce would expose you and commit you to a visible position; staying silent and voting with the majority is reversible.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: you have not been named by any active accusation today, though an earlier day 2 vote from one player named you once.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only live evidence is a dead sentinel's unverified night-1 watch claim and one investigator check on player_3 (Not suspicious), which is itself a dead player's claim.
query_dims.my_position: With the majority by voting, holding out from any personal accusation.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the necromancer, you privately know you struck player_5 (a chanteuse) through player_6's vigilante body, and that you hold the trailseer and vigilante bodies for later use; publicly no one knows your role and the sentinel's claim against player_5 is the live dispute.
query_dims.situation: Day 4 with five alive after a sentinel was lynched and the chanteuse and investigator were killed at night; the village is debating whether the dead sentinel's claim about a now-dead chanteuse was true, while you, the hidden necromancer, hold two dead bodies whose abilities you can use on future nights.
query_dims.target_landscape: Five players alive: three unclaimed town-aligned or unknown players and two others; the only public claim is a voted-out sentinel's night-1 watch that named player_5, already dead, and no independent evidence confirms it.

lessons.why: Same quiet-unclaimed-necromancer posture, but keyed on a sentinel report listing visitors to the necromancer's body; the seat's trigger is a claim about a dead chanteuse.
lessons.situation: A claimed sentinel or similar report publicly confirms a necromancer after a reanimated visit. The visited players claim roles while the necromancer stays unclaimed and quiet. Information landscape: Information-rich: a claimed sentinel report listing visitors, plus claims from a healer and a trailseer. Every report is unverified. Stakes: A necromancer is now known to exist, so each unclaimed player is a candidate vote. A tied or split vote only delays removal if I give the room nothing to hold onto. Consensus: The village agrees that a necromancer is active but is split on which visitor or quiet player to remove. Votes are likely to scatter or tie. My position: Holding out, with no stated read. I need to move toward the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A necromancer is confirmed, and I am an unclaimed player who has said nothing. Forward exposure: Silence fixes me in the role of unclaimed suspect with no defense on record. A modest, claim-based read can be changed later. A fabricated role claim cannot be undone if a living power role contradicts it. Target landscape: Claimed visitors (healer, trailseer) are under scrutiny from the sentinel's report. Unclaimed quiet players are the fallback targets, and I am one of them. Public vs private: The room has just learned that a necromancer exists. Privately I know I directed the body's visit, and no one can verify that I did.
lessons.action: If a visit by a dead player's body has publicly confirmed a necromancer and you are quiet and unclaimed, speak early with a specific read tied to the public claims. For example, question one claimant's timeline or ask who the sentinel's reported visitors could be. Take a stance that other players can engage with, and do not claim a role you cannot support against living power roles.

lessons.why: Final three or four; five are alive and no claim is demanded.
lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Two town power roles have claimed, their results back each other up, and the necromancer is pushed to state a role or be voted out. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed roles of the dead, public vote history, claimed night results and spent abilities leave very little room to bluff. Stakes: One elimination vote decides the game. If the necromancer is voted out it loses outright, and a failed claim leaves no later day to repair it. Consensus: The few remaining players are converging on a bloc of cross-verifying town claims, with the unclaimed or contradicted player as the obvious elimination. My position: Holding out alone against a forming two-player bloc. Heat: High to critical. Claimed town roles are demanding my claim, or I am the odd player out after their results cleared each other. Forward exposure: A role claim commits me to a night history that the claimed town roles can check against their own results and spent abilities. A claim that fails the check is nearly irreversible, but staying silent is already read as guilt in a small endgame. Target landscape: The claimed power roles (vigilante, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist) and any unclaimed player. Their claims are partly corroborated by revealed deaths and spent abilities, so each can be tested against the record. Public vs private: Privately a lone killer who has been attacking through a dead player's body, while publicly needing to pass as an ordinary town power role under direct claim demands.
lessons.action: When pressed to claim at the final three or four, give a specific role claim instead of stalling. Pick a still-living town role that no revealed death or other claim has already used, and tell a night story that fits every claimed result and the visit rules. For example, a Sentinel is never told of its own watch, and a Trailseer's follow is a visit others can cross-check.

lessons.why: Principle (steer only through public evidence, do not quote a body-derived result) transfers, but the seat has not shared any body-derived result.
lessons.situation: After a night attack or save, the necromancer holds results gathered through a dead town role and wants to redirect suspicion onto the visitors. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: the dead role's death is on record, so the room can tell which living roles could have produced such a result. Stakes: My win needs the room kept off me for many more days, so losing the cover of a hidden identity costs far more than anything the leaked result could gain. Consensus: The village is unsettled after a night attack and save, with no fixed target. The living roles are still working out what the visits mean. My position: Not yet in conflict, but I would be holding out alone if I spoke up with the hidden result. Heat: Zero before sharing. It would jump to universal accusation if I quoted the body-derived result. Forward exposure: Stating a result that only the dead role could have produced points straight at the necromancer, and the room cannot unsee it. A read built on public evidence can be dropped without penalty. Target landscape: The players whose visits I learned about (claimed healer, other claimants) are the targets, but the only support is a hidden source. Public evidence such as claim overlaps is available to use instead. Public vs private: Privately I hold a night result obtained through a dead role, such as who visited a door. Publicly, no living player holds that role, so quoting the result shows I am the necromancer.
lessons.action: If a dead player's ability gave you night information, steer suspicion only through reasons the room can see: public claims, votes, and contradictions between players. Do not quote the body-derived result, such as sentinel visitor names, when no living role could explain how you got it. Only a living claimed role could plausibly share such a result, and you cannot back that claim.

lessons.situation: A claimed information role accuses a player based on a night result, the accused disputes it, and the necromancer is tempted to step in and challenge the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead role with a concealed role, a specific claimed tracking report, and mechanical counter-claims from the accused. All of it is still unverified. Stakes: The board has many living players, so every public commitment matters for the endgame. A defense that turns out wrong leaves a damaging record, while a vote with the majority costs nothing. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.

Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.
lessons.action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.

lessons.why: Trailseer follows the likely retaliation target, but the investigator is only a claim here.
lessons.situation: A wolf was just eliminated by the vote, and the confirmed town investigator is the obvious target for wolf retaliation that night. The trailseer wants to preserve that investigator's last action in case they are killed. Information landscape: Info-rich: a wolf has been caught, the investigator is validated, and earlier night visits and claims are on record. Visit data on the likely victim is more valuable than a blind follow. Stakes: Losing the investigator without recovering their last check would remove a key information source. Seeing the investigator's visit, and getting it reported, can lead directly to the last wolf. Target landscape: The confirmed or strongly vetted info role facing retaliation, versus claimed protectors who were already attacked or saved, versus quiet unread players. The vetted role is the likeliest night victim and a natural way to find their last target.
lessons.action: When the trailseer's own role is likely to draw an attack, follow the player the wolves most want dead, such as the confirmed investigator who just exposed a wolf. If the target dies, the trailseer still learns whom they visited that night. That information can point suspicion at the visited player.

lessons.why: Night 1 blind follow; the seat has claims, a vote record and night reports.
lessons.situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.

lessons.situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The Trailseer must pick a first follow target blindly, while the wolves and a lone killer may also pick arbitrary opening kills, including the Trailseer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no voting record, no night history, only baseline impressions from Day 1. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and evil far from parity, so no single follow is decisive. The value is in collecting a first concrete visit link before wagons and claims form, and the Trailseer may be killed before reporting it. Target landscape: Nine unrevealed other players with no claims, votes or behavioral deviations; any pick is an exploratory behavioral guess, so choose an unread player who does not stand out.
lessons.action: On the opening night with no claims or reads, follow one unread, low-profile player to get a concrete movement baseline. If the result names a door, keep it as a checkable link to cross-reference against other night results and later claims. If it shows no visits, treat that as weak information, because a wolf carrier whose victim was concealed leaves no trace, and the target may also be a passive role.
